method.baseline: One primary project receiving sustained attention for twelve weeks, with ordinary advisor/coauthor feedback, public or already accessible data and checkpoints, and a bounded academic compute plan. Named contacts are not assumed to have committed labor, specialist labels, hardware, or new grants.
method.feasibility: Feasibility assesses a credible ML conference-paper contribution, including a distinct result, proof or evaluation, comparisons, and writing. It assesses the actual stated or explicitly narrowed source question. Easy implementation and an uninformative null pilot do not by themselves make a paper feasible.
method.impact: Impact is conditional on success of the SAME rated version, within its relevant scientific or practical community. Venue fit affects feasibility; impact is not penalized a second time for lying outside ML. Broad topic importance does not automatically transfer to a small diagnostic.
method.scope: The current main Sunay Storage notebook, including November 9-10 additions. Separate Foundational AI and Applied Math companion agendas and historical source archives are outside this pass.
method.caveats: Scores are judgmental planning indices on a 1–5 scale, shown to one decimal. Both assess the same stated scope. Component weights and the bottleneck cap are judgment calls. Small decimal gaps are weak evidence, not measured differences or acceptance probabilities. Genuine ties are retained. There is no combined feasibility–impact ranking.
method.coverage: 319 entry-level assessments: 272 active B entries, 13 shorter leads, 21 Hamed-discussion entries, 9 reflections, 3 mistakes/utility questions, and the financial-narrative addition. 259 receive both scores; 60 reading, reflection, tool, administrative, or established-component notes are N/A. Four repeated H discussions reuse the owning B assessment. Other related scopes remain explicitly identified; merged M headings are not extra projects.
method.evidence: Every entry and its first-pass assessment received a second review for source fidelity and score consistency. Targeted primary literature checks focused on close overlaps and consequential ratings, with full methods inspected for selected cases. Abstract-only and failed-access checks are distinguished in the review records. No entry has exhaustive novelty clearance.
method.existing: Established manuscript components are not converted into invented follow-on papers. Genuine open continuations and finishing working papers are scored on their stated remaining work; B055, B068, and B263 remain manuscript-completion candidates. An unanswered broad question can still receive a low score; it need not already be a complete proposal.
method.schedule: Use weeks 1-2 to settle the claim, closest baseline, resources, and first discriminating result. Weeks 3-6 develop the core result; weeks 7-9 test robustness and comparisons; weeks 10-12 write and revise. Reassess if the initial gate fails.
anchors: No credible twelve-week route with current formulation or resources.
An illustration or observation with little identifiable change to knowledge or practice.
A pilot is plausible; a paper depends on several unresolved steps or poor venue fit.
A useful narrow extension, application, or clarification.
A scoped paper is plausible, but a substantial technical, empirical, access, or contribution uncertainty remains.
A substantive contribution to a clear research community or task.
A distinct question, accessible proof or evaluation route, and a credible paper-sized outcome; uncertainty is not mainly about what the contribution is.
Addresses an important bottleneck with a result that could transfer across settings.
Unusually ready: substantial verified groundwork for a distinct claim; limited remaining uncertainty.
A realistic scoped result could materially change widely used methods or accepted understanding.

refinement.scale: 1–5, displayed to one decimal; weighted assessment indices, not probabilities or measurement precision

criteria.claim: How specific, distinct and paper-sized is the remaining contribution?
criteria.technical: How tractable is the central mathematical or algorithmic work within twelve weeks?
criteria.resources: How ready are the needed data, models, compute, participants and expertise? Do not assume contacts commit work.
criteria.validation: How achievable is convincing proof/evaluation with strong comparisons and writing within twelve weeks?

feasibility.aggregation: Weighted mean, capped at weakest component + 1.0, then rounded to one decimal. The cap prevents strength elsewhere hiding a severe bottleneck.

criteria.value: How consequential would the exact scoped result be if it succeeded?
criteria.reach: How broadly could that result transfer or be reused within its relevant scientific/practical community?
criteria.distinctiveness: How much new understanding or capability would it add beyond the literature already checked?

impact.aggregation: Weighted mean rounded to one decimal; conditional on success of the same assessed scope.

anchors.2: Weak / several unresolved dependencies / narrow increment
anchors.3: Plausible, substantive but bounded / meaningful uncertainty
anchors.4: Strong and well-supported / important reusable advance
anchors.5: Exceptional readiness or field-changing value, requiring concrete support

refinement.interpretation: Judgmental refinement of the existing audit, not a new exhaustive literature review. Half-point subcriteria expose why tied coarse scores separate. Small decimal gaps are weak evidence; retain genuine ties and duplicated scopes. N/A stays unscored. Retain the old integer pair for comparison. Pareto status is relative to these estimates, not a claim of objectively best research.

ideas.original_title: B001. Honest assessments of paper significance and learning from author behavior
ideas.original_text:
As a beginning graduate student I had trouble telling how much a researcher actually thought of a paper. There are good reasons to promote work one would rank well below one’s best, including supporting the student who did it. Could authors’ private assessments help a newcomer decide what to read? Su’s work on eliciting within-lab rankings is a starting point. Even an honest ranking within each lab is a start, but it still leaves the question of how to compare papers across labs.

One idea is to ask for ratings on a common scale and compare them with assessments by independent readers. Another is to look at what authors do: where they submit a paper, where they put it on their website, how much they promote it. How well do those choices predict the blinded assessment? Honest authors can disagree with readers, and different labs have different ways of publicizing their work.

Related work. Su’s isotonic mechanism uses an author’s ordering to refine noisy scores of that author’s papers [reference in Storage]. The ICML 2023 experiment collected such orderings and measured their agreement with review outcomes [reference in Storage]. For the question here, I would need a comparison that neither study supplies: can visible choices by authors in different labs predict what independent readers will judge significant?

ideas.original_title: B002. Extrapolating evaluations, with unpaired calibration as one route
ideas.original_text:
What can a benchmark tell us about tasks we have never evaluated? Tao and I discussed the broad extrapolation question. Soham suggested a version in which we have abundant AI judgments on the new task, and both human and AI judgments on each of several earlier tasks. On each earlier task the two samples come from the same population, but need not label the same responses.

Suppose the judgment is binary. If the AI judge has the same false-positive and false-negative rates across tasks, variation in historical pass rates might let us estimate the human pass rate on the new one. The hard part is deciding whether the judge’s errors transfer. Soham thought the more interesting target might be a whole performance curve conditional on response features. A little human evaluation on the new task could tell us how far to trust the transfer.

Related work. Rogan and Gladen correct a positive screening rate for imperfect sensitivity and specificity [reference in Storage], and black-box label-shift estimation learns a confusion matrix from labeled source predictions [reference in Storage]. In the unpaired version, the historical human and AI pass rates have to identify that channel through variation across tasks. For a task with no AI judgments either, Zhou et al.’s use of item-demand and model-ability profiles to predict performance on new items is a closer comparison [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B004. Disentangling what an evaluator rewards
ideas.original_text:
An LLM judge may favor an answer because it is longer or uses a particular phrase. Could we tell how much of a learned reward comes from those features and how much from the part of the answer we care about? Soham pointed out the problem of unmeasured confounders. If longer answers also tend to be better, regressing out length could discard a real difference.

I asked Davis whether compressing a matrix of benchmark scores, as in BenchPress, might incidentally reduce this sensitivity. Davis thought that intuition plausible but was unsure about generalization. Would it carry over to tasks outside the matrix? A useful comparison would change how an answer is presented while keeping its substance fixed. This bears on reward hacking too: a judge can look good until a model is given an incentive to exploit the cue.

Related work. Length-Controlled AlpacaEval estimates what a judge’s win rate would look like at equal response lengths [reference in Storage]. BenchPress reconstructs missing benchmark scores from a low-rank matrix of observed scores [reference in Storage]. To find out whether compression also suppresses a judge’s presentation bias, I would need pairs in which I change the presentation and independently check that I preserved the answer.

ideas.original_title: B003. Open-ended research evaluation and mathematical taste
ideas.original_text:
An AIME answer is easy to score. How do we score a research agent that produces a useful lemma, simplifies an argument, or finds a connection between two problems? Tao suggested thinking about what a benchmark for open-ended research in a particular field might look like. Edgar mentioned length, generality, unification and the ability to reach the same idea by different routes. Those criteria need not agree. Behrad suggested another question that came back to me when I saw a human–AI proof. Did the proof introduce a useful mathematical object or definition? I’d like to be able to give an argument credit for that contribution even when its final theorem could be proved another way.

I would especially like to see what happens if we hand models a correct proof and ask them to simplify it. Do the same models win as when we ask them to find a proof? Lean can check that the new proof establishes the same result. A shorter proof could still be harder for a person to understand.

I’d also like to try this on our own papers. I saw someone set limits on the methods the model could use and repeatedly ask it to simplify the proof it had just produced. At what point would I prefer to keep the preceding version?

Related work. ProofOptimizer already trains a model to shorten Lean proofs and checks the resulting proofs in Lean [reference in Storage]. Inglis and Aberdein found that mathematicians’ judgments of beauty and simplicity can diverge [reference in Storage]. I would use a verified simplification as a candidate, then ask mathematicians whether it exposes a reusable idea or makes the decisive step easier to understand.

ideas.original_title: B006. Choosing evaluation metrics and error tradeoffs
ideas.original_text:
A gross but memorable example of a false positive and a false negative is the automatic-flushing toilet in AGH. I’d take the false positive there. What tradeoff do we choose when we evaluate a language model? Sweeping a threshold gives an ROC curve, and the area under it is a convenient summary. I want to understand when that summary answers the question the user cares about, particularly if the two mistakes have very different costs.

Related work. Hand showed that AUC can implicitly average over a different distribution of misclassification costs for each classifier, making an apparently uniform comparison hard to interpret [reference in Storage]. In the toilet example I can say which mistake costs more. I’d like to know whether we can ask users the analogous question before comparing language models.

ideas.original_title: B007. Reliability of everyday AI use
ideas.original_text:
What do people actually ask AI to do, and how reliable is it for those particular tasks? Suppose someone asks for a numerical score on a piece of creative writing. Does the number stay reasonably consistent if they ask again? How many queries would they need before they could trust the answer? I’d start by asking users which judgments they already rely on.

Related work. WildChat records interactions with a public chatbot and gives a starting sample of tasks people actually bring to it [reference in Storage]. For the writing example, LitBench compares automated judges with human pairwise story preferences [reference in Storage]. I would measure agreement with readers and repeatability on the same story separately: a judge could give the same unhelpful score every time.

ideas.original_title: B008. Evaluating diffusion models with vision-language judges
ideas.original_text:
How are diffusion models evaluated? It seems like some simple questions about a generated image could be answered by a vision-language model acting as a judge. Which parts of the evaluation could we entrust to it?

Related work. TIFA already turns a prompt into questions that a vision–language model answers about a generated image [reference in Storage]. Davidsonian Scene Graph goes further by encoding dependencies among questions, so an answer about an object’s color need not count as evidence that the object was present [reference in Storage]. I would start by checking which question types still disagree with people on the same images.

ideas.original_title: B237. Qualitative questions, scaling, and interpersonal judgment
ideas.original_text:
If we make a model larger while keeping the training recipe much the same, do its answers to qualitative questions get better? Suppose I describe a disagreement with a friend. Changing a few words in my account probably shouldn’t reverse the advice. Learning what my friend saw, or what I hope to do about the disagreement, might quite reasonably change it. Can a more capable model tell the difference? I worry about a model that understands the situation well enough to make my side sound especially persuasive. I might like that answer and leave less inclined to repair the friendship. Whether I preferred the advice and whether it helped me are two different questions.

Related work. In randomized experiments, Cheng et al. found that people rated affirming AI advice more favorably, yet exposure to it reduced their reported willingness to repair a conflict [reference in Storage]. Wang, Insulla and Montanari varied the presentation of puzzles while preserving their valid solutions and compared human and model answer distributions [reference in Storage]. Across model sizes, does advice respond more to a genuinely new fact than to a change in how the same facts are presented?

ideas.original_title: B244. The cost of giving a model an image instead of text
ideas.original_text:
How much performance do you lose by giving an LLM a problem as an image instead of transcribing it into a text prompt? Take a problem where the transcription can carry all the information in the image. Is there something like a fixed cost to reading it visually, which becomes relatively small as the problem itself gets harder? A diagram whose geometry matters is a different case. We might lose part of the problem in trying to transcribe it.

Related work. VISTA-Bench compares text with renderings of the same words [reference in Storage], and CrossMath supplies text and image variants with the same task-relevant information [reference in Storage]. Sun and colleagues also found that image inputs can change the amount of reasoning a model produces, with results sensitive to rendering choices [reference in Storage]. To test the fixed-cost idea I would vary reasoning difficulty at fixed legibility and keep problems that genuinely require a diagram in a separate comparison.

ideas.original_title: B009. Self-distillation from a single expert demonstration
ideas.original_text:
Can a student learn from a single expert demonstration by extracting a rule, generating more problems with that rule, and fine-tuning on its own examples? With a proof, I’d like to know which details the student can discard before it stops being the same idea. Tao and I discussed this, and Mahdi found related work on SelfGuide.

Mahdi suggested a useful intermediate check. Give the student the rule it extracted and ask it to solve the original problem again. If it can’t, why expect the synthetic problems to teach the right thing? Passing that check still leaves the interesting question of whether the rule helps on a new problem.

Related work. SELF-GUIDE fine-tunes a model on task-specific examples it generates itself [reference in Storage]. Instruction Induction tests a complementary step by asking a model to infer a verbal rule from examples and evaluating how well the rule works on held-out inputs [reference in Storage]. With one proof as the demonstration, I would measure separately whether the rule regenerates that proof and whether its synthetic examples help on another one.

ideas.original_title: B010. Selective self-play and diversity in idea space
ideas.original_text:
A model makes many attempts at a math problem. Suppose it can’t find an obvious flaw in two of them. Which one is worth learning from? My first thought was to reward high surprise, −log p(y ∣ x), conditional on the attempt being “not wrong.” Sima pointed out that appending “Quack!” to an ordinary proof makes it unlikely without adding an idea. Could embedding distances or local token likelihood tell us whether an unusual step still belongs with its neighbors? I discussed those scores with Davis. Thomas’s distinction between diversity in tokens and diversity in strategies seems important here.

An argument can also go in circles while every step looks reasonable. I picture a non-backtracking walk in idea space. Sima suggested mixing a few such traces into ordinary training data. One later, AI-assisted suggestion was to check whether a selected trace actually improves held-out performance after a small update.

Related work. Lee et al. use a human-calibrated judge to distinguish different solution methods from different phrasings of one method. Surface diversity can hold steady while approach diversity declines, and directly rewarding the judge can train the model to exploit its preferences [reference in Storage]. Among attempts in which the model finds no obvious flaw, does my surprise score pick out a different strategy? I would separately check whether the argument is sound.

ideas.original_title: B011. Data-corrected self-distillation
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a teacher generates noisy labels. The student thinks some of them are wrong, replaces those labels with its own predictions, and trains on the corrected data. When does this help? Think of a glowing hotel review labeled one star. There are cases where I want a model to be able to correct the data it sees. The difficulty is that disagreement by itself doesn’t tell us who made the mistake. I’d like a toy model where we can see when the student fixes the teacher’s errors and when it just reinforces its own.

Related work. Reed et al. trained on a mixture of the supplied label and the model’s own hard or soft prediction, allowing the training target to change when those disagree [reference in Storage]. In the teacher–student version I would separate examples on which the teacher alone is wrong from those on which both models make the same mistake. Only the first group offers a correction that the student already knows how to make.

ideas.original_title: B012. Distilling fine-tuning into an in-context prefix
ideas.original_text:
Could we replace a fine-tuning run with a set of in-context examples? One way to try would be to sample diverse inputs and outputs from the fine-tuned model, then find a short prefix that makes the original model behave similarly on new inputs. The attraction is that we could deploy the adaptation without changing the weights. Would the same demonstrations work for a different model family? I discussed steering-vector transfer with Emre from Philippe’s group. The idea was to transfer from a smaller model to a larger one, by analogy with hyperparameter transfer. I’d distinguish those two kinds of transfer.

Related work. Wang et al. generate compact sets of demonstrations to represent a target dataset for in-context learning [reference in Storage]. Here I would optimize against the behavior of a particular fine-tuned model and test the resulting prefix on fresh inputs and a second base model. A distinct comparison is transfer of an internal steering direction: Agarwal reports that directions can transfer between independently trained models, with success varying across model pairs [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B173. A general control perspective on agent reliability
ideas.original_text:
A probe that calls for another rollout, a warning inserted into a reasoning trace, and a controller that deletes a token all intervene on a model while it is acting. Can we understand them as instances of one controlled stochastic process? Would model-predictive control suggest an intervention we would otherwise miss? There is a related question about what we want the controller to detect. I wondered whether an underspecified instruction leaves room for some preference acquired in training to determine the action. I don’t yet know how to identify that preference from the action alone.

Related work. FUDGE changes next-token probabilities using a prediction about the eventual text [reference in Storage]; a predictive safety filter changes a proposed control action when it cannot certify a safe continuation [reference in Storage]. Comparing their observations and interventions is one question. Inferring a preference from what the model then does is another: inverse reinforcement learning gives examples in which even knowing an optimal policy does not identify its reward [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B013. Entropy time series around mistakes and branching
ideas.original_text:
How does next-token entropy behave across generation tasks, from problem-solving to creative writing? What happens when a reasoning model makes a mistake? I can imagine a spike just after a wrong step, but does it last? If the model eventually backtracks, can we see that in the time series? We could introduce a mistake during generation and watch what happens next. A branch in a trace can also reflect several reasonable ways forward, even when nothing has gone wrong. I’d like to look at actual traces before deciding which pattern makes a useful uncertainty signal.

Related work. Wang et al. identify high-entropy tokens at forks in math reasoning traces and find that restricting reinforcement-learning updates to those tokens can preserve much of the performance gain [reference in Storage]. A fork can support several good arguments. I would compare its entropy trajectory with one obtained after inserting a known error into the very same prefix.

ideas.original_title: B027. Backtracking, roll-outs, and decoding objectives
ideas.original_text:
Is the most probable continuation the one we’d want a reasoner to follow? Holtzman and collaborators gave examples where human text doesn’t maximize model probability. I wondered whether a diversity term could explain some of the difference, and whether that objective would suggest a better decoding rule. If a branch goes badly, there is a second decision: how far back do we go? Entropy or a value estimate might say when to turn around. We still need to choose the earlier token or step from which to try again.

Related work. Holtzman et al. showed how likelihood-maximizing decoding can produce repetitive open-ended text and proposed nucleus sampling [reference in Storage]. Satori learns explicit search actions, including reflection and exploration of alternatives, inside an autoregressive trace [reference in Storage]. I would separate the choice of decoding objective from the choice of where to resume a failed proof, since optimizing one need not settle the other.

ideas.original_title: B014. Productive breaks through complementary reasoning tasks
ideas.original_text:
When I’m stuck on an algebra problem, switching to a geometric way of thinking can be a productive break. Could a reasoning model benefit from interleaving complementary tasks in one trace? This came up with Sima and Surbhi. One could intervene at test time or steer the representation, but which task should the model switch to? Sima pointed out that it may be hard for us to specify complementary tasks ahead of time. Perhaps the model has its own sense of which two tasks go together. I’d also like a toy model in which switching really helps.

Related work. In human experiments, an undemanding break helped people return to a previously seen creative problem [reference in Storage], and alternating two creative tasks reduced fixation relative to other switching schedules [reference in Storage]. I’d compare three equal-time interventions on an unfinished model proof: an easy diversion, a deliberately complementary problem, and extra work on the original argument. That would tell us whether the content of the break matters.

ideas.original_title: B015. Selective amnesia and efficient test-time search
ideas.original_text:
Once an autoregressive model has tried the same approach five times, every attempt is still in its context. Sometimes when I’m stuck I wish I could forget how I approached a problem and look at it as a beginner. Could a model learn to mask off selected blocks of old tokens? I discussed the idea with Surbhi. The goal would be to get out of a rut sooner while keeping the probability of solving the problem about the same.

Shiva suggested that human memory might retain a principle and discard the details of an attempt. It would be interesting to compare that kind of compaction with masking. Hiding an old token’s position need not erase information already carried into later states.

Writing a chain of thought also changes what the model will read a few steps later. I wonder how much of the benefit comes from arranging its own context as it goes. Masking an old attempt is one intervention, but simply writing down which parts of that attempt still matter might change what it tries next.

Related work. MEMENTO compresses each reasoning block into a short summary. The cached states of its summary tokens still carry information about the original block, and the authors find that removing that channel reduces accuracy [reference in Storage]. I would compare three ways to continue a stalled attempt at the same remaining compute budget: mask it, retain only the summary text, or retain the summary with its original cached states. Which one preserves a useful lemma without preserving the mistake?

Shiva suggested that human memory might retain a principle and discard the details of an attempt. It would be interesting to compare that kind of compaction with masking. Hiding an old token’s position need not erase information already carried into later states.

Writing a chain of thought also changes what the model will read a few steps later. I wonder how much of the benefit comes from arranging its own context as it goes. Masking an old attempt is one intervention, but simply writing down which parts of that attempt still matter might change what it tries next.

Related work. MEMENTO compresses each reasoning block into a short summary. The cached states of its summary tokens still carry information about the original block, and the authors find that removing that channel reduces accuracy [reference in Storage]. I would compare three ways to continue a stalled attempt at the same remaining compute budget: mask it, retain only the summary text, or retain the summary with its original cached states. Which one preserves a useful lemma without preserving the mistake?

ideas.original_title: B016. Does the reputation of a hard problem inhibit a model?
ideas.original_text:
Does knowing that a problem is famous and hard change how hard a model tries? The story of Dantzig mistaking unsolved problems for homework made me wonder whether telling a model less about a problem’s reputation might give it a similar advantage. Could we hide that information, or selectively unlearn it, without removing mathematical knowledge it needs? Given what models can already solve, I’m unsure whether this effect is appreciable in practice.

Related work. Lee et al. found that a linear probe on a model’s representations predicts the difficulty of math problems [reference in Storage]. That gives me a way to distinguish perceived difficulty from the causal effect of reputation. I would keep the problem fixed, change only the account of its history, and measure whether either the probe or the model’s persistence changes.

ideas.original_title: B017. Adaptive branching with a probe and a stronger verifier
ideas.original_text:
Revisiting an idea of Edgar’s: when should a reasoning model branch? A cheap probe could decide when to roll out several continuations. If they lead in genuinely different directions, we could call a stronger verifier to pick one. If they all say essentially the same thing, the verifier call seems wasteful. I had Ren’s KnowNo algorithm in mind, extended with rollouts. Could we conformalize both thresholds—the one for branching and the one for calling the verifier?

In July I wondered whether the probe could learn from the trajectory itself, including the base model’s hidden activations when available. Would a signal learned with the base model frozen still tell us when an intervention helps if we train the two together?

Related work. KnowNo uses conformal prediction sets to decide when a robot planner needs help [reference in Storage]. Kiyani et al. study when a weak verifier should accept, reject, or pay for a strong check, accounting for incorrect decisions and strong-check frequency [reference in Storage]. The extra decision here comes earlier: running several continuations creates the evidence on which the later verifier call depends.

ideas.original_title: B018. Complementary reward models and selective human intervention
ideas.original_text:
Can we train a process reward model that catches mistakes a person tends to miss? Sima studied complementarity in prediction sets, where we can see whether the answer was covered. In an open-ended reasoning trace, even deciding which step deserved criticism can be difficult. Shiva suggested letting the AI drive and having the human intervene selectively. Shayan disagreed about that division of labor.

We could also have several AI evaluators with different strengths. If the first monitor is unsure of its judgment, would asking a second one help us decide when to call the human or stronger verifier? Its value depends on what it catches that the first one misses.

Related work. Noorani et al. formalize how AI can correct mistakes in a human prediction set while limiting harm to cases the human already got right [reference in Storage]. Weak–strong verification gives a complementary way to account for the cost of escalating an uncertain decision [reference in Storage]. For proof traces I would need a criterion for a missed step error before I could measure either complementarity or harm.

ideas.original_title: B019. Active speed-reading and iterative retrieval pruning
ideas.original_text:
When I was studying for the SAT, a tutor suggested reading the questions first and then skimming the passage. An extreme version was to read just the first sentence of each paragraph. Could an LLM do something similar, starting with very little context and asking for the details it needs? Hamed, Sima and I discussed revealing more of the source over successive turns. Sima suggested going the other way: start with the material retrieved by a search system and let the model prune it. The retriever’s idea of relevance may differ from the reader’s. How much reading, and how many turns, does either approach save?

Related work. FLARE retrieves additional material when a tentative continuation contains low-confidence tokens, then regenerates the passage with that material [reference in Storage]. RECOMP instead conditions retrieval-augmented generation on a compressed version of the retrieved passages and can omit them entirely [reference in Storage]. These suggest two baselines for one reading task: measure what the model asks to see next and what it chooses to discard after retrieval.

ideas.original_title: B020. Semantic successive refinement and controllable summaries
ideas.original_text:
Sometimes I want the news without every detail in the newsletter. Could I turn a knob and get a shorter version, then expand just the claim I want to understand? I was thinking of adapting the factuality back-out idea, except that the score here would be relevance to me. The extra difficulty is that the model may have a poor idea of what I find relevant. I’d also like the different levels to fit together: when I ask for a little more detail, the earlier account should still make sense.

Related work. GranuSum controls the granularity of a summary by varying the events supplied to the generator [reference in Storage]. Equitz and Cover give a sharper benchmark in source coding: under a specified distortion measure, a coarse description can sometimes be refined to an optimal finer one without a rate penalty [reference in Storage]. For a newsletter I would first have to say what the reader counts as lost information, then test whether adding detail preserves the earlier account.

ideas.original_title: B021. Conformal token budgeting and auxiliary-work waste
ideas.original_text:
I noticed GPT spending a surprising amount of its reasoning budget searching PDFs. How much do searches, repeated steps and LaTeX formatting displace useful mathematics? Some searches are necessary. I’d first want to know when interrupting them changes the answer.

Edgar and Berkan discussed monitoring repetition and token-level p-hacking. Could we calibrate a stopping rule that responds to the particular problem? Surbhi pointed out why an overall token limit is unsatisfying: it can meet its marginal guarantee and still interrupt the wrong subtasks. The activation signal in B017 might help decide when to intervene. The question is what the monitor can actually tell at that point in the trace.

Related work. Xie et al. monitor uncertainty signals during reasoning and give a nonparametric rule controlling the probability of stopping prematurely on well-posed queries [reference in Storage]. I’d like to distinguish stopping the entire response from interrupting one low-value search. The relevant loss in the latter case is the change in the eventual answer after the rest of the reasoning is allowed to proceed.

ideas.original_title: B022. Curricula whose answers are easier to obtain than their solutions
ideas.original_text:
Walking home, I wondered where the training problems come from once a model reaches the frontier of human mathematics. Can we generate problems for which we know the answer but don’t know the solution? Think of an AIME problem whose numerical answer we can check even though we couldn’t find the derivation ourselves. Computationally intractable examples won’t teach much if the student never solves one. And we used to get away with “engineer’s induction” on the AIME: solve the first few cases and guess the pattern.

What makes a problem difficult for a particular model? It might require a long proof, or a short trick far from any the model has seen. I also wondered how simple or complicated a verified proof one can elicit at a given prompt complexity. That comparison depends on who is searching and how long they get to search.

Related work. Absolute Zero uses code execution to check self-proposed tasks [reference in Storage]. Dong and Ma’s STP rewards conjectures the current prover can solve only rarely, then trains on successful proofs [reference in Storage]. That is one concrete sense in which difficulty depends on the learner. For a problem where I know the numerical answer but lack a proof, I would fix the search budget and test whether the student finds an argument that transfers or gets the answer by guessing a pattern.

ideas.original_title: B024. How much should a teacher reveal?
ideas.original_text:
In an AI-assisted brainstorm with David, we considered a teacher who knows something the student is supposed to discover. A complete demonstration may show the right action while concealing the reason to search, check a result, or correct course. When should the teacher reveal the answer, and when would a hint teach more? Could students reach the same accuracy with fewer training examples, while still learning to search, check, and correct their own work?

A related situation came up in August. A user supplies a few images, clarifies what they mean and critiques the first attempt. Could the assistant ask for the next piece of information only when it needs it? Revealing everything up front costs the user time, but a poorly chosen question can cost a turn without bringing the assistant any closer.

Related work. Kaur et al. found that giving a teacher privileged context can degrade a thinking model trained by on-policy self-distillation, with changes concentrated around high-entropy branching decisions [reference in Storage]. Conformal Information Pursuit studies an interactive learner that chooses questions and uses their answers to narrow a prediction [reference in Storage]. I would vary what the teacher reveals at a branch and measure both the number of examples the student needs and the searches it can later perform unaided.

ideas.original_title: B025. Whimsical post-training for small-model efficiency
ideas.original_text:
Could a small model learn to produce proofs by recovering the order of contiguous blocks cut from a teacher’s proof? This is one of the more whimsical post-training ideas I had in mind. Dwip formalized a related multi-way preference problem. Edgar wondered whether rearranging blocks provides too little information. I would also check whether the model learns mathematics or merely uses grammatical cues. If the task does teach a reusable skill cheaply, small models might be the right place to look for the gain.

Related work. Poulsen et al.’s randomized study found comparable learning gains in less practice time for students who ordered proof blocks rather than writing induction proofs from scratch [reference in Storage]. An et al. found that the order of proof steps within training examples affects a model’s later success on propositional proofs [reference in Storage]. My experiment would make ordering itself the supervision, then ask the model to produce a fresh proof without being given its pieces.

ideas.original_title: B026. Dense feedback, credit assignment, and GEPA
ideas.original_text:
The GEPA authors describe dense natural-language feedback as a form of implicit credit assignment. Why not make the assignment explicit and derive a process reward for each step from what the feedback says? Converting a sentence about what went wrong into a single number could itself introduce noise. Another detail I like is that GEPA keeps scores for individual instances. Two prompts can have the same average and be good at entirely different things. This reminded me of MAP-Elites and of Behrad’s point about what gets lost when we average.

Related work. GEPA uses feedback on execution traces to propose revised prompts and retains candidates that excel on different examples [reference in Storage]. MAP-Elites similarly keeps high-performing solutions in distinct regions of a user-defined behavior space [reference in Storage]. Here the unresolved step is to identify which decision in a trace deserves credit for a particular piece of feedback, then test that attribution by changing the decision.

ideas.original_title: B028. Honest effort in reasoning models
ideas.original_text:
I assume a reasoning model feels some pressure during training to reach its answer in a bounded amount of time. If I ask it to try to prove a conjecture and it gives up, how could we tell whether it had exhausted a promising line of reasoning? It may have learned that stopping early pays. Could that pressure make it give up even when it knows it has hardly tried? How might we detect that and address it? I’d like to know what interpretability could tell us about that possibility, particularly since a failed proof says very little by itself about the effort that went into it.

Related work. Van der Weij et al. show that language models can be induced to underperform selectively on evaluations [reference in Storage]. That supplies positive controls in which capability is present and performance is deliberately suppressed. I would test whether a signal learned from those cases distinguishes premature stopping from an honest failed search on an unfamiliar conjecture.

ideas.original_title: B271. Reasoning between successive pieces of an answer
ideas.original_text:
Why should an LLM get just one opportunity to reason before it starts answering? It could think for a while, write the first part of the answer, then use another short reasoning trace to decide what to write next. I’d like to compare this with spending the same total number of reasoning tokens up front. Once the model has committed to part of its answer, does the next burst of reasoning help it follow through, or does the commitment make an early mistake harder to fix?

Related work. Quiet-STaR trains a model to generate internal rationales that help predict later tokens [reference in Storage]. PLANTAIN already interleaves hidden reasoning with visible output, beginning with a plan, and reports better benchmark accuracy than think-then-answer baselines [reference in Storage]. I would fix the total reasoning tokens, give no user feedback, and make the first visible piece part of the answer itself. Does the next burst of reasoning help complete the argument, or compound an early mistake?

ideas.original_title: B260. Self-paraphrase and fixed points of model improvement
ideas.original_text:
I have a vague feeling that a good AI ought to satisfy certain fixed-point equations. For example, suppose a model rewrites its own prompt without losing any information. Should its performance change? I’d be less surprised if a stronger model could help by doing the rewriting. The intuition is that there shouldn’t be an easy transformation a good model can apply to its own inputs to make itself better. If we could write down conditions like that, perhaps iterating the map would tell us how to improve a model that falls short.

How does this square with recursive self-improvement? I asked Davis whether toy models of learning from self-generated data could say anything about its limits. He doubted that such limits would be close enough to matter in practice.

Related work. OPRO improves prompts by showing an LLM previously tried prompts and their measured scores [reference in Storage]. Those scores supply information that a model rewriting an isolated prompt does not have. I would test the fixed-point intuition first with a meaning-preserving rewrite and no score feedback, then give the model one of those two advantages at a time.

ideas.original_title: B029. Steerable image editing and visual-style extrapolation
ideas.original_text:
Playing with an image editor, I wanted to change my hair and leave everything else alone. Why can’t the editor give me a deterministic check that it hasn’t touched a pixel outside the hair? Of course, I’d still have to tell whether it picked out the hair correctly and whether I liked the new style. Another edit I’d like is to take a photograph of a sign and generate letters that don’t appear on it, in the same font. That’s a different sort of control: the model has to infer a style and extrapolate it.

Related work. RePaint conditions denoising on the known region of a masked image [reference in Storage]. Once I have the hair mask, I can simply copy the original pixels outside it into the edited image and check them for equality. The questions that remain are whether the mask captured the hair and whether the new style looks right. For the sign example, Park et al. learn localized style representations to synthesize unseen glyphs from a few observed characters [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B030. Flat communication and evolving architectures
ideas.original_text:
In a bank, information can travel from an associate all the way up to the CEO. A flat company lets people talk to one another directly. If a hierarchy is something like a deep network, what would a flat learning architecture be? Companies also grow and shrink, or change who reports to whom, when their information needs change. Could a network usefully change its architecture as it learns? More specifically, could we co-train a family of competing networks and let competition change their architectures without a human directing each change? One concrete width question I raised in July was to start wide, remove neurons and retrain. Does that lead to a different width from the one that works when training from scratch?

Related work. NEAT evolves both network weights and topology, adding structure over generations [reference in Storage]. Liu et al. found that for several structured pruning methods, a discovered small architecture could perform comparably when trained from scratch [reference in Storage]. I would use that restart comparison to separate the value of the final wiring from the value of arriving at it through competition or gradual pruning.

ideas.original_title: B031. Weight implants from larger to smaller models
ideas.original_text:
How exactly do you do weight implants from a large model into a small one? Could we learn a low-rank version of each hidden layer by asking it to reproduce the next layer’s activations in the teacher? I’d like to understand what survives that transfer.

Related work. FitNets trains a thin student to match a teacher’s intermediate representations through a learned regressor [reference in Storage]. Jaderberg et al. fit low-rank expansions to approximate convolutional layers, including objectives based on reconstructed responses [reference in Storage]. I would compare copying such a factorization with relearning the layer from activation targets, then measure how errors accumulate across successive layers.

ideas.original_title: B270. How small a map connects two trained models?
ideas.original_text:
Davis showed me a learned map between two GPT-2 models trained from different random seeds. He was looking at the rate–distortion question. How much capacity does the map need before it can translate one model’s representations into the other’s with small error?

I wondered if we could work this out for a pair of random-feature models. Fix the size of the translating model and ask how well the best map of that size can do. How does the error change when we let the translator grow?

Related work. Model stitching connects the lower layers of one frozen network to the upper layers of another through a learned adapter and measures downstream performance [reference in Storage]. A translator can preserve that performance while reconstructing some hidden directions poorly. In the random-feature example, I would trace both errors as the translator’s rank or parameter budget increases.

ideas.original_title: B032. Post-hoc pitch smoothing for speech synthesis
ideas.original_text:
Cheap text-to-speech models occasionally make rapid, unnatural changes in pitch. Could simple smoothing after synthesis fix those jumps while keeping the inflection the speaker meant?

Related work. WORLD separates a speech waveform into fundamental frequency, spectral envelope and aperiodicity for resynthesis [reference in Storage]. That gives a controlled way to test the proposed fix: smooth only the pitch trajectory, hold the other components fixed, and ask listeners both whether the jump disappeared and whether the intended emphasis survived.

ideas.original_title: B033. Bayesian tool-set learning on interaction DAGs
ideas.original_text:
Suppose an olympiad problem calls for Cauchy–Schwarz and AM–GM. An agent proposes a set of tools and gets noisy feedback about how well it matches the tools the problem needs. This was the example Behrad and I discussed. Should we have several agents try different tools independently, or let the next one see what the first has learned? I picture a graph in which an edge is a call and a vertex is a place to branch or share evidence. To update beliefs, we need some account of what feedback each proposed tool set would receive under each possible answer. Then we can ask which graph makes the best use of a fixed amount of compute.

Related work. Graph of Thoughts represents model-generated thoughts and their dependencies as a graph, allowing intermediate results to branch and recombine [reference in Storage]. Lindley’s Bayesian design criterion assigns an experiment value through its expected information about the unknown state [reference in Storage]. To compare tool-use graphs I would need the observation channel for each proposed tool set and a terminal loss for choosing the wrong set.

ideas.original_title: B034. Work, span, and productive versus waiting time
ideas.original_text:
When two branches meet, the first one to arrive may spend some time waiting for the other. An agent that thinks for one minute and waits for four hasn’t done five minutes of inference. I’d like the graph to keep track of both clocks. The sum of the active call times measures work. The longest chain of calls that must happen in order gives the earliest completion time with enough processors. Counting a wait as extra thinking would quietly improve the precision of an observation in the model.

Related work. Blumofe and Leiserson analyze parallel scheduling in terms of total work and critical-path length, giving a work-stealing bound for fully strict computations [reference in Storage]. Those are useful clocks for this graph. A waiting branch can extend elapsed time without changing either its completed work or the precision of its most recent observation.

The longest chain of calls that must happen in order gives the earliest completion time with enough processors. Counting a wait as extra thinking would quietly improve the precision of an observation in the model.

Related work. Blumofe and Leiserson analyze parallel scheduling in terms of total work and critical-path length, giving a work-stealing bound for fully strict computations [reference in Storage]. Those are useful clocks for this graph. A waiting branch can extend elapsed time without changing either its completed work or the precision of its most recent observation.

ideas.original_title: B035. Sequentialization, context contamination, and equal-work experiments
ideas.original_text:
Ashwin asked why one agent couldn’t do everything a team does by taking the branches in sequence. If it can give each branch an isolated scratchpad and reproduce the same calls with the same information, it can reproduce the joint transcript. Parallel calls can still finish sooner. There might also be a statistical advantage if the failed attempts in a single growing context make later attempts worse. That’s an assumption about the model, and one I’d like to test.

I ran into a related question with long inputs. Direct transcription worked on my handwritten notes. When would splitting the input across calls help instead, and what dependencies would we lose at the split?

Related work. Tran and Kiela compare single- and multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning at equal thinking-token budgets and find that a single agent can outperform the tested teams [reference in Storage]. To isolate context contamination, I would also run the same multibranch policy sequentially with isolated scratchpads. A change in accuracy there and a change in wall-clock time under parallel execution answer different questions.

ideas.original_title: B036. Continuous-time reasoning particles and private beliefs
ideas.original_text:
Could reasoning trajectories really be trajectories through space and time? I imagined particles that carry beliefs, branch into different lines of attack, and share information when they meet. If the particles just copy their parent’s belief and independently carry out the usual calls, this is another way to draw the interaction graph. What would make it a genuinely interacting system? Repulsion between exploring branches or agents trying to infer one another’s private beliefs are possibilities. I don’t yet know what the right interaction law is.

Related work. Zhao et al. use twisted sequential Monte Carlo to maintain and resample partial language-model sequences under a specified sequence-level target [reference in Storage]. That supplies a concrete interacting-particle baseline with a known role for resampling. If branches also infer one another’s private beliefs or repel one another, I would want to specify how those interactions change the target or the decision risk.

ideas.original_title: B037. Power-law information and branching-versus-depth phase diagrams
ideas.original_text:
Given two units of compute, should an agent think twice as long or should two agents each think for one unit? Suppose all calls try the same tools, whose expected feedback differs between the two candidate answers, and return independent Gaussian observations with noise proportional to t^(−γ) after thinking for time t. Their information adds, so the comparison is between 2^(2γ) and 2. In this model, splitting wins below γ = 1/2, concentrating the time wins above it, and they tie at the boundary. This gives a simple account of what makes branching attractive. It depends on how precision scales with thinking time, even before we bring in agents with different skills.

Related work. Snell et al. compare allocating test-time compute to sequential revisions and to search over multiple candidate solutions, with the best strategy depending on the problem and model [reference in Storage]. The Gaussian calculation suggests a quantity to measure in those experiments: how quickly does the information in one branch grow with its thinking time, compared with the information in a fresh branch?

ideas.original_title: B038. Heterogeneous agent channels and concurrency capacity
ideas.original_text:
Natalie asked what happens when the agents have different capabilities. We can give each type its own observation model, cost of thinking and number of available copies. Now a second kind of agent might be valuable because it distinguishes possibilities the first one confuses, even if it is less accurate on average. I think of mathematicians who see the same problem through different representations. Does assigning a specialist to each representation still help if one versatile agent can translate between them? The comparison should account for the time and capacity used by both arrangements.

Related work. Pappu et al. find that heterogeneous self-organizing LLM teams can underuse an expert even when told which member has the relevant expertise [reference in Storage]. In this model I could separate two explanations by comparing a router that knows each specialist’s channel with one that has to infer it, while charging both for the same calls and concurrent capacity.

ideas.original_title: B039. Pruning Blackwell-dominated computation patterns
ideas.original_text:
Are there local patterns we can rule out without searching over the whole graph? Natalie suggested that some should be obviously wasteful. Suppose another call can be made at the same point, costs no more and produces an observation from which we can simulate the old one at every possible history. Any later agent could ignore the extra information and continue as before. This gives a Blackwell comparison that justifies replacing the inferior call in a design that does not already use its replacement, provided the schedule and downstream options stay the same. If the design already uses both calls, it may gain information from both observations.

Related work. Blackwell compares experiments by asking whether one observation can be simulated by garbling the other [reference in Storage]. If a design includes the weaker experiment and omits the stronger one, replacing it with the stronger one is justified when the replacement is available and preserves the schedule and downstream options. If both calls are already in the design, deleting the weaker one can lose a second informative observation.

ideas.original_title: B040. Stability of finite-budget topology recommendations
ideas.original_text:
Natalie asked how stable a recommendation about the best graph would be. If two designs are almost tied, a different noise model or a little Monte Carlo error might reverse the recommendation. For a finite list we can say exactly how much room there is: if the best design is ahead by Δ, errors smaller than Δ/2 in every estimated utility leave the winner unchanged. To use this for an actual recommendation we would need to know the size of the gap and how sensitively each design responds to the model assumptions.

Related work. Kim and Nelson give an indifference-zone procedure for selecting the best simulated system from a finite set when the best is separated from its competitors [reference in Storage]. That addresses Monte Carlo uncertainty in the ranking. A second stability check here would vary the assumed feedback channel itself, since no number of replicates under one channel can tell us whether another would reverse the ranking.

ideas.original_title: B041. Diminishing information and greedy graph growth
ideas.original_text:
Could we build an interaction graph by choosing a useful set of calls before any of the answers come back? Suppose we have a fixed library of experiments, and their observations are independent given the answer we are trying to learn. Then the expected information gained from adding one call cannot increase as the set we have already chosen grows. With a budget of equally costly calls, that gives us a reason to build the set greedily. The harder case is when an answer changes which call we want to make next. And even for a fixed set, does the information we gain help with the decision we ultimately need to make?

Related work. Krause and Guestrin give conditional-independence conditions under which information gain is submodular [reference in Storage]. Under a cardinality budget, the greedy approximation bound of Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher applies to a normalized, monotone submodular objective [reference in Storage]. For tool calls, I would check the independence model first and then ask how closely information gain tracks the loss of the final tool choice.

ideas.original_title: B042. Adaptive information gathering and version-space reduction
ideas.original_text:
Choosing the next call after seeing an answer is a different problem from choosing the whole graph up front. An informative outcome can make an apparently unpromising follow-up suddenly worth doing. For a greedy rule to have the usual adaptive guarantee, marginal gains must diminish even after conditioning on the particular outcomes so far. Ordinary diminishing returns in expectation don’t give that. One case to understand is a version space of possible answers that shrinks after each noiseless observation. How far can that intuition carry over to noisy agent calls?

Related work. Golovin and Krause formulate adaptive submodularity in terms of expected marginal gains conditional on partial observations and use it to justify adaptive greedy policies [reference in Storage]. Their version-space examples provide a starting point for the noiseless case. With noisy agent outputs I would check the conditional inequality on the actual observation channel, including histories where an unexpected answer makes a follow-up more valuable.

ideas.original_title: B043. Adjacency lifts, convex envelopes, and Lovasz risk relaxations
ideas.original_text:
Can we replace choices about which edges exist with continuous variables and optimize those instead? The answer depends on what the objective looks like on the space of graphs. Taking an exact convex envelope is a definition, but evaluating it can be as hard as the original problem. A Lovász extension is more promising if the set function really is submodular. I’d start by asking which of our risk objectives has that structure in a stated representation. In particular, if information gain is submodular, subtracting that gain from a baseline gives a supermodular risk. The sign matters for minimization.

Related work. Lovász’s extension is convex exactly when the underlying set function is submodular [reference in Storage]. That makes the sign consequential here: subtracting submodular information gain from a constant yields a supermodular risk, whose Lovász extension is generally concave. I would check the set function induced by the chosen edge representation before deciding what continuous problem to solve.

ideas.original_title: B044. Convex information-decay surrogates and validation after rounding
ideas.original_text:
In the Gaussian model, accumulating evidence helps separate rival answers. Could we score a fractional graph by a sum of exponentially decaying terms, one for each rival, and optimize that simpler score under the compute budget? The proposed objective is convex. Its value is a guide for choosing edges, rather than a certificate for the actual Bayes risk. Once we turn the fractional solution back into a graph that can run, we can evaluate the chosen calls under the original observation model. Does the graph still do well there?

Related work. Chernoff’s error exponent explains why a term that decays exponentially with separating information is a plausible design score [reference in Storage]. Joshi and Boyd relax a discrete sensor-selection problem for Gaussian estimation and round the result [reference in Storage]; here the checks after rounding are budget feasibility and decision risk under the original forward model.

ideas.original_title: B045. Spectral SDP as a communication-topology surrogate
ideas.original_text:
Bhaswar suggested the analogy with Boyd and Diaconis’s work on fastest-mixing chains. Perhaps a graph across which information propagates quickly would be a good architecture. On a symmetrized support, we can choose edge weights to maximize the Laplacian spectral gap under a compute constraint. How much of the original problem survives that simplification? A large gap says something about communication on the undirected graph. It does not capture which agent saw which evidence before choosing its next call.

Related work. Boyd, Diaconis and Xiao optimize the mixing rate of a reversible Markov chain on a fixed graph [reference in Storage]. Ghosh and Boyd study the closer objective of adding edges to increase algebraic connectivity [reference in Storage]. Neither objective records when an agent gets to condition its next call on an earlier answer.

ideas.original_title: B046. Edge-gated DAG-GNN topology search
ideas.original_text:
Could we learn the interaction graph itself? Fix an order for the synchronization points and allow a candidate edge only from an earlier point to a later one. Give each optional connection a learnable gate. A graph neural network could then pass messages along these connections and learn from the final task loss, with a cost for activating expensive edges. At the end we need a discrete graph that stays within budget. I’d judge it by running that graph, since training with partially open gates is easier than deciding which real calls to pay for.

Related work. DARTS relaxes discrete architecture choices during training [reference in Storage]; G-Designer already learns communication topologies for language-model agents with a graph neural network [reference in Storage], and ARG-Designer generates those topologies autoregressively [reference in Storage]. A useful comparison is how their discrete graphs perform against the gated, ordered graph at the same realized call cost.

ideas.original_title: B047. Dense ordered multigraphons and continuous risk summaries
ideas.original_text:
If the number of agents grows, is there a continuous object we can optimize in place of the whole graph? For a dense graph it is natural to retain the order of the vertices and specify how many parallel calls typically connect two positions. Long connections cost more in the level-weighted model, so the limiting cost has to remember distance as well as edge density. This approach can describe objectives determined by frequencies of small ordered patterns. Whether the final answer at the sink can be read from those frequencies is a separate question.

Related work. Orderons preserve the order information needed for ordered subgraph frequencies [reference in Storage], while multigraphons retain a distribution over edge multiplicities [reference in Storage]. Combining these ingredients would still require a convergence statement for the distance-weighted cost and a separate argument for any proposed sink loss.

ideas.original_title: B048. Continuum optimality conditions for interaction kernels
ideas.original_text:
What would a locally optimal continuum architecture look like? Following Bhaswar’s analogy with variational equations for random graphs, imagine moving a little edge capacity from one pair of positions to another without increasing the total cost. At an interior optimum there should be no profitable such exchange: the marginal reduction in risk has to balance the marginal compute cost. The first-order condition only has content once we choose a differentiable risk that reflects the agent system. Convexity would be a further assumption if we wanted it to establish global optimality.

Related work. Chatterjee and Diaconis derive graphon variational problems for exponential random graphs [reference in Storage], and Diao et al. develop directional derivatives of graphon functionals [reference in Storage]. Those results suggest how to perturb an edge kernel; the missing input here is a differentiable expression for the risk of the ordered agent system.

ideas.original_title: B049. Sparse ordered graphons and rescaled costs
ideas.original_text:
A large network can have many neighbors per agent and still have a vanishing fraction of all possible edges. Bhaswar pointed out that a dense graph limit loses the signal in that regime. We can rescale the edge intensity so that a long communication link still carries its intended cost in the limit. Passing from cost to performance is harder. A small dense patch can dominate the count of a pattern even in an otherwise sparse graph. What restrictions on those patches would give us a useful limiting risk?

Related work. Borgs et al. rescale sparse graphs and identify integrability conditions under which counts of fixed patterns converge [reference in Storage]. The orderon theory retains vertex positions in the dense setting [reference in Storage]; transferring a distance-weighted cost or a risk functional requires checking both order and sparse concentration.

ideas.original_title: B050. Bounded-degree local weak limits for interaction graphs
ideas.original_text:
If each agent communicates with only a bounded number of others, perhaps the right picture is what a typical agent sees within a few steps. Sample a vertex and record its neighborhood, including edge directions and durations. Convergence of those local views can describe average performance when the loss itself depends only on such a neighborhood. A final decision made at a distant sink can depend on the entire graph. Bhaswar’s point was that we should choose the large-network limit to match the information the question needs.

Related work. Benjamini and Schramm study limits seen from a uniformly sampled vertex [reference in Storage]; Aldous and Lyons extend this viewpoint to marked rooted networks [reference in Storage]. Direction and duration can be kept as marks, but convergence around a typical vertex gives no corresponding guarantee at a distinguished sink.

ideas.original_title: B051. Reliability-constrained interaction graphs under component failures
ideas.original_text:
What if an agent or a synchronization point fails before it passes its work along? A very good computation is useless at the sink if every path carrying its result breaks. My first question was whether increasing the failure probability would cause a switch from one deep chain to many parallel ones. A simple model independently removes internal vertices and keeps the source and sink available. Then we can ask both how much evidence gets through and how likely an open directed path from source to sink is to survive. Parallel paths buy reliability, but they use compute we might otherwise spend going deeper.

Related work. Lin, Yeh and Kuo compute network reliability when vertices as well as links may fail [reference in Storage]. Moore and Shannon study how circuit design can recover reliability from unreliable components [reference in Storage]. In this graph I would first calculate the probability that at least one directed path from source to sink survives. Even conditional on such a path, the information that reaches the sink can vary.

ideas.original_title: B052. Depth--width reliability crossing for two parallel-chain architectures
ideas.original_text:
Compare one long chain with several shorter, disjoint chains. Suppose a surviving long chain gives a better answer than a surviving short one, but a short answer is usable if any short chain makes it through. As internal failures become more likely, the deep design loses its advantage. The calculation in the draft gives a single crossing for this particular pair of designs and payoff. I’d like to understand how sharply the preferred design changes near the crossing. This restricted comparison leaves open the best architecture among graphs that can also branch and rejoin.

Related work. The series and parallel survival calculations go back to reliable switching circuits [reference in Storage], and Ghare and Taylor optimize redundancy in series systems [reference in Storage]. Here a surviving long chain earns a different payoff from a surviving short chain, so the single crossing concerns these two payoff curves and gives no ranking for graphs with shared vertices.

ideas.original_title: B053. Global depth--width transition for additive surviving-chain information
ideas.original_text:
Suppose every surviving branch contributes information, so that two successful short chains are worth more than one. Now we can ask how to divide the budget among equal-length chains. In the draft’s additive model, the value of a surviving chain is a fixed superlinear power of its length. With budget W for equal-length chains and independent failure probability p at each internal vertex, one nearly full-length chain wins as W grows and −Wlog (1 − p) tends to zero. When this quantity grows without bound, shorter chains and growing width win instead. The transition depends on the budget as well as the failure rate. It answers a different question from the payoff in B052, which only requires one branch to survive.

Related work. Classical redundancy allocation maximizes system reliability under resource constraints [reference in Storage]. Here each surviving chain contributes a payoff that grows faster than linearly with its depth. That assumption is what makes rare failures compatible with a preference for one long chain in the equal-length parallel-chain family. With a linear payoff, a fixed number of calls earns more in one-step chains whenever each additional step risks failure.

ideas.original_title: B054. Multi-agent reinforcement learning
ideas.original_text:
You can throw a bunch of virtuosos in a room together, but they won’t necessarily make great chamber music. What does a team of agents have to learn together that its members wouldn’t learn by training alone? I keep hearing how difficult it is to orchestrate several individually capable models. I’d like to understand which difficulties are really questions about multi-agent reinforcement learning.

Related work. Lowe et al. train agents with critics that see the other agents during training [reference in Storage], while QMIX fits a team value from the individual agents’ action values [reference in Storage]. These give two concrete comparisons for the chamber-music question: what information is shared in training, and which coordinated decisions can still be made by the agents separately?

ideas.original_title: B055. Conformal localization of proof errors
ideas.original_text:
If a mathematician has time to inspect only a few steps of a long AI-generated proof, which ones should we flag? Tao and I considered breaking the argument into claims, scoring each with a black-box verifier, then turning those scores into conformal p-values. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure selects a set to review. The relevant error here is sending a correct step to the human as a suspected mistake. A bound on the false discovery rate concerns the flagged set, not the correctness of the entire proof.

The September manuscript reports experiments on Hard2Verify, which has step-level labels for olympiad proofs. We were also looking for dependable annotations on research proofs. Tao raised concerns about the quality of one available set. A statistical guarantee cannot tell us whether the original annotator read a step correctly.

Related work. Benjamini and Hochberg give the reference rule for controlling the false discovery rate [reference in Storage], and Bates et al. show when conformal p-values sharing a calibration sample support that rule [reference in Storage]. Hard2Verify supplies human step annotations [reference in Storage]; a proof application still has to justify the relevant exchangeability and dependence conditions, particularly for several steps from one proof.

ideas.original_title: B269. False discoveries in a batch of mathematical announcements
ideas.original_text:
Davis asked how many of a frontier lab’s announced mathematical results people expected to hold up. I had a related question. Before other mathematicians have had the chance to check them, what false discovery rate are we willing to tolerate across the results the lab releases as true?

The unit matters here. One announced theorem can contain a long proof with a mistaken step and still be true. We’d need to say whether the lab is claiming the theorem, a correct proof of it, or both before we could count which announcements failed.

Related work. Benjamini and Hochberg control the expected fraction of false discoveries among rejected hypotheses under their assumptions on the p-values [reference in Storage]. Applying that criterion here requires a null and valid evidence for each announcement. A false theorem and an invalid submitted proof of a true theorem would yield different definitions of a false discovery.

ideas.original_title: B056. Dependence-aware conformal factuality
ideas.original_text:
A tweet can make several claims that amount to much the same thing. If we score every claim in isolation, could we discard useful information about which ones stand or fall together? Our conformal factuality work uses estimated entailment relations to pass evidence between claims, then calibrates a threshold for filtering them. Learning a better relation can help us keep more true material. The risk guarantee still comes from calibration under its stated assumptions.

In September we compared DeBERTa and Qwen for estimating the relations, separately from the choice of VERA or Qwen3-8B to score the claims themselves. The matched resplits let us see what changed when we switched one component. Our revised submission reports higher claim retention at a controlled expected false-negative rate on FABLES, FELM and an annotated Wikipedia dataset.

Related work. Mohri and Hashimoto calibrate a claim filter [reference in Storage]. Rubin-Toles et al. use a deducibility graph to select claims that satisfy their coherent-factuality criterion [reference in Storage]. Our September manuscript updates the scores of claims in an existing response by belief propagation on estimated entailment relations [reference in Storage]. Wang et al. intervene earlier: they calibrate a graph-level score to decide when to stop generation [reference in Storage]. For an already generated response, I would compare how many claims each filter retains at the same target expected false-negative rate.

ideas.original_title: B057. Risk-controlled post-processing of a policy
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a policy is already in use and we want it to meet a new risk constraint. How little can we change it? In the work Tao and I did with Hamed and Edgar, the objective is to leave the original action in place on as many inputs as possible while keeping the probability of a downstream loss of at least c at most ε. We estimate where switching to a fallback would most reduce the conditional probability of a downstream loss of at least c, given the input, then use calibration data to decide how often to switch.

One difficulty is that a fallback need not be better on every individual input. The observed loss can rise at some thresholds even when switching is useful on average. That matters for the calibration argument. We looked at both medical decisions and routing requests among language models.

Related work. Our post-processing paper characterizes the best agreement with a baseline under a chance constraint [reference in Storage]. With a general fallback its calibration result bounds expected excess risk under i.i.d. regularity assumptions; exact exchangeable control is a separate result for an exactly safe fallback. Learn then Test offers a comparison that tests candidate policies with a high-probability guarantee [reference in Storage].
