ideas.original_title: B058. Stochastic routing and mixture-of-experts connections
ideas.original_text:
When should a router pay for a stronger model? If the choice is made before either response is available, we care about the expected reduction in loss on this input relative to the extra cost. A router that first runs the weak model gets to use different information and has already paid part of the bill. Tao and I were interested in how to choose the route, then calibrate its risk on fresh labeled examples. The empirical loss along the routing path can be nonmonotone, which makes finding a satisfactory threshold harder than it looks.

I also wondered how this relates to stochastic routing and mixture-of-experts models. Randomly mixing two routes is a useful baseline. Our draft also uses calibration to mix two input-dependent routing rules: the first to meet the bumped risk budget and its immediate predecessor on the fitted path. How this relates to learning which expert to select in a mixture-of-experts model is still open.

Related work. Dekoninck et al. distinguish routing before inference from cascading after candidate answers are available [reference in Storage]. Our post-processing paper calibrates a switch from a baseline under a risk constraint [reference in Storage]. A mixture-of-experts gate allocates computation within a model [reference in Storage], whereas Noorani et al. use disagreement among generated responses to route without correctness labels [reference in Storage]. I would compare these rules at equal deployment cost, counting the weak samples used to route. DeSalvo et al. address a separate budget, the expert queries needed during training [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B059. Rectifying decision regions for multiple risk control
ideas.original_text:
Sima drew a problem with two scores and two risks. Once we sketched the decision regions, we could see why it didn’t fit directly into MultiRisk: her boundaries were hyperbolas, while a sequence of thresholds cuts along the coordinate axes. Could we change coordinates to straighten the boundaries? The same question comes up with the oblique splits of a decision tree. We would need a map that works for all the regions together. If it is learned from data, we’d still have to calibrate the resulting decisions without using the calibration data to choose a favorable transformation.

Related work. MultiRisk calibrates prioritized coordinate thresholds [reference in Storage]; Plassier et al. transform conformity scores to improve conditional coverage [reference in Storage], a different goal from straightening several boundaries at once. Learn then Test [reference in Storage] gives a comparison for a fixed family of candidate rules; using the same observations to learn a more favorable map would need its own validity argument.

ideas.original_title: B060. Induced conformal prediction from seed labels
ideas.original_text:
Suppose the labels in a prediction problem are related. Could we construct prediction sets for a few seed labels and use those sets to induce predictions for the others? Soham and I discussed this, and Edgar pointed to work on conformal structured prediction. The distinction I’d start with is between a rule we know exactly and one we learned from examples. In the first case a valid set can carry through a deterministic implication. In the second, an error in the implication itself can break the argument. Could we get away with computing sets for fewer labels? One idea was to choose seed labels greedily using residual variation. I wasn’t sure that was the right criterion.

Related work. Zhang, Li and Bastani represent sets of structured labels compactly, including through nodes of a known hierarchy [reference in Storage]. For a learned implication between labels, a separate risk check such as Learn then Test [reference in Storage] is one possible baseline; only a known implication automatically carries a joint seed-coverage event through to its image.

ideas.original_title: B061. Merging human and AI prediction sets
ideas.original_text:
In Sima’s human–AI complementarity problem, a policy chooses either the human’s prediction set or the AI’s. Why restrict it to switching? If both sets tell us something, could we combine them while keeping the required coverage, and when would simple switching already be optimal? I had in mind the corresponding problem of combining two confidence intervals or two sources of evidence about the same quantity. Work by Ramdas, Wang and Vovk on merging p-values and e-values might give us a useful place to start.

Related work. The published human–AI procedure already lets the system prune and augment a human set under counterfactual-harm and complementarity constraints [reference in Storage]. Gasparin and Ramdas merge dependent uncertainty sets with an explicit coverage cost [reference in Storage], and Vovk and Wang study merging scalar evidence [reference in Storage]. A fair comparison would put switching and merging under the same coverage and human-harm requirements.

ideas.original_title: B062. Symmetry-aware uncertainty and ambiguous protein structure
ideas.original_text:
Afnan told me about intrinsically disordered protein regions whose structure depends on what they interact with. In a setting like that, what would uncertainty about the predicted structure even mean? I wanted to understand which symmetries a molecular prediction procedure uses and how they relate to symmetry-based conformal inference. If the input is rotated, how should the set of plausible output structures move? I don’t yet know how much of the ambiguity comes from symmetry and how much from an unobserved interaction partner.

Related work. AlphaFold’s structure module builds rigid-motion symmetry into geometric prediction [reference in Storage], while SymmPI derives prediction sets under specified group symmetries [reference in Storage]. Oldfield et al. document different bound structures for disordered p53 regions with different partners [reference in Storage]: rotating a single plausible structure cannot represent that kind of ambiguity.

ideas.original_title: B063. Archive-valued estimation when the loss is revealed later
ideas.original_text:
When we fit an estimator, do we really have to decide on the loss in advance? Behrad’s account of Ben Recht’s criticism of average performance, and the way MAP-Elites keeps solutions that are good on different instances, made me wonder what we could return instead. Imagine storing a small set of estimators that make different tradeoffs between groups. When we learn which outcomes matter, we can choose among them.

Shayan and I discussed how the set itself might be revised as more of the loss becomes known. The constraint that makes this interesting is that we can afford to choose a stored fit but can’t simply redo the entire analysis once the loss arrives.

Related work. MAP-Elites stores the best solution found in each region of a chosen descriptor space [reference in Storage]. Omniprediction addresses the later choice of loss by post-processing one predictor over a specified loss and comparator class [reference in Storage]. The two make useful comparisons for a small archive: when does selecting one stored fit outperform a permissible post-processing of a single fit?

ideas.original_title: B064. Evidence under restricted stopping rules
ideas.original_text:
What if we knew that an experimenter could only look at the data at particular times? An evidence measure safe under arbitrary optional stopping protects against more behavior than this experiment permits. Could restricting the stopping rules lead to a more informative measure, especially at the allowed early looks? I discussed this with Junu, Ilia and Shayan. The analogy I had in mind was restricting the class of test functions used to define calibration. The question is what should replace that class here: which stopping rules are available, and which alternatives do we want power against?

Related work. O’Brien and Fleming calibrate tests for a prescribed sequence of interim looks [reference in Storage]; safe testing gives evidence that can be accumulated across optional continuations [reference in Storage]. An intermediate procedure needs to specify the permitted stopping times and compare power at those looks under a common null and alternative.

ideas.original_title: B065. Automated estimator discovery with risk certification
ideas.original_text:
Could an evolutionary search discover an improved estimator of a normal mean? Some familiar improvements make a surprisingly small change to the formula, so a simple language of symbolic mutations might be enough. I discussed this with Davis and Yan. The interesting part is how to judge a candidate. If it looks good on a handful of values of the true mean, it might have learned precisely where our check is weak. Could we use adaptive screening to find promising formulas and then prove that one has no larger risk for every mean, with a strict improvement somewhere? A search result and a dominance argument would play quite different roles.

Related work. FunSearch evolves candidate programs against a supplied evaluation criterion [reference in Storage]. James and Stein’s domination result for a multivariate normal mean [reference in Storage] and Stein’s unbiased risk identity [reference in Storage] offer a benchmark and a possible analytic check: a formula discovered on a finite grid still needs a risk comparison over the entire parameter space.

ideas.original_title: B264. Matching minimax bounds with an AI prover
ideas.original_text:
Mahdi and I wondered whether an AI system could help prove minimax rates. A problem Edgar tried with GPT gave us a concrete case. In a nonparametric regression with constant noise variance, how accurately can we estimate that variance when we don’t know the regression function? The available upper and lower bounds I had seen left a gap. Was the estimator leaving something on the table, or was the lower-bound construction too easy to distinguish?

I’d like to give a system the model, parameter class and loss, and ask for both arguments. An estimator with a proved risk bound would give it a rate to beat from below. When those rates disagree, could the system identify an avoidable loss in the estimator or construct a harder family of examples?

Related work. The July example is Aronow and Lopatto’s counterexample to the conjectured rate under rough random design [reference in Storage]. Their October manuscript credits AI with proof discovery and verification. For constant conditional variance, a design density bounded above and away from zero, and bounded conditional fourth moments, its upper and lower root-mean-square risk bounds agree up to a power of log n when the regression smoothness s exceeds one and the dimension d exceeds 4s [reference in Storage]. I could use this case to test whether a prover independently finds both the estimator and the hard alternatives.

ideas.original_title: B259. Statistical decisions built from tests
ideas.original_text:
Is there a formulation of statistical decision theory that starts with hypothesis tests and builds the other decisions out of them? Confidence sets are what made me ask. Invert a family of tests and you get the set of parameter values you couldn’t reject. Could a more general decision, perhaps a map from data to a subset of the parameter space, be written naturally in terms of elementary tests? What would we learn by writing it that way? A point estimate seems like the most natural example to try next, and I’m not sure what the answer is there.

Related work. Neyman’s confidence-set construction already builds a set-valued decision by inverting tests [reference in Storage]. Wald’s framework lets the action and loss be specified directly [reference in Storage]. For a point estimate, the interesting question is whether representing the action through tests preserves its risk or makes an optimal rule easier to find.

ideas.original_title: B066. Incomplete group augmentation and random designs
ideas.original_text:
After Morgane’s talk, Kyle and I were asking what an incomplete set of data augmentations really is. Is it a sample of transformations drawn from the full compact group, or do we apply every transformation in a smaller subgroup? Those descriptions need not give the same augmented data. I also asked about the size of the set of unmatched directions in the random-design version of her graph example. Morgane thought there might be a connection to Kyle’s Gaussian-mixture question. I’d like to understand the connection before treating the two models as equivalent.

Related work. Chen, Dobriban and Lee formulate augmentation as averaging over group orbits [reference in Storage], and Esmaili Mallory et al. study the dependence created by augmentations of a common observation [reference in Storage]. Huang et al. relate unmatched directions to the design’s variance pattern [reference in Storage]; sampling a few transformations, exhausting a subgroup, and sampling Gaussian-mixture components would need comparable design laws before that result could connect them.

ideas.original_title: B067. Universality for dependent data and graph models
ideas.original_text:
A common high-dimensional analysis replaces the design by a Gaussian one that is easier to study. What survives when the observations are dependent? In her FOLDS talk, Morgane discussed logistic regression with block dependence or mixing. Augmenting the same image several times is a good reason to care: the rotated cats in the training set aren’t independent cats. I wanted to understand how the Gaussian replacement deals with that dependence, and what rate it gives. I’d also like to know whether random graphs or graph neural networks admit comparably useful universality classes.

Related work. Esmaili Mallory et al. prove Gaussian universality for logistic regression under block dependence, finite-range dependence and specific mixing conditions [reference in Storage]. For a graph comparison, Deshpande, Abbe and Montanari connect mutual information in a two-group block model with growing degree to a Gaussian observation model [reference in Storage]; transferring a logistic-risk result to a GNN would require a new choice of observable and graph regime.

ideas.original_title: B068. Affine free operators: spectral edges and internal gaps
ideas.original_text:
A note I circulated in July considers two extensions of the spectral-edge formulas of Parmaksiz and van Handel for free operators. One allows a nonzero deterministic term in the operator. The other keeps the centered model and asks about the gaps inside the spectrum as well as the two outside edges. The proposed characterization uses stable real solutions of a matrix Cauchy-transform equation. These are distinct extensions: the second statement in the note is for the centered case.

Related work. Parmaksız and van Handel give explicit formulas for the outer edges when the free operator is centered [reference in Storage]. Lehner’s general recipe already covers quadratic polynomials with a deterministic term [reference in Storage]. For a nonzero mean the question is whether we can simplify that recipe enough to compute the edges. For the centered case I would compare the proposed test for an internal gap with the band and edge criteria of Alt, Erdős and Krüger, checking their hypotheses for the linearized operator [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B069. Extensions of high-dimensional learning analyses
ideas.original_text:
I had a few questions after talking with Behrad about his high-dimensional analyses. Is there a universality argument for the result? What becomes difficult when we go from one gradient step to several? I’d also like to understand in which space preconditioning ought to act. Thomas’s explanation using BatchNorm made me wonder whether equivariance tells us something about that choice. A related question from the conversation was whether filtering or denoising synthetic examples could help in weak-to-strong generalization.

Related work. Moniri et al. treat one gradient step [reference in Storage]; Moniri and Hassani have since analyzed the second step and shown how additional feature directions emerge in their scaling regime [reference in Storage]. Their separate weak-to-strong analysis [reference in Storage] is a starting point for testing synthetic-label filtering; results for two steps do not settle arbitrary depth, universality, or the choice of preconditioner.

ideas.original_title: B265. The auxiliary problem for a matrix CGMT
ideas.original_text:
Behrad asked me to think about a matrix version of the convex Gaussian min–max theorem. The appeal of the usual comparison is that the auxiliary optimization problem can be much simpler to analyze. Behrad thought it was easy to write down matrix variants and much harder to find one that buys us anything. His sticking point was concrete. What should the auxiliary problem look like in the matrix case, and for which primary problems would solving it pay off?

Related work. Bosch and Panahi use a Gaussian comparison for repeated features to compute learning curves for vector-valued regression [reference in Storage]. Agterberg and Vidal give a matrix CGMT for symmetric Gaussian matrix sensing and relate nuclear-norm estimation to spectral soft thresholding in a matrix denoising model [reference in Storage]. For Behrad’s question I would start with one of these auxiliary problems. What makes it easier to solve, and which of those simplifications survive in another matrix model?

ideas.original_title: B263. Weighting real and synthetic observations in linear regression
ideas.original_text:
Manit Paul and I studied a simple version of learning from synthetic data. We have some real observations, fit a linear model, then use it to generate more labels. How much weight should those labels get? They carry both error inherited from the original fit and fresh noise from generation. In our Gaussian model, a reward that knows which residuals to trust can make the synthetic data useful. Constructing such a reward from the real data is harder. In our MNIST comparison, pooling the available real labels gave lower test error than the selected filter at the same label budget. What information does the reward supply beyond what the original fit already learned?

Related work. Kazdan et al. distinguish successive replacement of real data from retaining real observations and accumulating synthetic generations [reference in Storage]. He, Xu and Cheng derive weights for iterative training with fresh real data at each round [reference in Storage]. Our working manuscript asks about a single real anchor and a reward based on residuals [reference in Storage]. I would compare the filter with pooling all available real labels, counting the labels used to estimate the reward in both budgets.

ideas.original_title: B070. Multiple testing as a bridge into econometrics
ideas.original_text:
When I asked Anjali how a statistician might find an interesting problem in econometrics, I mentioned recent work on the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Is there a feature-selection question in econometrics where controlling the false discovery rate would be useful? It was a possible point of entry. I’d first want to know which selection decisions econometricians actually struggle with.

Related work. Benjamini and Hochberg prove FDR control for independent test statistics [reference in Storage]; Barber and Candès target selection among regression variables with knockoffs [reference in Storage]. Harvey and Liu give a concrete financial application involving false and missed discoveries [reference in Storage]. Whether the unit is a tested strategy, a factor, or a conditional regression effect determines which comparison is appropriate.

ideas.original_title: B071. Double descent with variance profiles
ideas.original_text:
What happens to double descent when the training examples are dependent, synthetic or augmented? Morgane’s talk included designs with heterogeneous covariances and designs in which some feature variances vanish. I liked the bipartite graph picture: put observations on one side, features on the other, and draw an edge where the variance is positive. Which feature directions can be left uncovered? Outside the complete bipartite case I wouldn’t expect the singularity to depend only on whether p/n = 1. I’d like to understand the relevant matching condition for random designs, and whether this gives us a way to think about the synthetic-data problem Manit and I studied in B263.

Related work. Huang et al. already locate variance singularities using maximum matchings and the Dulmage–Mendelsohn decomposition of the variance-profile graph [reference in Storage]. Esmaili Mallory et al. analyze dependence from repeated augmentations in logistic regression [reference in Storage]; applying the matching criterion to a random or synthetic design requires specifying how its support and covariance arise.

ideas.original_title: B072. Conformal inference for difficult multichannel time series
ideas.original_text:
Conformal inference for a time series sounds especially difficult when it has several channels, some observations are missing, the distribution changes over time, and the noise variance changes with it. What coverage could we reasonably ask for in that setting?

Related work. Xu, Jiang and Xie build joint ellipsoidal prediction regions for multivariate sequences [reference in Storage]; Zaffran et al. distinguish marginal from missingness-pattern-conditional coverage [reference in Storage]; Gibbs and Candès target long-run coverage under distribution shift [reference in Storage]. A multichannel guarantee should say whether it concerns a whole response vector, a particular observation mask, or errors averaged across time.

ideas.original_title: B073. Combining evidence while saving computation
ideas.original_text:
Ilia and I discussed two versions of the problem of combining e-values: the inputs are independent, or their dependence is arbitrary. What useful cases lie between those extremes? A graphical dependence assumption might let us do better without having to know the full joint distribution. I also wondered whether we always need to compute every input. If part of the combination already settles the testing decision, could we stop and save the work? We’d need to know how the unfinished calculation is bounded, since a favorable partial answer alone isn’t grounds for stopping.

Related work. Vovk and Wang compare independent and dependent e-values [reference in Storage], and Wang characterizes admissible mergers under arbitrary dependence [reference in Storage]. Martingale-based sequential mergers [reference in Storage] require conditional validity as evidence is revealed; a dependence graph alone does not supply it. A different, computation-only shortcut is to stop when every possible completion yields the same testing decision.

ideas.original_title: B256. Benjamini--Hochberg under structured dependence
ideas.original_text:
For two-sided Gaussian tests with correlated statistics, by how much can Benjamini–Hochberg exceed its nominal false discovery rate? Could we express the excess as a function of the correlation structure? I wondered whether our proof-verification project (B055) had prompted Edgar to think about this, since I had seen a related question in an earlier discussion. I could be wrong about that connection.

I wanted a simple one-factor, two-block example to see where the inflation comes from. Davis subsequently shared Lihua Lei’s analysis of the one-factor setting. I also have a more speculative question. What happens to BH when the dependence among the p-values comes from something like an Ising model or an exponential random graph?

For the same Gaussian tests, I would compare ordinary BH with converting the p-values to e-values and running e-BH. At a given correlation structure, how much power would I give up for protection against dependence, and how far above the target would ordinary BH actually go?

Related work. Dobriban gives Gaussian factor models where two-sided BH exceeds its nominal FDR [reference in Storage]. Lei gives matching-order bounds for the worst case over one-common-factor Gaussian models: as q tends to zero, the inflation factor FDR/q grows on the order of the square root of log(1/q) [reference in Storage]. For a fixed correlation matrix and signal configuration, I would measure the actual inflation and compare power against e-BH after specifying a valid p-to-e conversion. Its FDR guarantee allows arbitrary dependence [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B074. A connection between the wild bootstrap and test-time search?
ideas.original_text:
Manit described an exchangeability-based correction to a naive bootstrap, using the wild bootstrap for SGD as an example. His aim was to get a finite-sample distribution-free guarantee while removing a slack term. For some reason the wild bootstrap reminded me of beam search. Is there a formal connection with test-time search? I would first want to say what is being perturbed in each procedure and which distribution we think it approximates. So far it’s an analogy.

Related work. Fang et al. perturb SGD updates to approximate a sampling distribution [reference in Storage]; Paul and Kuchibhotla study order-statistic inequalities with bootstrap and conformal applications, distinguishing their asymptotic bootstrap and finite-sample conformal results [reference in Storage]. Stochastic beam search instead samples sequences without replacement using Gumbel perturbations [reference in Storage]; the common use of randomness alone gives no bootstrap law for ordinary beam search.

ideas.original_title: B075. What could a zero-shot p-value mean?
ideas.original_text:
Junu and I wondered whether an LLM could give a p-value zero-shot. The Bayesian interpretation of pretraining was the intuition. But does the model mean it can calculate a specified test statistic and its null distribution, or is it just giving a numerical expression of its own uncertainty? For the latter number to be a p-value, we’d need to specify a null under which unusually small reports occur no more often than advertised. Guessing a conditional expectation, as in the paper we discussed, is a different task.

Related work. Engh and Aronow use model guesses of conditional means to improve causal estimation [reference in Storage]. A contrasting use of a model would be to compute a specified randomization test: Phipson and Smyth show how randomly drawn permutations can yield valid discrete p-values [reference in Storage]. That validity comes from the randomization law, which an uncalibrated numerical guess does not supply.

ideas.original_title: B076. Bayesian uncertainty-quantification reading pointers
ideas.original_text:
Joey recommended Andrew Gordon Wilson’s perspective on Bayesian uncertainty quantification and pointed me toward Jacob Gardner’s work. One question I came back to was why a Gaussian-process prior is so useful when the scientific function we are trying to optimize is itself deterministic. Which regularity of that function makes the prior useful for deciding where to evaluate next? Could a deterministic uncertainty set lead to comparable choices under the same evaluation budget?

Related work. Wilson and Izmailov discuss how a prior expresses assumptions about functions and generalization [reference in Storage]. For optimization, Srinivas et al. analyze GP-UCB both under a GP model and for a fixed function with bounded reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space norm [reference in Storage]; the fixed-function result is a concrete way to ask what the kernel assumes without treating the objective as a random draw.

ideas.original_title: B077. Sequential multi-risk control with prioritized actions
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a system can take several fallback actions in a fixed order. Once an early check fires, nothing reaches the later checks. Loosening the first threshold may therefore increase what the second stage has to handle. How can we choose all the thresholds so each action meets its own risk budget and the final policy is still useful? In our MultiRisk work, each risk averages its contribution over the whole stream of inputs. Conditioning only on the cases that reached a stage would give a different target. Yan, Hamed, Edgar and I studied how the priority order can be used in calibration.

Related work. Our MultiRisk paper uses priority to control several unconditional risk contributions simultaneously [reference in Storage], extending the single-loss calibration principle of conformal risk control [reference in Storage]. Learn then Test can evaluate families of candidate configurations under multiple risks [reference in Storage]; its high-probability certification differs from a marginal expected test-loss bound for the deployed recursion.

ideas.original_title: B078. MultiRisk: bumped empirical inverses and a symmetric threshold chain
ideas.original_text:
A tempting procedure is to choose the first threshold on the calibration sample, freeze it, and find the smallest second threshold whose empirical risk is acceptable. But the second loss now depends on a choice made using the same data. Can we still control its expected test loss? MultiRisk adds a worst-case test contribution to the empirical sum and works with slightly tightened risk levels. The proof compares the thresholds we can compute with auxiliary thresholds symmetric in the calibration and test points. The symmetry is how exchangeability enters. Only the thresholds learned from the calibration data are deployed.

Related work. Conformal risk control adds a worst-case contribution for the unobserved test loss before taking a single empirical inverse [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk uses several symmetric comparison thresholds because later losses depend on earlier fitted thresholds [reference in Storage]; the proof’s joint-sample thresholds are comparison devices, not extra test information needed for deployment.

ideas.original_title: B079. Tightness via anti-overshoot, weighted nesting, and jump counting
ideas.original_text:
If the procedure promises a risk below a budget, how far below it will we actually land? In a threshold problem, lowering the threshold by one step can move a whole block of observations across a boundary. An early move also changes which losses appear downstream. Our lower-bound argument keeps track of both effects. For score-based losses, absence of ties limits the jump at one threshold, and a nesting condition lets us charge downstream loss to the observations that moved earlier. Under those extra conditions the slack can be of order 1/n for a fixed number of stages. Upper control alone wouldn’t tell us that.

Related work. Conformal risk control derives a complementary lower bound when loss jumps do not pile up [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk has to count changes passed from one stage to later stages [reference in Storage]; near-tightness therefore uses assumptions on jumps and nesting beyond those sufficient for simultaneous upper control.

ideas.original_title: B080. Near-optimality from stable population inverses
ideas.original_text:
A feasible set of thresholds could leave a lot of useful predictions on the table. How does the calibrated objective compare with what we would choose if we knew the population risks? Two things have to go right. First, small errors in estimating risk must produce small changes in the thresholds. This depends on how the population risk crosses the budget at each stage. Second, the thresholds picked by the population recursion must themselves solve the decision problem we want to compare against. The draft separates these steps. A stability bound for the estimated recursion doesn’t establish the second claim.

Related work. Our MultiRisk preprint compares the fitted objective with a population minimizer under stated hypotheses. Lemma D.6 identifies when the population recursion solves its optimization problem, and Theorem 5.26 bounds the fitted objective under additional regularity [reference in Storage]. Bahadur’s quantile expansion gives a one-dimensional analogue for stability of the inverse [reference in Storage]. For a different utility I would check the population minimizer first, before trying to carry over the stability argument.

ideas.original_title: B081. Exact oracle recovery when scores have finite support
ideas.original_text:
For scores taking only finitely many values, two quite different numerical thresholds can induce exactly the same decisions. This suggests a simpler notion of stability. Suppose the budget lies strictly between two attainable risk levels at each stage of the population recursion. If the empirical risks are close enough, they pick out the very same threshold choices. We can then ask how many samples are needed to recover that population policy exactly. If a budget sits on a risk level, even a tiny sampling fluctuation can change the answer. Finite support on its own is insufficient.

Related work. MultiRisk gives the threshold recursion whose discrete decisions are to be recovered [reference in Storage]. For i.i.d. bounded losses, Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over the finite candidate risks give a direct baseline [reference in Storage]: a positive stagewise separation can preserve every comparison, whereas finite support alone supplies no separation.

ideas.original_title: B088. Rare-atom experiments exposing plug-in risk failures
ideas.original_text:
I wanted an example where the empirical risk looks reassuring for a perfectly understandable reason: a rare, expensive loss simply didn’t occur in the small calibration sample. The synthetic example puts a small probability on a large loss and routes cases through successive thresholds. The plug-in procedure can act as though the expensive outcome doesn’t exist. The worst-case correction can guard against it, but that protection also changes how many cases get through. The expectation-risk experiment and the earlier exceedance-probability experiment measure different things even when they use a similar mixture of ordinary and rare observations.

Related work. Conformal Risk Control adds a worst-case contribution for the unseen observation when calibrating a bounded, monotone loss [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk carries a related correction through a sequence of prioritized filters [reference in Storage]. The rare atom makes the cost of omitting that contribution observable even when the calibration sample contains no large loss.

ideas.original_title: B089. Synthetic scaling and fair baseline comparisons
ideas.original_text:
As the number of risk constraints grows, how much more conservative or expensive does calibration become? In the core synthetic example we can generate scores ourselves, set the budgets, and see exactly what fraction of cases the policy accepts. This makes comparisons with direct empirical thresholding and finite-grid testing easier to interpret. Here the fraction that passes all three filters is the objective loss, so smaller is better. LTT-Holm had lower values for all three stage risks but let 67.9% pass, compared with 47.0% for MultiRisk. I’d compare achieved risk, acceptance and calibration time together, keeping track of how finely each method was allowed to search. The six-constraint experiment asks how these tradeoffs change beyond the small three-score example.

Related work. MultiRisk uses the filter order to select thresholds recursively [reference in Storage]. Learn then Test certifies candidate settings through multiple testing [reference in Storage], while Pareto Testing screens settings before testing them on separate data [reference in Storage]. In this synthetic experiment the objective is to minimize the fraction passing every filter at the given stage-risk budgets. I would report that fraction alongside the number of threshold vectors each method considers.

ideas.original_title: B090. LLM abstention with safety and uncertainty scores
ideas.original_text:
When should an assistant abstain? In the PKU-SafeRLHF experiment we generated a response with Alpaca, used Llama Guard to score two groups of hazards, and used perplexity as a proxy for uncertainty. If a score crosses its threshold the assistant gives a fixed abstention response. We assigned a bounded cost to the answer it actually gives, using the Beaver reward model. For each abstention route, we average its reward-derived cost over all prompts, counting zero when that route is not taken. We likewise average the cost of the original answer times the indicator that we kept it. We report the fraction kept separately.

Related work. PKU-SafeRLHF records human judgments of response helpfulness and safety [reference in Storage]. Llama Guard supplies a separate model-based hazard classification [reference in Storage], and our MultiRisk experiment uses hazard scores to route responses [reference in Storage]. The comparison is the reward-derived cost contributed by each route, averaged over all prompts with zero contribution off that route. The kept-original objective is defined the same way. Keeping frequency is a separate outcome.

ideas.original_title: B091. Different LLM failures trigger different fallback outputs
ideas.original_text:
Abstention seems a blunt response to three different problems. If the first or second safety check fires, could the assistant regenerate an answer suited to that hazard? If uncertainty is the issue, could it give the answer with a qualification? We generated all four possible outputs before calibration, including the original answer. The checks use scores from the original, but the cost is the reward-based cost of the answer actually returned. With a budget of 0.20 for each of the three routes, the measured MultiRisk costs were 0.192, 0.117 and 0.170 in the representative experiment.

Related work. Our MultiRisk framework permits a different output modification at each stage of an ordered policy [reference in Storage]. Self-Refine gives a concrete example of improving an output through model-generated feedback and revision [reference in Storage]. To evaluate hazard-specific regeneration here, I would score the replacement itself and account for how often that branch is used.

ideas.original_title: B092. Fourteen-category scaling and score/assumption diagnostics
ideas.original_text:
What happens as we give each safety category its own threshold? We increased the number of active Llama Guard categories from three to fourteen. Giving each category the same budget is quite different from dividing a fixed total among all of them, especially when some hazards are rare. At the representative fourteen-category setting, with a budget of 0.20 per category, MultiRisk abstained on about half the prompts. Some score distributions were highly concentrated. Looking at the mass near the chosen thresholds could help explain why changing a threshold sometimes has little effect and sometimes moves many responses at once.

Related work. Llama Guard 3 defines fourteen hazard categories that can supply separate routing signals [reference in Storage]. The priority ordering in MultiRisk [reference in Storage] and the candidate screening in Pareto Testing [reference in Storage] give two ways to manage many constraints. A comparison has to specify whether each new category receives a fresh budget or a share of a fixed total.

ideas.original_title: B093. Early-exit routing for adaptive BERT inference
ideas.original_text:
Can a classifier stop at an intermediate layer when the rest of the network would add little? On AG News we fitted probes at eleven layers of BERT. An early exit incurs a loss if the probe is wrong on an example the full classifier would have gotten right. With a representative per-stage budget of 0.020, MultiRisk used about a fifth of the full compute. Its accuracy was 0.911, compared with 0.952 for the full classifier. Limiting each route’s contribution to excess error can still cost several points of accuracy overall.

Related work. DeeBERT lets an example exit at an intermediate classifier [reference in Storage], and Jazbec et al. calibrate early exits against a specified quality loss [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk supplies separate risk budgets across the ordered exits [reference in Storage]. The experiment here budgets the contribution of each layer to errors the full classifier would have avoided.

ideas.original_title: B094. Audit total output quality separately from the calibrated objective
ideas.original_text:
Does optimizing the quantity we calibrated improve the answer someone actually receives? In our LLM abstention experiment, MultiRisk had the smaller calibrated objective, but the Beaver reward model gave its outputs lower quality scores than those from Learn then Test with Holm correction. We saw a much smaller quality gap in the intervention experiment. Beaver was also part of the evaluation, so an independent judge could rank the outputs differently. The early-exit experiment gives us a cleaner check of overall classification accuracy because we have the true labels.

Related work. Gao et al. compare a proxy reward with a separate reference reward as optimization pressure grows and find that the two can diverge [reference in Storage]. Our MultiRisk procedure controls the particular routed losses supplied to calibration [reference in Storage]. A separate judgment of all returned responses would tell us whether the ranking survives a change of evaluator as well as a change of objective.

ideas.original_title: B082. VaR control by reducing losses to exceedance indicators
ideas.original_text:
What if the deployment requirement is about a bad outcome in the tail, rather than the mean loss? The (1 − α)-quantile is at most β exactly when the probability that loss exceeds β is at most α. We can feed the indicator of exceedance into the expectation-risk procedure. For a sequence of fallback actions we must check that this transformation keeps the monotonicity and feasible endpoints the recursion needs. The resulting target is the marginal tail probability on a new case. A particular calibration sample may do better or worse.

Related work. MultiRisk supplies the expectation-risk recursion once each loss is replaced by its exceedance indicator [reference in Storage]. Quantile Learn-Then-Test [reference in Storage] and quantile risk control [reference in Storage] offer comparisons based on high-confidence population-quantile guarantees. The quantity to compare here is the marginal exceedance probability of the deployed priority rule, including calibration randomness.

ideas.original_title: B083. General quantile-based risks from finite bundles of VaR constraints
ideas.original_text:
An upper bound on one quantile says little about the rest of the tail. Could we control a weighted average of quantiles by bounding exceedance probabilities at several loss levels? For bounded nonnegative losses, the risk can be written as an integral of a function of the tail probabilities. Before calibration, choose a grid whose last point bounds the loss almost surely and assign exceedance budgets at the left endpoints so the resulting upper sum stays within the risk budget. The stage threshold has to satisfy every component. A finer grid better approximates the integral, while the choice of how much budget to give each component still matters.

Related work. Snell et al. bound quantile-based risks using confidence bounds on the loss distribution [reference in Storage]. Here the calibration primitive is instead MultiRisk [reference in Storage]: a predetermined finite bundle of exceedance constraints has to imply the tail-integral bound and remain feasible at each stage of the priority recursion.

ideas.original_title: B084. CVaR budget allocation: constant, linear, and power profiles
ideas.original_text:
For CVaR we care about the average size of losses in the upper tail. In the finite-grid approach, we can give every loss level the same exceedance budget. We could instead allow more exceedances at moderate losses and make the very largest losses rarer. Which allocation leaves the most useful decisions available while still bounding the tail average? The draft compares equal budgets with decreasing profiles, including a linear profile. Those options change the conservatism of the bound. They must be chosen in a way consistent with how the calibration data will be used.

Related work. Rockafellar and Uryasev express CVaR using an auxiliary threshold and expected excess loss [reference in Storage]; quantile risk control bounds tail functionals from distributional information [reference in Storage], and conformal risk training gives an OCE-based alternative [reference in Storage]. These are comparisons for the cost of replacing the tail integral with a finite grid and allocating its budgets before calibration.

ideas.original_title: B085. Direct exchangeability-based CVaR calibration: unfinished routes
ideas.original_text:
Can we control CVaR directly by exchangeability, without replacing the tail integral by a grid? One idea was to bound the tail quantile and calibrate a truncated mean. I couldn’t see how to carry the quantile bound through a threshold chosen from the very same data.

A second attempt, suggested by Gemini, averages the largest calibration and test losses and bounds the missing test contribution. There’s a specific gap: changing the threshold also changes the event on which we take the conditional expectation. Pointwise ordering of the losses doesn’t order those two conditional means. Could a random choice of index repair the step? I left that open.

Related work. Snell et al. bound tail risks from confidence bounds on the loss distribution [reference in Storage], while Yeh et al. control CVaR through an optimized certainty-equivalent construction [reference in Storage]. Both offer comparisons for a direct proof, but neither supplies the missing inequality between means conditional on two different, threshold-dependent tail events.

ideas.original_title: B086. OCE alternatives: tune a tail threshold on holdout data or during training
ideas.original_text:
Some tail risks can be written as the infimum, over an auxiliary threshold t, of the expected value of a transformed loss. For any fixed t this gives an expectation we can try to control, but choosing t poorly leaves a loose bound. Could we learn a useful threshold during training or choose it on a separate held-out sample before calibration? This direction came from reading about conformal risk training. The attraction is that we might use the form of the risk directly without having to control a large collection of tail probabilities.

Related work. Ben-Tal and Teboulle develop the optimized certainty-equivalent representation [reference in Storage]. Yeh et al. use it for conformal risk control and training, including for CVaR [reference in Storage]. Farzaneh and Simeone combine a synthetic likelihood model with held-out calibration to control the OCE risk with high probability [reference in Storage]. In MultiRisk [reference in Storage], I would ask how to estimate the auxiliary thresholds while preserving the simultaneous marginal guarantees for the ordered decisions.

ideas.original_title: B087. High-probability sequential QRC using disjoint calibration splits
ideas.original_text:
The marginal guarantee averages over the calibration sample and the next test case. What if we want high confidence, after drawing the calibration data, that all the population risks meet their budgets? One simple two-stage route is to split the data. Choose the first threshold on the first split, then calibrate the second on observations the first choice hasn’t seen. A finite set of candidates lets us account for the search and the two risk statements. The cost is fewer observations at each stage and a penalty for considering many candidates. This was a preliminary approach to the stronger guarantee.

Related work. Learn then Test uses a held-out sample to test which candidate settings meet population risk targets with high confidence [reference in Storage]. Quantile Risk Control constructs confidence bounds from loss order statistics, including bounds for tail functionals [reference in Storage]. In the two-stage sketch, the question is how much the second bound costs once the first threshold has been selected on a separate split.

ideas.original_title: B095. Tail-risk experiment continuation and reproducibility
ideas.original_text:
The expectation-risk experiments leave open what happens in the tail of the loss distribution. I would like to keep the same abstention and intervention tasks, the same splits and the same competing methods, then ask how much answering or routing costs at a specified upper quantile. For conditional value at risk, how does dividing the budget equally across the component constraints compare with allowing unequal allocations? The tail-risk draft describes the comparisons and the planned plots. The numerical tables from the expectation-risk experiments answer a different question.

Related work. Snell et al. bound loss quantiles using order statistics [reference in Storage], and Rockafellar and Uryasev give an auxiliary-threshold representation of CVaR [reference in Storage]. Applying these ideas to the ordered policies of MultiRisk [reference in Storage] would require evaluating the loss distribution of each selected policy. The reported means on the existing splits do not determine its upper tail.

ideas.original_title: B096. What calibration metrics should measure
ideas.original_text:
What makes a calibration metric useful? I wanted a metric we could estimate and compute that would bound gaps in decision risk. I wanted to understand the discontinuity of ordinary expected calibration error and study smooth and cutoff calibration error [reference in Storage]. Edgar mentioned open problems in this area.

I asked Shayan whether there is a similar tension for rank calibration. If an uncertainty score is only meant to order examples, which measures stay the same under a smooth, strictly increasing change of scale? Which can we estimate without having to learn the entire curve of accuracy conditional on the score? Edgar, Hamed and I had tried semiparametric calculations for a class of such measures. We hadn’t settled on which quantity we actually wanted.

Related work. Rossellini et al. show that cutoff calibration error can be estimated and has a decision-theoretic interpretation [reference in Storage]. For an uncertainty score whose numerical scale is arbitrary, Huang et al. instead ask whether average generation quality declines as reported uncertainty increases [reference in Storage]. I would like to know which decision-risk bounds, if any, survive that move from probabilities to ranks.

ideas.original_title: B097. Why some signal decompositions are natural
ideas.original_text:
What lets me pick out the bass line in a rock song? There are countless ways of writing a signal as f = g + h. My first thought was to ask for the two parts to be as regular as possible, say by minimizing the larger of their norms. But the equal split g = h = f/2 already attains the smallest possible value, and I haven’t isolated an instrument. What makes the decomposition I actually hear a natural one?

Related work. Smaragdis and Brown factor a nonnegative time–frequency representation of polyphonic music into recurring spectral patterns and their activations [reference in Storage]. This gives a concrete alternative to splitting a waveform by smoothness. A useful test would be whether the recovered patterns group into the bass line a listener actually hears.

ideas.original_title: B098. Equivariant quantile regression and conformal prediction
ideas.original_text:
Ordinary conformal prediction gives the same prediction set if I pass the scores through a strictly increasing function and transform the threshold accordingly. Why can we lose that property when we fit a threshold by quantile regression? Even if the predictor class is closed under the transformation, the pinball loss and any regularizer can rank the candidate fits differently. Could we modify the fitting objective to recover equivariance for a specified class of transformations? I’d like to understand the unregularized case first and then come back to LR-QR.

Related work. Regression quantiles are fitted by minimizing asymmetric absolute loss [reference in Storage]. Our LR-QR method also regularizes the fitted threshold using information about the covariate shift [reference in Storage]. A strictly increasing map preserves the ranks of the observed scores, but can change the sizes of the residuals being minimized. I would check equivariance of that optimization before adding the regularizer.

ideas.original_title: B099. Causal estimands that are difficult under privacy
ideas.original_text:
When I think of causal estimands, I think of average treatment effects. Averages seem comparatively friendly to privacy. Are there natural causal quantities practitioners care about that are much harder to estimate privately? Ask Soham.

Related work. Niu et al. construct differentially private learners for conditional average treatment effects and compare the accuracy of several estimators [reference in Storage]. Subgroup effects give a concrete place to start: a small subgroup can offer much less information than the population used for an overall average. A lower bound for a specified subgroup estimand would separate a cost of privacy from the cost of estimating heterogeneity even without privacy.

ideas.original_title: B100. Interpreting coverage under distribution shift
ideas.original_text:
When I compare coverage lower bounds for conformal prediction under covariate shift, including the one for our LR-QR algorithm, I struggle to see which method has the advantage. Empirically the differences can be clear. Does one bound identify a setting where the others are too pessimistic? I would like to ask James Wang or Surbhi Goel about their clipped version of weighted conformal prediction [reference in Storage]. A difference in set size or in which subgroups are covered might matter to a user even when both methods have the same nominal coverage.

Related work. Weighted conformal prediction uses the target-to-source density ratio to reweight the calibration observations [reference in Storage]. LR-QR learns a threshold using likelihood-ratio regularization [reference in Storage]. Wang and Goel fit a clipped density ratio, bound the expected undercoverage, and use a data-dependent increase in the coverage target to correct for it [reference in Storage]. I would compare the guarantees on the same shift, alongside set size and coverage in the regions carrying the largest weights.

ideas.original_title: B255. Synthetic data for locally efficient conformal prediction
ideas.original_text:
Shayan once drew a picture for me: if we could collect more examples near X = x, perhaps we could get better coverage near x. What if we have no way to collect those labels, but we can generate synthetic ones? With a perfect generator I could keep drawing from Y ∣ X = x until I knew that conditional distribution quite well. With an imperfect one, could some debiasing still give us smaller prediction sets or better local coverage while preserving marginal validity? Are there fundamental limits on what synthetic data can buy us here?

Even evaluating conditional coverage is a problem. If we could estimate its error well, could we improve a predictor using that estimate while constraining its marginal coverage?

Related work. Chen and Li use paired trusted labels to correct synthetic-label quantile learning. An independent trusted split gives marginal coverage. They identify conditional-coverage error as a gradient of profiled pinball risk and quantify when synthetic labels help [reference in Storage]. Braun et al. give a diagnostic for conditional miscoverage [reference in Storage]. Wang et al. conformalize conditional draws at a test input [reference in Storage], and Zheng and Zhu already allocate those draws across inputs to reduce set size at a fixed average budget [reference in Storage]. Distribution-free conditional coverage itself has limits even with real labels [reference in Storage]. With separate costs for real pairs and generated draws, where should I buy each to improve coverage near a chosen input while retaining marginal validity?

ideas.original_title: B211. Natural-language proof verification and co-scientist systems
ideas.original_text:
Edgar’s interest in AI co-scientists made me wonder what system we might actually build. One possibility is a verifier for proofs written in ordinary mathematical language. If a model is grading a solution to a functional equation, does it check the argument or just look for the right final answer? An olympiad-style rubric might help us tell. Another route would be to break a proof into natural-language steps and their implications, so that the verifier checks one block at a time. How much structure do we need before this becomes useful, short of fully formalizing the proof in Lean?

Related work. ProofGrader evaluates natural-language competition proofs against expert scores using reference solutions and marking schemes [reference in Storage]; Co-Scientist instead generates and critiques research hypotheses [reference in Storage]. For a proof assistant, I would hold the conclusion fixed and change one implication, then ask whether the grader can locate the error as well as lower the score.

ideas.original_title: B101. Recursive proof verification and repair
ideas.original_text:
How would I check a long proof if I could ask another model for help a limited number of times? I’d start with the main argument and break a doubtful passage into smaller claims. A localization procedure would tell me which parts to inspect. A repair procedure would try replacing a bad step and then check that the replacement still fits the argument. The May sketch assumes the verifier’s confidence becomes better calibrated on smaller steps. A smaller step might be easier to check; when does that intuition actually justify the assumption? Junu and I also discussed how the choice of which claim to inspect next affects error control. The fixed-claim multiple-testing version is in B055.

Related work. Block Verification first translates an argument into self-contained modules and judges each module [reference in Storage]. StepProof instead breaks a natural-language proof into smaller subproofs amenable to formal checking [reference in Storage]. The distinction I want to measure is the benefit of choosing which doubtful passage to split or repair next when the available checks are limited.

ideas.original_title: B104. Localization utilities, risks, and algorithmic comparisons
ideas.original_text:
Pointing to a whole proof is little help to someone looking for one bad step. Pointing to a single line is useful only if the mistake is actually there. How should we value a report that narrows a mistake to a paragraph, or finds two of three distinct mistakes? I would want to distinguish false accusations, missed mistakes and the amount of text a human still has to read. Reporting both a paragraph and a sentence inside it should not count as two discoveries of the same error. If we attempt a repair, we also have to check whether the resulting proof is correct.

Related work. Focused BH adjusts a multiple-testing procedure for the filter determining which discoveries are ultimately reported [reference in Storage]. ProcessBench supplies annotated first mistakes in mathematical solutions [reference in Storage]. Those annotations could test whether a report points to the right region, while questions about missed second errors or redundant ancestor–descendant reports need richer labels and an explicitly chosen loss.

ideas.original_title: B103. Bayesian recursive proof localization
ideas.original_text:
A Bayesian version would maintain a distribution over where the proof’s mistakes are. After each verifier call, update that distribution and decide whether to check another claim, split the current one, attempt a repair, or hand the proof back. If we knew how the verifier and decomposer behaved and had a fixed budget, we could work backward from the value of the final report to choose an action now. What would be a credible model for those responses, especially when a repair changes the proof we are checking?

Related work. Smallwood and Sondik give the finite-horizon dynamic program for decisions made from a partially observed state [reference in Storage]. A module verifier such as Block Verification [reference in Storage] supplies one possible observation about a proof. The difficult modeling choice is the transition after a repair: the old verifier responses still describe the old proof, and some of its dependencies may have changed.

ideas.original_title: B102. Adaptive refinement and evidence-based localization
ideas.original_text:
In a proof with several doubtful regions, where should the verifier spend its next call? My May sketch gives one answer. Split the region where seeing the subclaims would most improve the eventual report, taking account of how many false alarms we will tolerate. By the time we test a subclaim, we have already selected its parent for closer inspection. Can we construct evidence that stays valid conditional on what prompted that choice? The sketch considers e-values for this purpose. Both their validity under selection and the performance of the greedy rule depend on assumptions about the verifier.

Related work. DAGGER controls false discoveries when a prespecified graph governs which hypotheses can be tested next [reference in Storage]. For a child selected after inspecting its parent, I would need its e-value to have null expectation at most one conditional on the selection history [reference in Storage]. Whether choosing the most informative split greedily is efficient is a separate question, for which adaptive submodularity gives a benchmark [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B105. A possible data--parameter duality
ideas.original_text:
The symmetry of η^(⊤)θ made me wonder whether a Bayesian model might admit a useful duality between data and parameters. We can always factor a joint distribution in either order. Is there a family in which exchanging the roles tells us something about inference?

Related work. Letac defines a dual natural exponential family through an inverse relationship between the two mean maps and shows that a dual measure need not exist [reference in Storage]. That gives a precise case in which exchanging coordinates has content. For a Bayesian analogue, I would ask what choice of prior makes the reverse conditional belong to the proposed dual family.

ideas.original_title: B106. Embedding hierarchies together with their labels
ideas.original_text:
I can picture a hierarchy of classes and subclasses, each with its own attributes, much more readily than I can picture the continuous representation a network learns. Could we embed a tree with scalar or vector labels in Euclidean space while preserving both the hierarchy and the labels? What dimension would it take? I’d like to compare this with hyperbolic embeddings and ask Alan Chang about the metric-embedding side of the question.

A related example I discussed in July was a photograph with one corner of a building hidden. The opposite corner might tell us much more about the missing patch than its immediate neighbors. In what geometry would those two corners be close? The idea of simplifying a video model came up separately with Behrad (B219).

Related work. Sarkar constructs low-distortion embeddings of trees in the hyperbolic plane [reference in Storage], and Nickel and Kiela learn hyperbolic embeddings for observed hierarchies [reference in Storage]. These are useful benchmarks for preserving tree geometry. I would specify separately which distances or predictions involving the attached attributes must also survive the embedding.

ideas.original_title: B107. Representation recovery and transfer beyond one validation task
ideas.original_text:
I asked Thomas about a doctor with a small collection of brain MRI scans labeled healthy or diseased. Suppose synthetic scans improve her classifier even though some show anatomical artifacts. Has she learned a better representation? Thomas pointed out that if the held-out scans faithfully represent the patients and task she cares about, the gain in accuracy is already useful. My worry was what happens when she asks a different question or sees a different patient population. Could we generate brain regions separately and combine them in a way that respects their structure?

I also asked whether, in the linear model y = FGx, we could view the updates to the row space of G as motion on a Grassmann manifold. Thomas described a related retraction onto the Stiefel manifold in his algorithm.

Related work. Tripuraneni et al. study transfer through a shared linear representation [reference in Storage]. Zhang et al. show how non-isotropic covariates can bias the representation update and introduce a correction [reference in Storage]. For the MRI question, changing the task and changing the hospital test different things: Zech et al. observed cross-hospital degradation even for a fixed pneumonia-prediction task [reference in Storage].
ideas.original_html:
I asked Thomas about a doctor with a small collection of brain MRI scans labeled healthy or diseased. Suppose synthetic scans improve her classifier even though some show anatomical artifacts. Has she learned a better representation? Thomas pointed out that if the held-out scans faithfully represent the patients and task she cares about, the gain in accuracy is already useful. My worry was what happens when she asks a different question or sees a different patient population. Could we generate brain regions separately and combine them in a way that respects their structure?

I also asked whether, in the linear model y=FGxy=FGx, we could view the updates to the row space of GG as motion on a Grassmann manifold. Thomas described a related retraction onto the Stiefel manifold in his algorithm.

Related work. Tripuraneni et al. study transfer through a shared linear representation [reference in Storage]. Zhang et al. show how non-isotropic covariates can bias the representation update and introduce a correction [reference in Storage]. For the MRI question, changing the task and changing the hospital test different things: Zech et al. observed cross-hospital degradation even for a fixed pneumonia-prediction task [reference in Storage].

ideas.original_title: B108. What part of deep-learning theory is statistical?
ideas.original_text:
How much of what we call deep-learning theory is statistical? In the interpolating regime, some of the questions that interest me seem to be about solving systems of nonlinear equations. Understanding why a fitted system has a solution feels quite different from understanding what the data tell us about a new observation.

Related work. Montanari and Subag analyze algorithms for solving random systems of real polynomial equations in specified dimensional regimes [reference in Storage]. Belkin et al. exhibit models whose test risk changes substantially as capacity grows through and beyond interpolation [reference in Storage]. Finding a solution and predicting its out-of-sample error are different mathematical tasks even when both start from an interpolating fit.

ideas.scope: Learn object-specific update rates in a small interacting dynamical system and compare trajectory prediction at matched compute.

ideas.original_title: B109. Principled choices in world-model objectives
ideas.original_text:
Why use a pointwise loss to train a world model when we care about a whole trajectory? I had similar questions about stop-gradient updates and exponential moving averages. What property of the dynamics makes these choices sensible?

One thing I keep coming back to is that the objects in a scene move on different time scales. A cyclist passes a pedestrian, they interact briefly, and then each goes on moving at a different pace. Could a model learn which objects evolve together and when a faster group needs information from a slower one?

Related work. PlaNet’s latent overshooting objective trains predictions across several future steps [reference in Storage]. Clockwork VAEs instead assign different update frequencies to levels of a latent hierarchy for video [reference in Storage]. The street-scene example suggests an additional test: can the model learn which objects belong at each time scale and when interactions between scales become important?

ideas.original_title: B110. Specialist models, physical intelligence, and useful robots
ideas.original_text:
Xiaohan and I were talking about small specialist models versus large general models. I suspect the comparison looks different for digital and physical tasks. Coding seems a peculiar example of specialization since so much of it is structured language. A model that predicts something from a biological sequence seems a better test. On the physical side, which robots would actually improve someone’s life? A robot that keeps an older person company is one example I’d like to think about (B197).

Related work. ESMFold uses representations learned from protein sequences to predict atomic structure [reference in Storage]. RT-2 combines vision-language pretraining with robot-action data to test transfer from web knowledge to physical control [reference in Storage]. These give concrete digital and embodied comparisons, provided the training data, action repertoire and criterion for a useful outcome are specified for each.

ideas.title: New skills versus sharpening an existing policy
ideas.scope: Separate improved elicitation from learning new compositions using controlled pretraining mixtures and executable reasoning tasks.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Executable tasks support controlled experiments, but finite samples cannot establish absent latent skills; robust operational claims need careful controls.
ideas.impact_reason: The study could clarify composition versus elicitation in a controlled setting, sharpening post-training evaluations without settling general capability creation.
ideas.gate: Define a claim observable under finite sampling; distinguish absent support from merely very low base-model success probability.
ideas.rated_version: Separate improved elicitation from learning new compositions using controlled pretraining mixtures and executable reasoning tasks.

audit_evidence.does_not_establish: Does not establish sample-optimal curricula or identify entirely absent pretrained skills from finitely many failed samples.

ideas.original_title: B111. New skills versus sharpening an existing policy
ideas.original_text:
Does post-training teach a genuinely new skill, or make a model more likely to use a skill it already had? Thomas pointed out a distinction I like. A model might know each of the moves in a solution without ever sampling them in the right sequence. Rewarding successful traces gives very little guidance if every attempted composition fails. Could feedback on a prefix tell the model which part of a strategy was worth keeping? Before claiming that training taught a new skill, I would like to know what we can already elicit from the pretrained model. Thomas also warned that a length penalty can discourage precisely the long attempts a hard new problem needs.

Related work. Zhao et al. vary pretraining mixtures and observe RL amplifying behaviors already present in those mixtures [reference in Storage]. Park et al. find transfer to unseen expression-tree shapes in a controlled Countdown task [reference in Storage]. These results motivate measuring both the base model’s probability of producing a correct trace and its ability to reuse known moves in a previously unseen composition.

ideas.original_title: B115. Minimal synthetic curricula for composition
ideas.original_text:
An AI-generated suggestion in my notes with David was to start with skills the model already knows separately. At the same difficulty and budget, which extra examples most efficiently teach compositions from a structural family the model has not seen? A model that has learned each primitive may still fail on an unfamiliar arrangement of those primitives. Short executable programs or Countdown problems would let us distinguish teaching a new composition from showing the model a harder instance of an old one.

Related work. SCAN tests whether a learner can execute new combinations of commands built from familiar primitives [reference in Storage]. In Countdown, Park et al. use expression trees to distinguish transfer to unseen structures from transfer to longer inputs [reference in Storage]. A curriculum comparison could use those distinctions to count how many added examples are needed to reach the same accuracy on a held-out family of compositions.

ideas.original_title: B112. Continual learning through RL, optimizer design, and loss landscapes
ideas.original_text:
A friend suggested continual learning as a direction, and I wanted to ask Thomas and David about it. Thomas’s work on optimizers got me wondering how the geometry of the loss changes when an RL agent has to keep learning. Is there a good problem here where understanding the optimizer would tell us something about what the agent keeps or forgets?

Related work. Dohare et al. find that networks trained on successive problems can lose the ability to learn later ones and test an intervention that replaces low-utility units [reference in Storage]. In a changing RL task I would measure adaptation to the next task separately from retention on earlier tasks. An optimizer can improve one quantity while doing little for the other.

ideas.scope: Measure joint context–compute performance frontiers on a controlled family of tasks with known training support.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Small models and task generators make a bounded study feasible; a useful theory beyond a descriptive frontier is uncertain.

ideas.original_title: B113. What counts as in-distribution when context and compute change?
ideas.original_text:
What does out-of-distribution mean for a modern model? Thomas asked me this, and I wish we had a better answer. A task might look far from the training data under a density or transport-distance definition, yet be within the model’s reach given more examples in context or more time to reason. How do we describe that dependence on the information and computation available at test time?

Related work. Snell et al. find that the relative payoff from different test-time compute strategies varies with problem difficulty [reference in Storage]. Xie et al. give a setting in which demonstrations in the prompt provide evidence about a latent task [reference in Storage]. I would vary the demonstrations and the inference budget independently before labeling a task beyond the model’s reach.

ideas.original_title: B257. Learning from self-generated reinforcement-learning environments
ideas.original_text:
Davis and I were discussing whether problem-solving conversations might be useful for training a model indirectly. Suppose another system used them to construct environments in which the model could practice. That was a conjecture about one possible route for the information. What I’d like to understand is the learning problem it suggests. If an algorithm can choose or generate new tasks for itself, perhaps without gold-standard rewards, what would let it generalize to ever broader domains? Synthetic data, active learning, and domain randomization all come to mind, but I don’t know which analogy captures the important part. I asked Hamed whether we could make sense of this in a simple theoretical model.

Related work. PAIRED trains an environment generator using the performance gap between two agents, producing increasingly difficult but solvable tasks and improving transfer in its experiments [reference in Storage]. It supplies a concrete objective for self-selected environments. If a conversation supplies the task description but no trustworthy reward, how would we tell that the generated task was solvable or useful?

ideas.scope: Compare deletion of an early observation with retraining while retaining later updates in an order-dependent learning model.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A linear or convex sequential model is manageable; a result beyond existing deletion guarantees needs a precise order constraint.
ideas.impact_reason: Would clarify when preserving later learning makes unlearning harder, with a concrete algorithmic rather than metaphorical interpretation.
ideas.gate: Exhibit a noncommutativity or information limit absent from ordinary batch deletion.
ideas.rated_version: Compare deletion of an early observation with retraining while retaining later updates in an order-dependent learning model.
ideas.audit_reason: Keep: training-order-sensitive deletion is a concrete narrowing. It must be compared to formal unlearning rather than interpreted literally as reversing physical time.

ideas.original_title: B114. Comparing learning, unlearning, and forgetting
ideas.original_text:
I asked Ivi whether unlearning is fundamentally harder than learning. I had the arrow of time in physics in mind. Can a model learn something from experience and then undo that particular change while still remembering what it learned afterward? I would like to revisit this alongside continual learning.

Related work. Ginart et al. formulate data deletion by comparing the released model to the result of training without the deleted observations and study algorithms that can make deletion cheaper than full retraining [reference in Storage]. That comparison gives the time-reversal analogy a target: keep the effect of the later data while removing the contribution of the earlier observation.
