ideas.title: Which facts does a model retain as it learns?
ideas.scope: Track a controlled transition from memorized facts to a shared rule using held-out consequences and causal interventions.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Training small models is possible; observing a fact graph or separating compressed memorization from rule learning is substantially harder.
ideas.impact_reason: A controlled mechanism would be a substantive learning-dynamics result; the small task does not yet establish general knowledge organization.
ideas.gate: Define an intervention that distinguishes a learned rule from successful recall, rather than relying on probe accuracy.
ideas.rated_version: Track a controlled transition from memorized facts to a shared rule using held-out consequences and causal interventions.
ideas.audit_reason: The observable fact-to-rule transition is unresolved; small-model mechanism evidence cannot inherit the impact of general knowledge acquisition.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Training small models is feasible; distinguishing causal rule acquisition from compressed recall is the essential unresolved measurement problem.
ideas.I_note: A controlled fact-to-rule mechanism would deepen learning-dynamics understanding, with the first task supporting bounded knowledge-organization claims.
ideas.original_title: B253. Which facts does a model retain as it learns?
ideas.original_text:
Can we estimate the set of facts an LLM has memorized, say in its MLPs? I picture a discrete set that changes during training. Perhaps the model initially memorizes several facts separately, then discovers some simpler fact that accounts for all of them. In that case, did the old facts disappear, or did they get folded into something else? I wonder if we could describe what happens during training as a large graph of facts getting successively coarser. I don’t know how to observe that graph, even at a single checkpoint.

Related work. Chang et al. follow how exposure to a fact during pretraining changes predictions on probes, including ones testing generalization [reference in Storage]. If several formerly separate facts get folded into one rule, I would want a probe whose answer follows from that rule but was never shown during training. Getting the old answers right at a later checkpoint cannot by itself distinguish the two accounts.

ideas.original_title: B272. Which old episodes should an agent remember?
ideas.original_text:
I have only a hazy sense of most of elementary school, but I can still recall a few moments quite clearly. It reminds me of a geological record in which a handful of events far in the past leave traces we can still see. How should an agent with a long history decide which episodes to keep?

Perhaps the density of retained events ought to fall as we go further back, even while particular old episodes remain worth keeping. The hard part is deciding what makes an episode formative when the agent may only discover its importance much later.

Related work. Generative Agents score stored observations by recency, relevance and importance when deciding what to retrieve [reference in Storage]. Keeping a record but retrieving it rarely is different from deleting it under a fixed memory budget. For the geological-record analogy, I would measure the later cost of deleting an old episode that initially seemed unimportant.

ideas.original_title: B116. When should synthetic examples share a context?
ideas.original_text:
An AI-generated idea in the brainstorm with David concerns how we pack synthetic examples into a context. Suppose several examples are different views of the same hidden program. Keeping them together could make that program easier to infer, but it could also give the model many copies of essentially the same evidence. With exactly the same training examples, when would grouping related ones help on a new program, and when would shuffling them be better?

Related work. Kim et al. improve pretraining efficiency by stitching related synthetic rephrasings into longer documents [reference in Storage]. Zhu et al. show on a stylized reasoning task how additional context can improve the learning signal even when no prediction loss is charged on that context [reference in Storage]. Holding the token multiset and loss masks fixed would help isolate the effect of grouping examples that share a hidden program.

ideas.original_title: B117. Predicting cross-model effects of selected data
ideas.original_text:
An AI-generated suggestion in my brainstorm with David was to use a cheap model to predict how selected training data would change another model’s behavior. For instance, examples that favor a particular formatting habit in one model might have little effect on a second model if it represents that habit differently. Could a comparison of their representations predict the direction of the change before we fine-tune the second model? In the proposed pilot, we would make that prediction for held-out model families before fine-tuning.

Related work. Aden-Ali et al. use logit-linear selection to construct datasets that induce particular behaviors after fine-tuning and demonstrate effects that transfer across architectures [reference in Storage]. I would ask for a forecast before training a held-out model family: can a comparison of the two representations predict the sign and magnitude of the behavioral change, including failed transfers?

ideas.original_title: B118. When do small-model dataset rankings transfer?
ideas.original_text:
Another AI-generated question from the discussion with David was whether a small model can rank candidate training datasets for a larger one. The ranking we really care about may only emerge after the larger model adapts to its downstream task. Could a short learning curve or the alignment of the training and downstream gradients tell us when a cheap proxy will pick the wrong dataset?

Related work. DoReMi learns domain weights with a small proxy and uses the resulting mixture to train a much larger language model [reference in Storage]. Mohri et al. find regimes in which a sufficiently trained larger model benefits from data that quality filtering would discard [reference in Storage]. A ranking diagnostic should predict reversals as scale and adaptation budget change, alongside the regret from actually following the proxy’s choice.

ideas.original_title: B120. Sampling Gaussian mixtures: seminar follow-up
ideas.original_text:
Jiaoyang asked me why diffusion models or Langevin dynamics can work as well as they seem to for sampling from high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures. Which properties of the mixture make that possible? I’d like to ask Morgane where the difficulty lies and whether Lester’s or Sinho’s work on sampling speaks to it.

Related work. Ge, Lee and Risteski prove sampling guarantees for simulated tempering with Langevin dynamics on a class of distributions close to equal-variance Gaussian mixtures [reference in Storage]. Chen, Kontonis and Shah study a different information model: from samples of a general mixture they learn a score-based sampler, with complexity depending on the number of components and target accuracy [reference in Storage]. I would compare the two only after saying what we know about the density and how its modes are separated.

ideas.original_title: B121. Composite optimization and the choice of parametrization
ideas.original_text:
In Mateo Diaz’s seminar the objective was h(F(x)), with h convex and F smooth. For recovery of a low-rank positive semidefinite matrix one can optimize over a matrix or write it as XX^(⊤) and optimize over the factors. We are looking for the same matrix, yet the parameterization can change how quickly gradient descent gets there. It reminded me of Alex L.-N.’s example of estimating a covariance matrix through its inverse. What does the talk’s restricted good-conditioning assumption mean in one of these concrete examples? I’d also like to understand how the Levenberg–Marquardt step compensates for the parameterization.

Related work. Díaz, Jiang and Labassi develop a preconditioned subgradient method for a convex loss composed with a smooth map [reference in Storage]. Under their regularity assumptions it can recover local linear convergence even when the map is poorly conditioned or overparameterized. In the positive semidefinite factorization example, I would check which condition concerns the loss on matrices and which concerns its representation by factors.

ideas.original_title: B122. Learning stable proximal updates
ideas.original_text:
A backward Euler step for gradient flow can be written as minimizing the objective plus a quadratic penalty for moving away from the previous iterate. This was the connection to proximal operators in Mateo Diaz’s talk. Shervin asked why the backward step could remain stable at step sizes where the forward step fails. What if the proximal operation is too expensive and we learn it instead? Another participant asked how error in a learned proximal map enters the convergence bound. I wondered where else in generative AI forward or backward steps could be viewed as proximal updates.

Related work. Rockafellar’s proximal-point analysis allows inexact updates under controlled error [reference in Storage]. Fang, Buchanan and Sulam construct learned networks that are exact proximal operators for a learned regularizer [reference in Storage]. The remaining distinction is between exactly implementing that learned map and approximating the particular backward step the original dynamics require.

ideas.original_title: B124. Channel-dependent attention readouts
ideas.original_text:
In an attention readout, the same weight on an earlier token multiplies every coordinate of its value vector. What if one coordinate ought to be copied from one token and another coordinate from a different token? We could give each channel c its own weights q_(t)^((c))(i), so that v_(t, c) = ∑_(i < t)q_(t)^((c))(i)v_(i, c). A single readout with shared weights cannot in general select each coordinate from a different token; giving each channel its own weights would allow that.

Related work. In a standard attention head, each token receives one weight for its entire value vector [reference in Storage]. DiSAN already implements feature-wise attention with a separate distribution across tokens for each feature [reference in Storage]. The remaining comparison is how many ordinary heads and what output map are needed to represent a specified channel-wise selector.

ideas.original_title: B125. Bayesian interpretation of in-context learning
ideas.original_text:
TabPFN is pretrained on many tabular tasks. When it sees labeled examples (x_(i), y_(i)) in context, one way to understand its prediction for a new x is that it first infers which task produced the examples. Could inferring a latent task from a small dataset in this Bayesian sense explain other instances of in-context learning?

Related work. TabPFN is explicitly trained to approximate posterior prediction on small tabular tasks drawn from a designed prior [reference in Storage]. Xie et al. give a different route to implicit Bayesian inference, through language-model pretraining on sequences sharing a latent concept [reference in Storage]. The comparison turns on where the prior over tasks comes from and which observations identify the task at inference time.

ideas.original_title: B273. Text as side information for image denoising
ideas.original_text:
I can take a blurry picture of the pub I can barely see from my apartment, give it to a model, tell it something about the scene and ask it to denoise the image. What would change if I kept the pixels fixed and gave it different information in words? It felt to me like a kind of Bayesian denoising.

Behrad asked whether the evidence would make the prior largely irrelevant once the posterior concentrated. To make the question precise I’d need to say what observation the blur represents, what the text tells us about the clean scene, and what feature of the reconstruction ought to change as a result.

Related work. TextIR already conditions image restoration on a user’s description and demonstrates the approach for tasks including super-resolution and inpainting [reference in Storage]. For the blurry pub, I would vary the reliability of the text at fixed pixels. When the words conflict with visible evidence, which details does the reconstruction recover and which does it invent?

ideas.original_title: B126. Foundational supervised-learning, NLP, and alignment notes
ideas.original_text:
For ESE 3060, I started with the distinction between fitting a predictor to a sample and predicting the label of a fresh observation. In classification, why do we fit a probability vector with cross-entropy when the final decision is just its largest coordinate? The population optimum of log loss gives the conditional class probabilities.

In the NLP notes I wanted to compare learning separate center and context vectors from co-occurrences, as in word2vec, with factoring a transformed word-count matrix. Which singular vectors are we using? The alignment notes give another optimization example, trading off expected reward against KL divergence from the base policy.

ideas.scope: Explanatory question about recovering token and position information from additive embeddings.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The present entry asks how established embeddings work; it has no specified new lower bound or empirical hypothesis.
ideas.impact_reason: A useful learning exercise, with no distinct research contribution yet.
ideas.gate: Choose an unresolved finite-precision or expressivity question before treating this as a paper.

ideas.original_title: B127. Positional embeddings and preservation of information
ideas.original_text:
How are position and token identity incorporated into the initial embedding of a language model? When the two vectors are added, why isn’t their separate information lost? I was hoping for an explanation in terms of high-dimensional geometry.

Related work. The original Transformer adds a position vector to each token embedding and uses sinusoidal features that allow fixed relative offsets to be represented linearly [reference in Storage]. DeBERTa keeps content and relative-position representations separate in its attention scores [reference in Storage]. A comparison can therefore distinguish exact recovery of both inputs from the weaker condition that a layer can compute the position-sensitive interaction it needs.

ideas.scope: Test whether retrieval-margin changes explain rounding-versus-dimension-truncation tradeoffs at a fixed storage budget.

ideas.original_title: B128. Nearest-neighbor retrieval, quantization, and dimension barriers
ideas.original_text:
Ashwin described preprocessing a database by recursively splitting it with hyperplanes. A nearest-neighbor query follows the splits until only a small cluster remains to search. At Pinecone another concern is how to store the retrieval vectors. Why can rounding their coordinates be less damaging than throwing away dimensions? I wanted to ask Hamed about that tradeoff. Matryoshka training approaches it from the other side, by encouraging the first k coordinates to remain useful even when later ones are dropped. I’d like to show Ashwin Kiril’s dimension-barrier paper and ask about the connection to Eric Lei’s work.

Related work. Product quantization compresses a vector with codebooks for its subvectors and uses those codes for approximate distance calculations [reference in Storage]. Matryoshka training instead makes prefixes of a representation useful at several dimensions [reference in Storage]. Bangachev et al. relate retrieval dimension to the margin separating relevant from irrelevant pairs [reference in Storage]. That margin gives a common quantity to inspect after rounding a vector or truncating it.

ideas.scope: Prove operator convergence for a graph estimated from signals in one restricted manifold-sampling model.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Graph identification and continuum approximation introduce coupled errors; a tractable estimation model is not yet selected.
ideas.impact_reason: Would connect learned graphs to consistent downstream operators, but likely within a specialized assumptions regime.

ideas.audit_reason: The inferred-graph operator error is an actual remaining mathematical question, but a joint sampling/estimation regime and rate are unspecified.

ideas.original_title: B129. Graph-signal generative models and continuum consistency
ideas.original_text:
Berkay described inferring an underlying graph from signals observed on it. He also studies how to generate graph signals, and raised the harder question of what model to use for generating the graph itself. I had a related question. If a sequence of graphs approximates a smooth manifold, under what conditions do the signals approach functions on that manifold and the operations we perform on them approach their continuum counterparts? Amit Singer’s work on graph Laplacians was the example I had in mind.

Related work. Dong et al. infer a graph Laplacian by favoring graphs on which the observed signals are smooth [reference in Storage]. Singer analyzes convergence to a manifold Laplacian when the graph is built from sampled points under specified kernel and sampling assumptions [reference in Storage]. If the graph is itself inferred from signals, we additionally have to bound the effect of that estimation on the operator whose limit we study.

ideas.scope: Analyze the estimation cost of guidance terms for one nonstandard flow-matching path and compare against diffusion guidance.
ideas.feasibility_reason: General guidance formulas already exist; identifying a tractable estimator with a distinct advantage remains open.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify when flow guidance is implementable, but broad diffusion-training questions must remain outside the first paper.

ideas.original_title: B130. Diffusion theory, dynamical regularization, and flow matching
ideas.original_text:
Shervin helped me separate two questions about diffusion. Sinho Chewi and collaborators ask how an error in the learned score, together with discretization of the reverse SDE, affects the distribution we sample. Mézard and collaborators ask how long we can train before the score starts fitting individual examples rather than the smoother population distribution. The dynamical regularization paper made the latter concrete for me by relating the empirical score to a smoothed training sample.

I also wanted to understand a difference with deterministic flow matching. Diffusion has a particularly convenient way to guide a sample toward a class because Bayes’ rule relates the conditional score to the unconditional score and a classifier gradient. What carries over if we choose a different path from noise to data?

Related work. Chen et al. bound sampling error given an approximate score [reference in Storage]; Bonnaire et al. instead study when training moves from learning a distribution to memorizing examples [reference in Storage]. Feng et al. already derive guidance for general flow matching [reference in Storage]. For the noise-to-data path I choose, which quantities does their guided velocity require, and can I estimate them as readily as a classifier gradient?

ideas.original_title: B131. Optimization-learning agenda
ideas.original_text:
I would like to understand Adam well enough to see where it could be improved. Which questions are best understood as dynamical systems, stochastic processes or control problems? My reading list began with Peter Bartlett’s and Stephen Wright’s plenaries and Mark Schmidt’s ICML talk. I’d also like to hear Behrad’s and Thomas’s perspectives and see whether Jason Altschuler runs a reading group on this.

Related work. Adam rescales each update using running estimates of first and second gradient moments [reference in Storage]. Reddi, Kale and Kumar give a convex example where Adam fails to converge and a modification that retains longer-term information [reference in Storage]. I would start by following those moment estimates on their example before deciding which part of the dynamics to change.

ideas.title: When a representation becomes readable and steerable
ideas.scope: Compare readout and steering across layers and contexts while checking interference with a second concept.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Open models enable interventions, but causal specificity and novelty beyond linear-representation theory require careful design.
ideas.impact_reason: A reproducible separation or diagnostic would improve representation analysis; small-model layer comparisons alone do not settle the general geometry.
ideas.gate: Find a systematic failure beyond existing readout/steering geometry and show that it predicts held-out context or concept-interference failures.

ideas.audit_reason: The cited primary paper already links reading and steering geometrically; useful novelty must concern cross-context failures or concept interference.

audit_evidence.does_not_resolve: A new context-dependent failure or multi-concept interference result beyond that geometry.

ideas.original_title: B132. When a representation becomes readable and steerable
ideas.original_text:
Misha’s steering talk left me with a geometric question. Why should adding the same vector to many different hidden states move a model from English to French? Why should those two clouds of representations be translates of each other? Shervin’s talk and the linear-representation paper made me want to reconcile the claim that a concept occupies a subspace with two others. Can a linear probe read it out, and can adding a vector actually change it? A good readout alone doesn’t tell me how to intervene.

At which layer does a probe start to work? Is the change sharp enough to detect by subsampling? I also wanted to ask Uday and Shervin about steering several concepts at once, where an intervention intended for one may affect another.

Related work. Park, Choe and Veitch relate linear readout and intervention through a choice of geometry [reference in Storage]; Rimsky et al. measure what changing an activation along a contrast vector actually does [reference in Storage]. For a language switch I would compare probe accuracy and intervention success layer by layer, and ask whether the same intervention preserves a second concept across contexts.

ideas.feasibility_reason: Success needs both a novel learned mechanism and a mathematical payoff; neither is currently available as a starting point.

ideas.original_title: B133. Interpreting new mathematical intuitions
ideas.original_text:
If a model develops a kind of mathematical intuition that humans don’t have, could mechanistic interpretability help us recognize it? I wonder whether some intuitions might be as hard to translate as trying to show someone what four dimensions look like.

Related work. Davies et al. used learned patterns to help mathematicians formulate conjectures [reference in Storage]; Nanda et al. reconstructed a modular-addition algorithm from a small transformer’s weights [reference in Storage]. I would want to know whether reconstructing a mechanism can give a mathematician a usable new conjecture or proof idea when the useful pattern has no familiar name.

ideas.scope: Discover reusable definitions from a fixed formal-proof corpus and evaluate transfer to held-out theorem families.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Formal proof tooling, abstraction search and meaningful held-out transfer are substantial independent workstreams.

ideas.original_title: B266. Finding new definitions across a family of proofs
ideas.original_text:
Behrad asked whether AI had invented anything like a group, a communication channel or a rigid body. Suppose a model has already solved a large collection of problems. Could it recognize that several of its proofs keep rebuilding the same object, then compress those proofs by giving the object a definition? I’d be especially interested in examples where the proofs come from fields that use different language.

How often do people actually introduce concepts that useful? I suggested making a timeline for some abstractions in wide use today, distinguishing when someone introduced one from when other mathematicians started using it. The size of the mathematical community has changed a great deal over the same period.

Related work. DreamCoder learns reusable program abstractions by compressing solutions to earlier tasks and using the resulting library to solve later ones [reference in Storage]. For mathematical definitions, shorter old proofs would be one test. A stronger one would be whether the definition suggests a proof in a different field that the system had not previously solved.

ideas.title: Do unfamiliar words in reasoning traces carry new concepts?
ideas.scope: Intervene on unusual reasoning expressions with multiple controlled paraphrases and matched familiar-expression edits.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Trace interventions are affordable, but obtaining representative unusual expressions and separating semantics from rewrite disruption remain major uncertainties.
ideas.impact_reason: Could distinguish useful internal conventions from dispensable wording, without establishing that the model invented a human-unknown concept.
ideas.gate: Establish semantic equivalence or a controlled task with known concepts; accuracy loss under every attempted paraphrase is not sufficient.
ideas.rated_version: Intervene on unusual reasoning expressions with multiple controlled paraphrases and matched familiar-expression edits.
ideas.audit_reason: Matched edits make a useful experiment; paraphrase sensitivity alone cannot distinguish a novel concept from expression or distribution sensitivity.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Trace edits are cheap; representative expressions and semantic-equivalence controls are the difficult parts of convincing validation.

ideas.original_title: B254. Do unfamiliar words in reasoning traces carry new concepts?
ideas.original_text:
Shayan shared an example that made me wonder about the “alien words” that show up in a model’s reasoning. Does one of those words stand for a new concept that helps the model, or is it as dispensable as some of the self-reflection in a reasoning trace? My first thought was to intervene on the trace: replace each unfamiliar expression with the closest ordinary grammatical wording and see what happens to accuracy. If a replacement works, perhaps the model didn’t need that particular word. If every replacement hurts, I’d want to know whether it is the concept that was useful or whether we simply haven’t found a good translation.

Related work. Lanham et al. tested how a model’s final answer responds to changes in its chain of thought, including paraphrases and introduced mistakes [reference in Storage]. I would compare an unfamiliar expression with several ordinary paraphrases and with edits to familiar expressions of similar length. That last comparison measures how disruptive a rewrite is even when no putatively new concept is involved.

ideas.title: From consumer bins to a continuum
ideas.scope: Derive a continuum limit for a specified binned consumption-rank transition model and test discretization error.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The starting micro-model is not yet specified; rank-only closure may fail, and ML-conference relevance is indirect.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve numerical or conceptual economic modeling if the limit preserves economically relevant transitions.
ideas.gate: Obtain the exact transition model and test whether rank alone gives a closed state description.
ideas.rated_version: Derive a continuum limit for a specified binned consumption-rank transition model and test discretization error.
ideas.audit_reason: Continuum limits are not themselves novel; the source-specific question is whether ranks close a Markov transition law as bins refine.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: The actual transition model and rank-only closure are unspecified; continuum analysis cannot yet be tied to a credible ML-paper result.
ideas.I_note: A valid limit could improve that economic model, with transfer constrained by the specific rank-transition assumptions.
ideas.original_title: B134. From consumer bins to a continuum
ideas.original_text:
In the Sargent–Humphrey talk, why put consumers into percentile bins? I wondered whether we could let the bins get finer and describe a consumer by a quantile of a continuous consumption distribution. Then we’d have to rewrite the micro model, which says what happens to someone who starts in a particular bin. What happens to their rank as they move? An infinite-state Markov process could still run in discrete time. This reminded me of hydrodynamic limits in statistical mechanics, where many local movements have a tractable aggregate description. I would ask Humphrey first what goes wrong in taking this limit, then perhaps Varadhan or Kavita Ramanan about the probability.

Related work. Arellano, Blundell and Bonhomme use conditional quantiles to model earnings transitions and their transmission to consumption [reference in Storage]. Achdou et al. link household decisions to a population distribution in continuous time [reference in Storage]. For the binned model, the issue is whether refining the bins yields a transition law on consumption ranks alone, even if the time step stays fixed.

ideas.original_title: B278. When forecast error undoes consumption smoothing
ideas.original_text:
On the treadmill I started picturing consumption smoothing as averaging the cash I expect to receive in the future. I had in mind a one-sided kernel that puts less weight on more distant payments. But what I would feed into that average is my forecast of the cash flows. I don’t get to average the amounts that will actually arrive.

When I revise those forecasts, could the error wipe out the smoothing I thought I was getting? I’d like to understand when the weighted-average picture makes sense in the first place and how sensitive its conclusion is to the pattern of forecast errors.

Related work. Hall derives a consumption implication from households optimizing under uncertainty: under the paper’s assumptions, predictable information should already be reflected in current marginal utility [reference in Storage]. That gives the kernel analogy a test. Which changes in consumption reflect genuine news about future income, and which reflect forecast errors that were predictable before the revision?

ideas.scope: Calibrate one finite-horizon safety event when changing a controller changes its own trajectory distribution, under explicit overlap assumptions.

ideas.original_title: B135. Robust control with learned dynamics
ideas.original_text:
Could modern work on learning dynamics give us a way back into the Hansen–Sargent problem of making decisions under model misspecification [reference in Storage]? I had in mind the control work around Hamed, George Pappas and Nik Matni, especially Charis Stamouli’s and Thomas Zhang’s defenses. A richer learned model might suggest a better controller. What can we still say about that controller’s behavior when the estimated dynamics are wrong? I’d like to understand whether a finite-sample conformal guarantee could cover a safety event along a trajectory, where the controller’s earlier actions help determine which states it visits next.

Related work. Hansen and Sargent study policies that withstand specified model distortions [reference in Storage]. Dean et al. bound the control cost of learning linear dynamics [reference in Storage], and Lindemann et al. calibrate predictions of external agents’ motion for safe planning [reference in Storage]. Two different robustness benchmarks are worst-case loss over a Wasserstein ball around empirical data [reference in Storage] and hedging under parameter uncertainty in a specified family of price processes [reference in Storage]. Which trajectories can I use for calibration when my own policy changes the states I visit?

ideas.original_title: B136. High-dimensional GMM and useful instrument construction
ideas.original_text:
I spent a morning walk talking through Hansen’s GMM, especially how an instrument turns a conditional moment restriction into an unconditional one. In a high-dimensional problem, which functions of the data should we use as instruments in the first place? I asked Emre whether we could bring together Dobriban–Wager-style asymptotics, Amit Singer’s GMM work with Liane Xu, and Xiaohong Chen’s work on the choice of basis functions. I don’t yet know which calculation would make that connection useful.

Related work. Hansen’s GMM results characterize how to weight a given set of moments [reference in Storage]. Ai and Chen approximate unknown functions in conditional moment models with growing sieves [reference in Storage], and Belloni et al. construct instruments from a large dictionary when the optimal instrument is approximately sparse [reference in Storage]. A useful comparison would ask which approximation or sparsity assumption is plausible for the proposed dictionary before taking a high-dimensional limit.

ideas.scope: Study post-search inference for a learned discontinuity direction under an explicitly specified treatment-assignment mechanism.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Automated search is feasible, but a credible assignment assumption and valid inference after selection are separate unresolved problems.

ideas.original_title: B137. Discovering effective randomization
ideas.original_text:
Natural experiments often get their force from finding a part of an observational dataset where the treatment was effectively randomized. Can we automate any of the work of finding those comparisons? Regression discontinuity made me wonder whether we could learn a direction in which a comparison becomes credible, especially when the running variable is unclear. A balanced-looking subset by itself wouldn’t convince me. I’d want to know what the assignment mechanism was, and how much evidence survives the fact that we searched over directions or subgroups to find it.

Related work. Herlands et al. already search multidimensional observational data for local treatment discontinuities [reference in Storage]. Cattaneo, Frandsen and Titiunik make explicit the assignment assumptions behind randomization inference in a window around a cutoff [reference in Storage]. After searching for a direction, what independent evidence about assignment would justify that comparison, and which observations could still be used to estimate the effect?

ideas.original_title: B258. Geometric matching for treatment effects
ideas.original_text:
What’s the dream scenario for causal inference? For every Robey in the control group, we’d have an identical Robey in the treatment group. We’d know the individual treatment effect, at least for the people in the study. Generalizing beyond them would still take some structure. In practice we can’t clone Robey, so we learn about him by looking at other people, or we average over people and aim for an ATE or a smoothed conditional effect. I asked Behrad whether a geometric matching estimator could bring us closer to that ideal. What would make two people close in the sense that matters for this comparison?

Related work. MALTS learns a distance for matching in which covariates important for predicting outcomes receive more weight, and uses matched groups to estimate conditional average treatment effects [reference in Storage]. In the Robey example, closeness in such a metric gives a plausible comparison unit. Saying what it reveals about one person’s missing potential outcome would require additional assumptions.

ideas.original_title: B138. Natural experiments with network effects
ideas.original_text:
When Twitter began showing me automatically translated posts, I found myself reading people from communities I hadn’t previously encountered. Could we use the change as a natural experiment? Did people just read different posts, or did they start replying to different people? One person’s response could change what others see.

My main interest is which statistical tools economists are missing when standard assumptions for natural experiments fail on a network. If we can’t obtain the platform data, a controllable artificial world like those Percy Liang’s group studies might let us try a method. I’d ask Sikata or Duncan which real question the method ought to answer, and look at Shuangning’s work with Stefan.

Related work. Aronow and Samii link an assignment design and a definition of network exposure to the causal contrast one can estimate [reference in Storage]; Li and Wager analyze treatment effects under interference on random graphs [reference in Storage]. For translation I would need the rollout rule as well as the pre-rollout network: seeing a translated post is one exposure, while replying to a new community changes who can be exposed next.

ideas.scope: Characterize identification and estimation of a population treatment effect under a specified referral-sampling mechanism.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A finite-network toy model permits theory and simulation; transport assumptions and recruitment information must be made explicit.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify what extra data referral surveys need, with useful identification limits for a neglected sampling design.

ideas.audit_reason: Referral-sampling correction does not identify a causal estimand; recruitment, treatment assignment, and transport assumptions must be separately explicit.

ideas.original_title: B139. Causal inference from referral-based survey recruitment
ideas.original_text:
At La Colombe in Dilworth Park I met a Yale MBA student trying to get more people to take a survey. He wanted respondents to forward it to their friends. I hadn’t seen data collected this way. If who enters the sample depends on who knows whom, under what conditions can we consistently or efficiently estimate a causal effect in the population? What would we need to know about how the invitations spread? Hanan suggested talking to Karun. Shuangning Li’s work on causal inference with networks also came to mind.

Related work. Volz and Heckathorn use network degree to relate recruitment to sampling probability under a random-walk approximation [reference in Storage]. Gile treats finite populations and sampling without replacement [reference in Storage]. Those results concern who enters the sample. For the causal effect I would separately ask what assumptions identify the effect among recruits and what invitation, refusal, or network information would let me transport it to the intended population.

ideas.original_title: B140. Synthetic economic agents over time
ideas.original_text:
Diebold asked whether LLM-generated people could substitute for some observations of real people in an economic simulation. Getting a plausible answer to a survey question is one thing. Can a simulated person make a plausible sequence of decisions as circumstances change? He was especially interested in the time-series case and suggested talking to Karun Adusimilli. How much real data would it take to correct a simulator’s errors?

John Mulvey’s interest in simulating a market with LLMs made me wonder about a narrower use. I asked Behrad whether backtests already model the decisions of individual participants and, if so, whether replacing some of them with LLM agents would tell us anything useful about a strategy. I’d be more persuaded by a revealing stress scenario than by a precise market forecast. B144 asks a different question about evaluating the argument for a policy.

Related work. Horton runs economic experiments with simulated agents [reference in Storage], Park et al. compare interview-based agents with the people they represent [reference in Storage], and Sun et al. train behavioral simulators using verbal feedback [reference in Storage]. Bashari et al. combine synthetic and real observations while controlling inferential error [reference in Storage]. Could a real person’s follow-up decisions detect simulator bias when an earlier choice changes their circumstances? For the backtest, Cont and Vuletić use generated market moves to choose hedge instruments and ratios [reference in Storage], which gives me a benchmark for what adding individual traders would buy.

ideas.title: World models and rational inattention
ideas.scope: Compare representation loss and decision loss in a small rational-inattention model with a fixed payoff and information budget.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A finite or linear-Gaussian model is manageable; linking it convincingly to JEPA-style training remains uncertain.
ideas.impact_reason: Could show precisely when predictive representations discard decision-relevant information.
ideas.gate: Produce a new separation or decision-aware objective beyond standard information-bottleneck formulations.
ideas.rated_version: Compare representation loss and decision loss in a small rational-inattention model with a fixed payoff and information budget.
ideas.audit_reason: A fixed payoff makes the JEPA/rational-inattention comparison concrete; generic representation compression is not by itself a new economic result.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Finite or Gaussian decision models are manageable with modest resources; the challenge is a new separation from information-bottleneck and rational-inattention baselines.
ideas.I_note: The scoped result could distinguish predictive compression from decision sufficiency, with broad analogy alone adding little novelty.
ideas.original_title: B141. World models and rational inattention
ideas.original_text:
A person doesn’t need every pixel in a scene to decide what to do next. Is there a connection between what a JEPA-style world model learns to ignore and what an economic agent ignores when attention is costly? Which details can a world model discard while still supporting the same decision? Which information would a rationally inattentive agent actually pay to acquire [reference in Storage]?

I wondered whether this could give someone with Hamed’s information-theory background a way into economics. A related question in September was when a person with limited computation should use someone else’s forecast of one quantity to help predict a different one.

Related work. I-JEPA learns representations by predicting masked parts of an image in embedding space [reference in Storage]. Sims instead chooses information subject to a capacity constraint and evaluates it by the decisions it supports [reference in Storage]. I would fix a decision and its payoff, then ask whether details discarded by the representation are also details an agent would decline to pay for.

ideas.scope: Characterize coherent forecasts when announcing a probability changes effort and therefore the probability of the event.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A restricted response model is tractable, but fixed-point reporting and its incentive conflict already have direct precedents.

ideas.original_title: B275. A forecast that changes the probability it predicts
ideas.original_text:
Junu asked me the probability that we would keep our proof-verification submission in. He wanted to know whether it was worth putting more time into the paper. But his effort would affect whether we withdrew it. If I told him 80 percent and that answer changed his decision, what probability had I just given him?

I wonder whether a coherent answer would have to be a fixed point. After Junu hears the number and chooses how much to work, the probability of keeping the submission in would have to agree with the number I announced. I had a similar worry about behavioral research more broadly. Once a finding becomes known, people can change the behavior that produced it.

Related work. Perdomo et al. model predictions that change the distribution on which they will be evaluated [reference in Storage]. Oesterheld et al. address the binary-report problem directly: a fixed-point report agrees with the event probability it induces, and a proper scoring rule can give an expert an incentive to report something else [reference in Storage]. In the submission example, Junu’s response to the announced probability is precisely the map one would need to estimate.

Related work. Perdomo et al. model predictions that change the distribution on which they will be evaluated [reference in Storage]. Oesterheld et al. address the binary-report problem directly: a fixed-point report agrees with the event probability it induces, and a proper scoring rule can give an expert an incentive to report something else [reference in Storage]. In the submission example, Junu’s response to the announced probability is precisely the map one would need to estimate.

ideas.title: Beyond simple mean-field interactions
ideas.scope: Analyze one heterogeneous interaction model in which a graph-dependent aggregate improves on a scalar mean field.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Graphon and sparse-network limits are established fields; a useful new observable and tractable interaction class remain to be chosen.
ideas.impact_reason: Could identify behavior lost by averaging, but a narrowly solvable model would have a specialized audience.
ideas.gate: Choose one economic or learning system and demonstrate that its key effect disappears under the simpler mean field.
ideas.rated_version: Analyze one heterogeneous interaction model in which a graph-dependent aggregate improves on a scalar mean field.
ideas.audit_reason: The broad question is substantive, but graphon and sparse-graph limits already exist; a specific observable beyond these precedents is needed.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: No economic or learning system and new observable have been fixed; existing graph limits do not supply that missing choice.

ideas.original_title: B142. Beyond simple mean-field interactions
ideas.original_text:
In a mean-field model each agent can interact with the rest of the population through an average. What kinds of economic behavior are lost in that simplification? I was thinking about the passage from Curie–Weiss to Sherrington–Kirkpatrick in statistical physics. Can richer interactions among heterogeneous agents still leave us with something tractable in the aggregate? I first encountered mean-field games through Alex Vladimirsky at Cornell. Philippe Rigollet’s survey gave me a separate analogy, with tokens interacting through repeated self-attention. I would like to know what takes the place of the interaction and the observable in each case.

Related work. Carmona et al. let different agents face different neighborhood aggregates through a graphon [reference in Storage]; Lacker and Soret show in a particular dynamic game how sparse and dense graphs yield different limits [reference in Storage]. The interacting-particle description of self-attention supplies a second comparison [reference in Storage]: the question is which household, neighbor or token states determine the interaction, and which aggregate still predicts the outcome of interest.

ideas.title: Purchasing power after an AI productivity gain
ideas.scope: Combine an automation task model with heterogeneous consumption baskets to track purchasing-power changes across households.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Requires substantial economic modeling and calibration, with no clear new ML contribution or verified data setup.
ideas.impact_reason: Could illuminate distributional effects of AI productivity, but the scoped contribution is primarily economics.
ideas.gate: Establish a novel mechanism beyond existing automation-incidence models and select an appropriate venue.
ideas.rated_version: Combine an automation task model with heterogeneous consumption baskets to track purchasing-power changes across households.
ideas.audit_reason: A model of purchasing power is explicitly requested, but this is still a broad economic agenda with no distinct ML-paper contribution.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: The economic agenda lacks a specified new mechanism and verified calibration setup, with particularly weak readiness for an ML-conference evaluation.
ideas.I_note: A credible distributional purchasing-power result could matter in economics; its value is not reduced merely because the venue fit is poor.
ideas.original_title: B279. Purchasing power after an AI productivity gain
ideas.original_text:
Behrad asked what happens to people’s ability to make a living if AI makes goods much cheaper to produce. I brought up comparative advantage and thought about asking Francis Diebold. Behrad then pointed out that firms still need customers who can afford the output. If income becomes more concentrated at the same time as prices fall, who ends up able to buy more?

I’d like an economic model in which we can follow both effects of the productivity gain. Knowing which tasks people retain doesn’t yet tell me what the income from those tasks can buy.

Related work. Acemoglu and Restrepo separate the labor displacement from automating existing tasks from the demand for labor created by new tasks [reference in Storage]. To answer Behrad’s question, I would take the wage and employment changes implied by a task model and combine them with changes in the prices of the goods different households actually buy.

ideas.title: Economic analogues of generalization beyond support
ideas.scope: Determine what fixed preferences, information, or dynamics imply about behavior outside previously observed environments.
ideas.feasibility_reason: This is a genuine extrapolation question, but the informative restriction and distinct result beyond revealed-preference theory remain unspecified.
ideas.impact_reason: A useful identification result could connect learned-agent extrapolation with economic reasoning under policy changes.
ideas.gate: Choose a concrete off-support decision and show what the stated invariances identify beyond existing demand bounds.
ideas.rated_version: Determine what fixed preferences, information, or dynamics imply about behavior outside previously observed environments.
ideas.audit_reason: Restored numerical scores: the source explicitly asks what restrictions predict off support; it is broader than an explanatory analogy.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Off-support behavior is a clear motivation, but the invariant restriction and concrete decision target still need selection before proof work.

ideas.original_title: B143. Economic analogues of generalization beyond support
ideas.original_text:
Thomas TCK Zhang asked whether a model can learn behavior beyond the support of its pretraining. If we treat a model as an economic agent, is there an analogous question in microeconomics? How do we reason about what an agent will do in an economic environment it has never encountered? I’d like to know whether the analogy with control buys us anything.

Related work. Blundell, Browning and Crawford use revealed preference to bound demand after a price change, without extrapolating a fitted demand curve [reference in Storage]. Lucas explains why a change in policy can also change the decision rule one hoped to extrapolate [reference in Storage]. For the learning analogy I would specify what remains fixed across environments—preferences, information or dynamics—and ask what those restrictions alone predict off support.

ideas.title: Agentic assessment of economic hypotheses
ideas.scope: Evaluate retrieval-assisted critiques of historical economic forecasts using strictly contemporaneous evidence and separate analogy-quality labels.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Public forecast archives support a pilot; temporal leakage and credible evaluation of causal arguments are substantial bottlenecks.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve evidence discipline in forecasting, while correct outcomes alone would not validate a policy mechanism.
ideas.gate: Use a prospectively held-out outcome set or otherwise defensible knowledge cutoff; date instructions and self-reported ignorance do not establish no leakage.
ideas.rated_version: Evaluate retrieval-assisted critiques of historical economic forecasts using strictly contemporaneous evidence and separate analogy-quality labels.
ideas.audit_reason: Dated retrieval restricts the evidence supplied, not the model knowledge already learned; analogy quality and forecast calibration need separate labels.

audit_evidence.supports: Financial factual recall can violate stated historical cutoffs; date instructions and self-reports are unreliable leakage controls.
audit_evidence.does_not_resolve: A leakage-free benchmark: unsuccessful recall also cannot certify absence of relevant hindsight knowledge.

ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Public forecasts are accessible, but credible pre-outcome model knowledge and independent analogy-quality labels make evaluation the limiting step.
ideas.I_note: Better evidence discipline would help economic forecasting, while accurate outcomes do not validate the narrative causal mechanism.
ideas.original_title: B144. Agentic assessment of economic hypotheses
ideas.original_text:
When an economist predicts the effect of a policy, I want to know the economic context, the proposed policy and the predicted effect. Could an agent help assess the argument? Suppose the forecast concerns stagflation. There may be historical periods with stagnation and others with inflation, yet very few that look exactly like the proposed setting. Could the agent find relevant episodes, explain which parts of each analogy hold, and make a case both for and against the forecast? Behrad’s work on debate made me think of the last step. I wondered about testing such a system on past forecasts whose outcomes we know.

Related work. Halawi et al. combine retrieval and reasoning to forecast events, scoring predictions against their outcomes [reference in Storage]; Moniri, Hassani and Dobriban use an independent model to judge debates between language models [reference in Storage]. I would give an agent only information available before a historical forecast and assess the choice of comparison episodes separately from forecast accuracy: correctly predicting inflation would not establish that the proposed policy caused it.

ideas.title: Why competitors share or withhold information
ideas.scope: Study information disclosure by competing learning agents in one market-entry game.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A small game is tractable; connecting disclosure to learning and finding a result beyond classical information-sharing theory remain unresolved.
ideas.impact_reason: Could explain a specific interaction between information release, entry, and competition; the cart-to-frontier-AI analogy alone adds little.
ideas.gate: Identify one learning-specific mechanism absent from the existing disclosure model.
ideas.rated_version: Study information disclosure by competing learning agents in one market-entry game.
ideas.audit_reason: The source contains market-design research questions, but the common-information game and welfare target are not specified; a single setting is essential.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: A small disclosure game is tractable, but the learning-specific mechanism and welfare comparison are not yet defined.
ideas.I_note: A new learning-entry interaction would be substantive; classical disclosure incentives alone would not be distinctive.
ideas.original_title: B145. Why competitors share or withhold information
ideas.original_text:
A halal-cart owner near Drexel told me about finding a place for his cart. How could someone entering that market tell whether the price for two parking spaces was reasonable? As far as he knew, there was no central source to consult. A newcomer could ask an incumbent, who might have little incentive to answer. One vendor told me that the hours a cart could operate differed from street to street. A spot near 34th Street might bring more foot traffic but fewer hours to sell. Could I tell from the rents what vendors are willing to pay for each advantage? That made me think of AI companies that compete on cost and performance yet publish technical reports or release some models. What features of a market make it worthwhile for competitors to share information? Would requiring them to disclose it change how the market develops?

Related work. Rosen’s hedonic model explains why prices vary with bundles of attributes without making a rent gradient alone a demand curve [reference in Storage]. Shapiro shows how rivals’ incentives to exchange cost information depend on the form of competition [reference in Storage]. For a cart location or a model release, I would first identify who holds the information and whether revealing it helps a rival enter, changes a price, or does both.

ideas.scope: Predict joint research output beyond individual-record baselines using only information available before first collaboration.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Bibliographic data permit a benchmark; defining complementarity independently of prestige and selection is the main obstacle.
ideas.impact_reason: A credible prospective measure could improve collaboration recommendations, but observed productivity cannot establish partnership causality.
ideas.gate: Use temporal and author-disjoint evaluation; control topic, career-stage and selection baselines, and describe results as predictive rather than causal.
ideas.rated_version: Predict joint research output beyond individual-record baselines using only information available before first collaboration.
ideas.audit_reason: Pre-collaboration prediction is testable; observational selection and changing team composition prevent interpreting residual output as causal partnership value.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Temporal bibliographic prediction is buildable; selection, prestige and career-stage controls are the main obstacle to convincing interpretation.

ideas.original_title: B146. Predicting complementary research partnerships
ideas.original_text:
Could we have predicted the productivity of Kahneman and Tversky together, or Hansen and Sargent, from what we knew about them separately? Academic hiring usually assesses one person at a time. What would we need to know about two people’s work to recognize a promising partnership before they’ve written anything together?

Related work. Anderson and Richards-Shubik jointly model economists’ choice of collaborators and their research output [reference in Storage]. A prospective test would use only work available before two people met, and distinguish predicting that they will collaborate from predicting that their joint work will outperform what their individual records suggest.

ideas.title: Representational convergence and algorithmic herding
ideas.scope: Test whether representation similarity predicts correlated decisions and losses in a controlled market simulator.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Open models and synthetic markets permit controlled comparisons; separating representation effects from common inputs needs careful interventions.
ideas.impact_reason: An identified link between representations and common trading exposure would improve agent evaluation; simulation alone does not establish systemic financial risk.
ideas.gate: Produce an intervention that changes representation similarity without trivially changing task quality.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether representation similarity predicts correlated decisions and losses in a controlled market simulator.
ideas.audit_reason: Representational similarity need not imply identical decisions; matched information and portfolio constraints must isolate a relation beyond behavioral similarity.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Open models and market simulators are accessible, but an intervention isolating representation similarity from common inputs and task quality is difficult.
ideas.I_note: An identified representation-to-exposure link would improve evaluation of correlated agent decisions, while simulated losses do not establish systemic risk.
ideas.original_title: B147. Representational convergence and algorithmic herding
ideas.original_text:
If models trained in different places converge on similar representations, will they also tend to make the same decisions? I raised the question with Thomas and Ivi because trading systems that look independent might still take correlated positions. What would have to be true for the similarity inside the models to show up as a common exposure in the market?

Related work. Huh et al. document alignment between representations learned by different models [reference in Storage]. Kleinberg and Raghavan show in a hiring model how reliance on a common ranking can correlate decisions [reference in Storage]. To connect the two in a market, I would compare internal alignment with agreement in trades on the same information, then check whether portfolio constraints amplify or undo that agreement.

ideas.title: Useful cooperation and harmful coordination
ideas.scope: In one repeated trading game, vary information or coordination channels and measure competitive efficiency and any task-specific cooperation benefit.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A small multi-agent experiment is feasible, but a welfare target and incentive-sensitive mechanism must distinguish it from existing tacit-collusion studies.
ideas.impact_reason: A clear tradeoff in one game could guide multi-agent evaluation; general coordination safety claims require substantially broader evidence.
ideas.gate: Define welfare and a useful cooperative task, reproduce no-communication collusion baselines, and distinguish collusion from correlated mistakes.
ideas.rated_version: In one repeated trading game, vary information or coordination channels and measure competitive efficiency and any task-specific cooperation benefit.
ideas.audit_reason: Tacit trading collusion without communication is already demonstrated; communication limits cannot be presumed to eliminate harmful coordination.

audit_evidence.supports: Informed RL traders can sustain collusive profits without communication; information rents and learning biases provide mechanisms.
audit_evidence.does_not_resolve: A new intervention preserving useful cooperation, or guarantees across market designs.

ideas.original_title: B178. Useful cooperation and harmful coordination
ideas.original_text:
What happens when many AI agents start trading in the same market? They could learn similar representations and make the same mistake at the same time, even if they never communicate. That’s one reason I want a better account of their interactions than we can get by evaluating each trader separately (B147). Collusion raises a different question. In discussing this with Hamed, I kept coming back to the fact that some tasks need agents to cooperate. What interactions should they be allowed to use, and what would count as their working together to evade a restriction or harm someone else? I’d like to know which limits on communication or changes in incentives leave the useful cooperation possible.

Related work. Pricing algorithms can sustain supracompetitive prices in simulated repeated competition without explicit communication [reference in Storage]; Dou, Goldstein and Ji study tacit collusion among trading algorithms in a simulated financial market [reference in Storage]. Neither identical orders nor shared losses alone diagnose collusion. I would ask what happens to trading behavior under a change in information, incentives, or the ability to coordinate.

ideas.title: Venture investing with no realized outcome data
ideas.scope: Derive partial-identification bounds for an unusual asset using synthetic predictions and explicitly imperfect comparables.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The statistical formulation is possible; validating transport from observed firms to an unprecedented firm is fundamentally difficult.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify what synthetic valuation can establish, but a toy bound may have limited valuation relevance.
ideas.gate: State a defensible link between comparable-firm errors and the target asset.
ideas.rated_version: Derive partial-identification bounds for an unusual asset using synthetic predictions and explicitly imperfect comparables.
ideas.audit_reason: Synthetic valuations do not create outcome information; a transport restriction on errors of genuinely comparable firms is indispensable.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Partial-identification algebra is possible, but defensible comparables and evidence for transport to the target firm are the binding limitations.

ideas.original_title: B148. Venture investing with no realized outcome data
ideas.original_text:
How does a venture investor make a principled decision before the outcome exists? Calling this a problem with zero data can obscure what evidence we do have about earlier companies. What is missing may be an earlier company sufficiently like this one. I wondered whether synthetic observations could help value an illiquid private asset, and what real evidence would be needed to debias that valuation. Generating a thousand guesses at the same price wouldn’t by itself tell us how far off they are.

Related work. Cochrane corrects for the selective observation of venture outcomes when estimating returns [reference in Storage]. Prediction-powered inference uses measured outcomes to correct prediction errors for a specified population quantity [reference in Storage]. To price one unusual firm, I would have to justify why errors on the available comparables inform this firm’s error; extra simulated prices alone supply no such link.

ideas.title: Human judgment when financial models outrun comprehension
ideas.scope: Test whether elicited investor beliefs retain predictive value after trading decisions are delegated to bots.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Requires suitable participants or existing delegation data; a simulator cannot by itself answer the human-judgment question.
ideas.impact_reason: Could reveal when human expertise complements automated decisions, within the tested delegation setting.
ideas.gate: Secure an evaluation with measured human beliefs and independently observed decisions.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether elicited investor beliefs retain predictive value after trading decisions are delegated to bots.
ideas.audit_reason: Human-versus-delegated behavior is a genuine comparison, but paired decisions and an operational investor-judgment measure are not currently available.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Matched human beliefs and delegated trading decisions are not available; suitable participants or existing data are required before validation can proceed.
ideas.I_note: A clean test of retained human judgment could inform financial human-AI collaboration, within the particular delegation setting.
ideas.original_title: B149. Human judgment when financial models outrun comprehension
ideas.original_text:
Markus Brunnermeier’s Jackson Hole paper on AI in finance and Raghuram Rajan’s discussion led me to ask what happens to human judgment when the instruments we use begin to elude our understanding. In finance the gap can matter to the institutions responsible for economic stability, as well as to the person making the decision. Where does justified confidence in a model begin to outrun what we understand about it?

Could we make explicit some of the judgments a fundamental investor makes about other people’s behavior, while automating the quantitative part of the analysis? I would want to know whose psychology the resulting model is meant to capture. Would the same judgments still carry information if most people delegated their trades to bots?

Related work. Brunnermeier asks how agentic AI changes financial markets and the institutions charged with their stability [reference in Storage]; Rajan’s discussion distinguishes a system’s ability to anticipate human responses from a human’s ability to anticipate the system [reference in Storage]. For an investor’s judgment about other traders, I would test whether it predicts behavior when humans place the trades, then whether it retains predictive value when those same humans delegate the decision.

ideas.original_title: B276. Dismissal rules for competing investment desks
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a fund has several competing desks and can tolerate only so much loss in a year. I heard about two ways it might decide which managers to dismiss. Under one rule a manager can be dismissed for falling sufficiently far below the benchmark. Under the other she can be dismissed for landing near the bottom of the firm’s own rankings. What bets will a manager take once she knows which rule applies?

I can imagine hugging the benchmark instead of making a good longer-term bet, or leaving after a particularly good year. Which dismissal rule would the firm want once it accounts for those responses? I have a related question about compensation. What purpose does the fixed management fee serve alongside a share of the gains?

Related work. Brown, Goetzmann and Park relate managers’ interim performance to subsequent portfolio risk and fund survival [reference in Storage]. Goetzmann, Ingersoll and Ross value performance-fee contracts with high-water marks [reference in Storage]. The experiment I have in mind would fix the compensation contract and vary only whether dismissal depends on the external benchmark or on the returns of the other desks.

ideas.scope: Determine what a cutoff comparison can reveal about overstatement of winning estimates, separately from the causal effect of winning.

ideas.original_title: B150. The winner's curse near a cutoff
ideas.original_text:
I wanted to explain the winner’s curse and ask whether a regression discontinuity could help us study it. The distinction I’d have to get straight first is between an unusually high winning estimate and the effect of winning itself. If an award goes to everyone just above a cutoff, comparing people on either side might tell us what receiving the award did. What would it tell us about how much the winning estimates overstated their value?

Related work. Andrews, Kitagawa and McCloskey study inference for an option selected using noisy estimates [reference in Storage]. In a regression discontinuity design, by contrast, the cutoff can identify a local effect of receiving treatment under suitable assignment assumptions [reference in Storage]. To measure overstatement of the winning estimate I would need a second measure of underlying value, or an explicit model of its measurement error, separate from what the award itself changes.

ideas.original_title: B151. Delivery-platform incentives, welfare, and physical risk
ideas.original_text:
A delivery incident made me think about the workers who bear time pressure and physical risk to provide convenience to customers. Are these the kinds of important problems that applied mathematicians should try to formulate? How do the worker’s circumstances affect the trade-off?

Related work. Useche, Robayo and Orozco-Fontalvo relate riders’ reported crashes to fatigue and working conditions in a survey [reference in Storage]. Lee et al. also find that a rider’s own higher-pressure days are associated with riskier riding and more near misses [reference in Storage]. To ask whose convenience is being paid for, I would want variation in delivery deadlines or pay that lets us measure the same policy’s effects on injury risk and take-home earnings.

ideas.original_title: B152. The economic purpose of a local sugar tax
ideas.original_text:
I got a surprisingly large bill at Malai, the ice-cream shop off Rittenhouse Square, and asked the cashier about it. That conversation left me with wondering why Philadelphia has a sugar tax and what it is meant to accomplish.

Related work. Philadelphia introduced its sweetened-beverage distribution tax to fund services including pre-K [reference in Storage]; an expensive ice-cream purchase alone does not establish that the tax was charged. Seiler, Tuchman and Yao trace how the Philadelphia tax affected prices and purchases, including shopping outside the city [reference in Storage]. Funding services and changing consumption are distinct objectives, with different evidence for each.

ideas.original_title: B153. Statistical finance beyond a trading strategy
ideas.original_text:
I asked where statistics could help in academic finance. Francis Diebold’s work on volatility, forecast evaluation and connections among banks gave me some examples. I am particularly interested in what an interpretable model can tell us in an economic environment outside the historical sample. Trading isn’t the only use for that kind of analysis. A financial engineer might instead design a product that helps someone pay for college at a particular time.

For trading strategies, I asked Behrad whether there is a scaling law from a small academic backtest to performance when real money trades at scale. He pointed out a selection problem. A trader might keep a strategy private while it works and publish it only once the opportunity has passed. What could we infer about scaling from the strategies that make it into journals?

Related work. Diebold and Yılmaz use forecast-error variance decompositions to measure connectedness across financial firms [reference in Storage], an application with a different target from trading profits. For the trading question, McLean and Pontiff distinguish post-publication decay from out-of-sample decay [reference in Storage], while Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz estimate execution costs from actual trades [reference in Storage]. Neither a published return series nor trading costs on their own reveal which profitable strategies were never disclosed.

ideas.original_title: B277. Pricing a contract on who leads during a match
ideas.original_text:
Suppose I want a contract that pays if England leads Argentina at any point in a match. England could lead early and still lose, so its chance of winning at the final whistle doesn’t pin down what the contract is worth. How much of the usual options-pricing argument would carry over to this prediction market?

I wondered whether a single price or Elo rating summarizes enough about a team. Two teams with similar ratings could pose very different matchups for Argentina. What would the state have to include for us to price a claim on the path of the score?

Related work. Dixon and Robinson model scoring intensities during a soccer match using the score, time remaining, and team-specific attack and defense parameters [reference in Storage]. Such a process gives a model probability for England ever taking the lead. Turning that probability into a traded price requires an additional assumption about risk, liquidity or replication.

ideas.original_title: B154. Bayesian and frequentist perspectives in economics
ideas.original_text:
What is the status of frequentist versus Bayesian econometrics? Microeconomic reasoning feels naturally Bayesian to me, and I was thinking of Aaron Roth’s work on agents with beliefs. Does that intuition carry over to how an econometrician would fit or assess a model of those agents?

Related work. Manski shows how eliciting subjective probabilities helps distinguish what a decision maker believes from what they prefer [reference in Storage]. Sims considers a different use of probability: representing a policymaker’s uncertainty about economic models and forecasts [reference in Storage]. In one example I would label whose belief each probability represents before asking whether Bayesian or frequentist evaluation better answers the econometrician’s question.

ideas.original_title: B155. Approachable problems in optimal control and mean-field games
ideas.original_text:
I asked Ananya Parashar, who had worked with Ludovic Tangpi, which problems in optimal control a newcomer might reasonably try. I kept hearing people in finance talk about mean-field games and forward–backward equations. I’d like to understand an economic example well enough to see where the interesting mathematical problem begins.

Related work. Carmona, Fouque and Sun solve a game in which each bank chooses how fast to borrow from or lend to a central bank. Its incentive depends on its reserves relative to the other banks’ average [reference in Storage]. I could work out one bank’s response at finite population size and then see what becomes simpler in the mean-field limit.

ideas.original_title: B219. Predictive models and first-principles explanations are complements
ideas.original_text:
While the people working from first principles are deriving a model of the economy, policymakers still have decisions to make. An econometric model fitted to observations can help them. And if the first-principles derivation succeeds, I hope it will improve the models we fit to data. I don’t see why the two groups shouldn’t be rooting for each other.

I suggested an example from video prediction to Behrad. A simple dynamics model might get the gross motion of the objects right. For something it handles badly, say what happens when two objects collide, could we learn the missing part from data?

Related work. Lucas showed why an observed economic relationship can change when a policy changes the decisions people make [reference in Storage]. For the video example, Ajay and colleagues combined a physics simulator with a learned interaction model for contact-rich manipulation, including planar pushing [reference in Storage]. The latter is a concrete precedent for learning what a simulator misses; predictive accuracy alone would still not settle the effect of an economic intervention.
