ideas.original_title: B156. AI-assisted first-principles models
ideas.original_text:
At Fine Hall I saw the poster for Felix Otto’s lectures on magnetization ripples in thin films. What appealed to me was the prospect of explaining a complicated physical pattern from a model of the underlying interactions. Alongside questions about safety and risk control, I’d like to use AI to build models of that kind.

Could we try something similar in economics? I would like to understand when a bottom-up account of how people make decisions gives a prediction that a top-down statistical model, such as a vector autoregression, misses. And if the derivation really does require a great deal of mathematical labor, will one mathematician direct many agents, or will several mathematicians work together?

Related work. Ignat and Otto derive a stochastic equation for magnetization ripples from a micromagnetic model [reference in Storage]; Schmidt and Lipson instead infer candidate physical laws from observations [reference in Storage]. In economics, Del Negro and Schorfheide use an equilibrium model as a prior for a VAR [reference in Storage]. An AI-assisted derivation would earn its keep if a stated assumption about individual decisions improved a prediction on data withheld from both models.

ideas.original_title: B157. How sensitive is economic model assessment?
ideas.original_text:
In Zhiheng You’s seminar I wondered how much a judgment about an economic model depends on the other predictions we regard as plausible. Take the certainty equivalent of a lottery with two prizes. It should lie between the prizes and increase when the lottery becomes more attractive. There are still many functions with those properties. We can draw alternatives from a constrained Gaussian process, but why that distribution? Wayne suggested that a tabular foundation model might supply another prior.

If we keep the economic restrictions but change the distribution over eligible predictors, how much does the model’s restrictiveness change? Completeness instead uses error on the test-data distribution. In what sense are these two measures complementary? The same issue arises in supply and demand because a natural prior in structural coordinates need not look natural after we pass to reduced form.

Related work. Completeness measures how much predictable variation a model captures in observed data [reference in Storage]; restrictiveness asks how well it can fit a specified distribution of alternatives [reference in Storage]. Fudenberg, Gao and You already vary the GP kernel and replace GP draws with spline draws, preserving the qualitative lottery-model ranking in their checks [reference in Storage]. Would a learned prior or a prior chosen in structural coordinates change that ranking while leaving the economic restrictions and the data for assessing completeness fixed?

ideas.original_title: B242. Municipal spending transparency and its actual effects
ideas.original_text:
A post about Fair Lawn’s mayoral election made me wonder how much of a town’s spending a resident can actually understand. Could a visualizer show where the money came from, what it paid for, and which decisions an elected official could have made differently? Philadelphia’s fireworks and subway entrances were the examples that got me thinking about this. If residents had better information, would it change what officials spend, or does the research give us reason to expect a smaller effect?

Related work. Seven coordinated field experiments found no overall effect of typical nonpartisan information campaigns on voter behavior [reference in Storage]. In Ugandan local governments, giving politicians financial information and training improved oversight and services only where local leaders were not aligned with the dominant party [reference in Storage]. For a town budget display, I would therefore distinguish whether residents understand a decision, whether they act on it, and whether the next budget changes.

ideas.original_title: B227. Human mathematical ability and the changing role of proof work
ideas.original_text: I think of Hugo Duminil-Copin solving, one after another, the percolation problems Michael Aizenman had put on his blackboard. The questions are concrete enough to describe. That takes nothing away from the depth of thought it took to solve them. Some of my own work uses tools from much the same part of probability, analysis, and combinatorics, and I find I can live with a model taking over some of that proof work. Then I open a paper on the Langlands program to a random page and have a rather different feeling about what it means for a human being to do mathematics.

ideas.scope: Model delegation separately for formulation, execution, and verification under scarce AI compute.

ideas.original_title: B248. Human contributions under scarce AI compute
ideas.original_text:
I can still do mathematics in a world with Terry Tao in it. Could something like comparative advantage also leave room for human work in a world with very capable AI? Even if a model could make conceptual breakthroughs, its compute would still be scarce. For an urgent frontier problem, asking a human to work alongside it might only slow it down. There is also work in which we supply something the system needs to know: how a design feels to use, for example, or whether a course of physical therapy has made it easier to move. Physical intuition might matter in engineering too, though a model may already have picked some of it up from human data.

Rakesh’s question about substitution and complementarity made me wonder about dividing up a single task. When writing a paper I might delegate coding and proof writing while keeping formulation and verification. If different tasks have the same recurring stages, could Meena’s model allow a different rate of delegation at each stage?

Related work. Korinek and Suh study how the pace of automation relative to capital accumulation changes the demand for human labor [reference in Storage]. At the level of one workflow, Jagadeesan, Hashimoto, and Kleinberg model how much a person uses an LLM and how much they post-process its output in response to detection [reference in Storage]. The stage-specific question is whether different delegation rates for formulation, execution, and verification would reveal complementarity that a single rate conceals.

ideas.title: AI for evaluating economic and financial narratives
ideas.scope: Extract explicit predictions from dated investor narratives and test whether evidence-based assessments improve forecast calibration beyond simple textual and financial baselines.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Public commentary is available, but reliable outcome labels and protection against model hindsight are substantial evaluation work.
ideas.impact_reason: Could make narrative assessment testable; influence on portfolios and market prices remains a separate, harder causal question.
ideas.gate: Confirm enough resolvable dated claims and demonstrably pre-outcome model checkpoints; compare forecast calibration and evidence grounding with existing finance benchmarks.
ideas.rated_version: Extract explicit predictions from dated investor narratives and test whether evidence-based assessments improve forecast calibration beyond simple textual and financial baselines.

audit_evidence.does_not_establish: That a particular narrative corpus is temporally clean.

ideas.original_title: AI for evaluating economic and financial narratives
ideas.original_text:
Use AI to evaluate the credibility or plausibility of narratives, especially those that investors and traders use to make portfolio decisions. Decompose a narrative into factual premises, proposed causal mechanisms, and testable predictions; assess the supporting evidence, competing explanations, and uncertainty. Separately, study how narratives spread, influence portfolio choices, and affect financial markets. A central distinction is between a narrative being well supported and being influential: an incorrect narrative can still move markets.

A first project could evaluate dated investor letters or market commentary using only information available at the time, then test whether the assessments help distinguish which explicit predictions subsequently hold.

ideas.title: Fruit flies: risk learning and decaying memory
ideas.scope: Test identifiability of location-specific memory versus generalized arousal in a simple return-to-food model.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Mathematical analysis is feasible; biological conclusions require controlled observations and domain support not yet established.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify an experiment, but a standalone toy fit has limited ML reach.
ideas.gate: Secure suitable observations or restrict the claim explicitly to experimental identifiability.
ideas.rated_version: Test identifiability of location-specific memory versus generalized arousal in a simple return-to-food model.
ideas.audit_reason: The bowl-specific versus generalized-arousal contrast is explicit; no animal-facility access or existing dataset has been verified.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: A small identifiability model is feasible, while suitable controlled observations and biological interpretation lack verified support.
ideas.I_note: The bowl-memory versus generalized-arousal distinction mainly informs a bounded experimental question.
ideas.original_title: B159. Fruit flies: risk learning and decaying memory
ideas.original_text:
I moved a cup near the fruit flies gathered around an old bowl of yogurt on my desk. They lifted off in a small spinning cloud. A few minutes later fewer had come back, and moving another cup seemed to reduce their number again. Perhaps each fly remembers the bowl as a risky place, especially if it was disturbed twice. How quickly would that memory decay? I wondered what kind of dynamical system this would be, and whether the individual flies need anything as sophisticated as Bayesian updating.

Related work. Tully and Quinn measured retention after flies learned to associate an odor with a shock [reference in Storage]. Gibson et al. found that repeated visual threats can instead leave flies in a defensive state that outlasts the stimulus [reference in Storage]. To distinguish memory of this bowl from generalized arousal, I would compare returns to the disturbed bowl and to an otherwise equivalent undisturbed one after the same delay.

ideas.original_title: B160. Flocking versus individual learning
ideas.original_text:
While I was looking out the window thinking about the flies, a flock of birds lifted off from the church next door. How much of what I had seen at the bowl was individual learning, and how much was one fly taking its cue from another? If they follow other flies, do they follow the whole crowd or just their nearest neighbor?

Related work. Ferreira and Moita show that the movement of other flies supplies a visual safety cue after a threat [reference in Storage]; Ballerini et al. found that neighbor rank rather than a fixed physical radius better described interactions in starling flocks [reference in Storage]. For the flies at the bowl, varying which neighbors can see one another while holding the disturbance fixed could separate individual memory from local social cues.

ideas.title: Inferring goals and measuring animal intelligence
ideas.scope: Characterize when inverse planning distinguishes goals from sensory and movement constraints.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Finite environments permit counterexamples and estimators, but new identification results beyond standard inverse planning are needed.
ideas.impact_reason: Could prevent misleading goal or intelligence claims from observed trajectories.
ideas.gate: Produce two observationally equivalent mechanisms and an informative additional measurement.
ideas.rated_version: Characterize when inverse planning distinguishes goals from sensory and movement constraints.
ideas.audit_reason: Goal inference with unknown sensory/motor costs is typically confounded; a useful paper must characterize that ambiguity rather than label speed intelligence.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Finite inverse-planning examples are accessible, but useful identification conditions must improve on familiar goal-cost confounding.
ideas.I_note: A rigorous ambiguity and measurement result could prevent misleading goal or intelligence inferences across behavioral settings.
ideas.original_title: B161. Inferring goals and measuring animal intelligence
ideas.original_text:
I wondered whether the time an animal takes to get from A to B while pursuing a physical goal could tell us something about its intelligence. But how would I know the animal was trying to get to B? Are animals always pursuing some task when they’re awake? For that matter, are we?

Related work. Baker, Saxe and Tenenbaum use inverse planning to ask which goal would make an observed path sensible under specified action costs [reference in Storage]. Before treating travel time as intelligence, I would check whether the path still favors that goal over an alternative once the animal’s possible sensory and movement constraints are allowed to vary.

ideas.scope: Derive a task-preserving coarse abstraction of a specific small neural circuit.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Choosing the circuit, abstraction, and validated responses is itself substantial; current notes supply no concrete construction.
ideas.impact_reason: A task-preserving abstraction of one small circuit could clarify an important mechanism; it would not yet explain intelligence generally.

ideas.audit_reason: A task-preserving coarse circuit model is an admissible narrowing, but biological validation and abstraction discovery exceed the demonstrated groundwork.

ideas.original_title: B162. A bottom-up abstraction of intelligence
ideas.original_text:
Could we start with a primitive brain and try to say what it does, abstracting away much of the biology? I was thinking of the way von Neumann architecture lets us describe a computer without specifying every component that implements it. What would the corresponding level of description be for intelligence?

Related work. Marr and Poggio distinguish describing a computation from describing the circuitry that realizes it [reference in Storage]. Lappalainen et al. make that distinction concrete: a fly connectome combined with a visual task predicts neural responses [reference in Storage]. I would ask which response to a changed visual input a coarser description still predicts before treating it as an abstraction of the circuit, let alone of intelligence.

ideas.scope: Compare feature-binding and temporal-interference models using a controlled two-signal task.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The experiment is compact, but human-subject access and a contribution beyond established attention phenomena are unverified.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify one failure mechanism; broad implications for AI are not yet justified.
ideas.gate: Specify predictions that distinguish the models rather than reproduce a known attention effect.

ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.

ideas.original_title: B163. Human mistakes and attention overload
ideas.original_text:
A few days ago I looked in quick succession at two traffic lights, one green and one red, and confused which one applied to me. What happens in my head when I make a mistake like that? Did the second signal override the first, did I retrieve the wrong one, or is there a more useful computational meaning of attention overload?

Related work. Treisman and Schmidt show that divided attention can make people report the right features in the wrong combination [reference in Storage]; Raymond, Shapiro and Arnell show that reporting one target can impair detection of the next at short intervals [reference in Storage]. To distinguish those explanations for the lights, I would vary their separation in time and ask separately which colors I saw and which signal each color belonged to.

ideas.scope: Test whether richer individual profiles predict behavior in new situations better than five trait scores.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The source gives a predictive comparison, but suitable repeated observations, reliable outcomes, and novelty beyond existing behavioral profiles are unverified.
ideas.impact_reason: A convincing comparison could establish when richer assessments capture useful individual variation beyond trait averages.
ideas.gate: Find repeated observations with genuinely held-out situations and compare predictive gains against measurement reliability and model complexity.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether richer individual profiles predict behavior in new situations better than five trait scores.
ideas.audit_reason: Restored because the source explicitly supplies an out-of-situation predictive test; the accompanying reading request does not erase that research question.
ideas.audit_uncertainty: Primary checks are targeted, not an exhaustive novelty review; project access and completed groundwork were not assumed.
ideas.F_note: Prediction models are manageable; repeated individual observations and genuinely held-out situations are the main unverified resource requirement.

ideas.original_title: B164. Richer individual representations in psychometrics
ideas.original_text:
When a questionnaire puts someone in a Myers–Briggs category or assigns them five personality scores, what do we miss about that person? Are there forms of personality assessment that give us a richer individual representation? I wanted to look at Kocielnik and colleagues’ paper on psychometric evaluation of language models with that question in mind.

Related work. Fleeson uses repeated observations to describe each person’s distribution of behavior, including the variation hidden by a trait average [reference in Storage]. Kocielnik et al. test when a language model’s questionnaire responses predict its behavior under matched evaluation conditions [reference in Storage]. For a person, the test of a richer profile would be whether it predicts what that person does in new situations better than five scores do.

ideas.scope: Study whether caregiving opportunities predict patience beyond the caregiving relationship.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Longitudinal confounding and participant recruitment make a convincing three-month ML paper unlikely.

ideas.rated_version: Study whether caregiving opportunities predict patience beyond the caregiving relationship.
ideas.audit_reason: The original question concerns human developmental effects, not simulated-agent behavior. F1 remains appropriate without longitudinal data or an established design; impact is narrow.

ideas.original_title: B165. Caregiving roles and the formation of behavior
ideas.original_text:
As an older sibling I know the feeling of letting my younger brother be the impressive one, or letting something pass because I want the best for him. Sometimes being a big sibling feels like being a parent in training. When I see the same patience in someone else with a younger sibling, I find it recognizable and appealing. I wonder how much of that habit comes from years of looking after someone.

Related work. Tavassoli, Recchia and Ross observed siblings at home over two years, recording opportunities to help as well as how children responded [reference in Storage]. That distinction matters for my example: having more occasions to look after someone is different from becoming more patient per occasion, and neither alone shows that the habit carries over to other relationships.

ideas.scope: Test whether spontaneously imagining a respected evaluator changes behavior during anger.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Measuring spontaneous cognition and separating its cause from its consequences require a specialized behavioral study.
ideas.impact_reason: A focused finding could inform self-regulation; relevance to model alignment would remain conjectural.
ideas.gate: Specify an observable intervention and a behavioral endpoint distinct from self-report.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether spontaneously imagining a respected evaluator changes behavior during anger.
ideas.audit_reason: The spontaneous-cognition target is harder than experimentally prompting an imagined evaluator. Preserve that distinction; a priming experiment alone would not answer the stated question.
ideas.F_note: Spontaneous imagined evaluation requires specialized behavioral access and identification; a prompted priming study would answer a different question.
ideas.I_note: The finding could illuminate a narrow self-regulation mechanism, with no established transfer to model alignment.
ideas.original_title: B166. Internalized approval as self-regulation
ideas.original_text:
A couple of times when I was angry, I found myself wondering whether someone whose judgment I respect would approve of what I was about to do. Both times it changed what I wanted to do. What struck me was that I hadn’t deliberately stopped to ask for a second opinion. The question seemed to arise on its own.

Related work. Baldwin, Carrell and Lopez found that priming a familiar evaluator could change how people judged themselves [reference in Storage]. My example raises a narrower question: does imagining that person’s judgment change what I actually do in anger when nobody has supplied a cue?

ideas.rated_version: Calibrate synthetic-reader ratings using a small set of the same reader’s real judgments and held-out poems.
ideas.audit_reason: A bounded reader-specific calibration study is coherent. Treat poems as sampling units and distinguish repeated judgments from independent people; simulator draws cannot remove common bias.
ideas.F_note: A reader-specific pilot is inexpensive, but repeated real ratings and cross-poem error transfer must be measured rather than assumed.
ideas.I_note: Calibrating shared simulator bias could help personalized evaluation, though one reader and literary domain limit reach.
ideas.original_title: B167. Poetry, taste, and synthetic copies of a reader
ideas.original_text:
I got such different reactions to a poem I wrote that I wondered what a quantitative assessment would even mean. If I care about one particular reader’s taste, I wish I could sample a thousand independent copies of that person, ask each to rate the poem, and average their answers. Of course, a thousand synthetic readers might all get the same thing wrong. How could I debias the average? I had much the same question about using synthetic data to value an illiquid asset (B148).

Related work. Park et al. compare interview-based agents with the individuals they simulate, giving a closer benchmark than agreement with a demographic average [reference in Storage]. Prediction-powered inference estimates and corrects average prediction error using real labels [reference in Storage]. For this poem, ratings of other poems by this reader could help only if their errors carry over; independent draws from one simulator cannot reveal a shared bias.

ideas.title: Learning habits that expand the problems one can see
ideas.scope: Study whether learning a new mathematical technique changes which problems people formulate.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The outcome is difficult to measure, and a credible comparison needs participants, task design, and longitudinal evaluation.
ideas.impact_reason: Potentially useful educational evidence, but a short study would support only a narrow claim.
ideas.gate: Define a blinded measure of newly noticed questions and recruit a feasible comparison sample.
ideas.rated_version: Study whether learning a new mathematical technique changes which problems people formulate.
ideas.audit_reason: A small study cannot establish that new techniques expand mathematical perception generally. The low scores correctly reflect measurement and recruitment dependencies.
ideas.F_note: A reliable blinded measure of newly noticed mathematical questions is missing, alongside participant and longitudinal-design dependencies.
ideas.I_note: A short study could contribute narrow educational evidence, but would not establish a general account of mathematical perception.
ideas.original_title: B168. Learning habits that expand the problems one can see
ideas.original_text:
I asked Vedant how he learns best. In applied math we can get a long way with “bare hands,” and I worry that solving everything on my desk with the tools I already know keeps me from noticing the interesting problems those tools don’t let me see.

Related work. Bilalić, McLeod and Gobet tracked chess experts’ attention when a familiar solution obscured a better one [reference in Storage]. I wonder about a step earlier in mathematics: after learning a new technique, do I notice a question that I would previously have passed over, even before trying to solve it?

ideas.title: Preventing specification fishing by AI analysts
ideas.scope: A protected-evidence controller for a specified family of adaptive analyses, compared with sample splitting and Thresholdout on false positives and power.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Protected evidence access is implementable, but a new statistical or efficiency result beyond split-sample and reusable-holdout baselines remains unverified.
ideas.impact_reason: Could make automated empirical analysis more trustworthy while preserving useful exploration.
ideas.gate: Specify the null, query family, data assumptions and leakage path; prove the guarantee or honestly label an empirical mitigation; compare power at equal evidence budgets.
ideas.rated_version: A protected-evidence controller for a specified family of adaptive analyses, compared with sample splitting and Thresholdout on false positives and power.
ideas.audit_reason: Retain. Reusable holdout is a concrete inferential baseline, not a proof that the full agent/controller proposal already exists. Do not say adaptive inference already solves the unrestricted scientific-agent task. The novelty hurdle is an agent-specific statistical or utility result beyond enforcing an existing interface.

audit_evidence.sections_read: Section 4, Algorithm Thresholdout, Theorem 9, Section 4.1; PDF pages 6–7
audit_evidence.findings: Thresholdout permits unrestricted training-data exploration but mediates holdout access. Theorem 9 concerns bounded queries phi:X->[0,1], an iid holdout, tolerance tau, failure probability beta, query count m, and an overfitting budget B. Before budget exhaustion, it bounds the probability that any answer differs from its population expectation by tau. The mechanism adds noise and stops when its budget is exhausted. The displayed sample requirement depends on log(m/beta)/tau^2 and B. The authors explicitly distinguish the experimental parameterization from their proved mechanism.
audit_evidence.limits: This is not automatically a p-value theorem for arbitrary regression specifications, causal identification, dependent data, unrestricted holdout exposure, or semantic warnings. Translating a fixed-null target into a valid query/test and matching power is substantive remaining work.

audit_evidence.sections_read: Experimental design and replication sections of author repository
audit_evidence.findings: Four empirical designs, eight framing/nudge prompts, two models and ten repetitions produce 640 sessions; scripts and logs enable studying search behavior. This supplies a concrete behavioral baseline.
audit_evidence.limits: The linked working-paper PDF returned 404. Its full statistical analysis was not checked; repository evidence does not establish a corrective validity guarantee.

ideas.F_note: Protected-evidence interfaces and behavioral baselines are available; a valid agent-specific guarantee or power advantage beyond Thresholdout remains the core work.
ideas.I_note: Trustworthy adaptive empirical analysis is a widely reusable target, while established reusable-holdout guarantees limit the novelty of interface enforcement alone.
ideas.original_title: B169. Preventing specification fishing by AI analysts
ideas.original_text:
An AI analyst eager to support my hypothesis might keep trying specifications until one gives the answer it thinks I want. Tao pointed out that in economics this often means trying many models on the same data. A well-meaning analyst can do it without recognizing the statistical problem.

I asked Mahdi whether we could teach an agent explicit principles of good data analysis through self-distillation. Shiva and I discussed a controller that would insert a warning when a trace shows fishing and then let the agent continue. If the model learns to recite the warning mechanically, remove it on traces where the search is legitimate. Can we teach the agent to recognize when its own search has changed the meaning of the evidence it reports?

A later AI-assisted sketch asked whether restricting the analyst’s queries could keep false positives under control when it tests a fixed null after an adaptive search. A warning about suspicious reasoning alone gives no such guarantee.

Related work. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn show how undisclosed analytic choices inflate false-positive rates [reference in Storage]. Dwork et al. give mechanisms for controlled holdout reuse [reference in Storage] and show that privacy-preserving perturbations can protect estimates of adaptively chosen statistical queries [reference in Storage]. I would evaluate a warning by whether the agent discloses its search and checks its preferred specification on suitably protected evidence while still pursuing legitimate alternatives.

ideas.title: Statistical optimal transport for constrained generative models
ideas.scope: Bound distribution error from estimating a constrained target separately from error caused by projection during sampling.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Simple constraint sets allow analysis and experiments; a new rate or decomposition beyond existing constrained sampling is needed.
ideas.impact_reason: Would clarify when enforcing feasibility distorts the intended sample distribution.
ideas.gate: Choose one constraint class where existing guarantees leave an identifiable statistical gap.
ideas.rated_version: Bound distribution error from estimating a constrained target separately from error caused by projection during sampling.
ideas.audit_reason: The statistical-versus-projection-error split is coherent, but could be a triangle inequality without new insight. Require an actual rate, lower bound, or failure regime before considering F4.
ideas.F_note: Simple constraint sets support analysis, but a useful rate, lower bound or failure regime must turn the decomposition into more than a triangle inequality.
ideas.I_note: Separating statistical and projection distortion would inform constrained generation, with novelty concentrated in the nontrivial regime or rate.
ideas.original_title: B119. Statistical optimal transport for constrained generative models
ideas.original_text:
Emre’s group works on statistical optimal transport. Could those tools help with a constrained sampling problem in diffusion models or flow matching? I wanted to ask Shervin, Romina or someone in Alejandro’s group which constraints actually arise.

Related work. Chen and Lipman train flow-matching models directly on manifolds [reference in Storage]. Christopher et al. incorporate feasibility constraints through projection during diffusion sampling [reference in Storage]. A concrete statistical question would fix a constraint set and distinguish error in learning the distribution on that set from error introduced by the constraint-enforcement step.

ideas.title: Steering diffusion without degrading useful safe outputs
ideas.scope: Quantify safe-mode distortion from diffusion steering when the safety classifier is imperfect.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Low-dimensional examples and frozen generators are feasible; a useful theorem and realistic mode-level evaluation are harder.
ideas.impact_reason: Could expose a central failure hidden by aggregate safety and quality metrics.
ideas.gate: Show a reproducible loss of safe modes and a correction at matched unsafe-output rate.
ideas.rated_version: Quantify safe-mode distortion from diffusion steering when the safety classifier is imperfect.
ideas.audit_reason: The conditional safe law is a defensible target. Avoid implying preservation of every safe mode from a single discrepancy bound; classifier error and feasible sampling must be explicit.
ideas.F_note: Frozen generators and low-dimensional examples support a first study; realistic mode-level validation under classifier error is the main burden.
ideas.I_note: Safe-mode loss is consequential and can be hidden by common aggregate metrics, giving the scoped result broader safety relevance.
ideas.original_title: B170. Steering diffusion without degrading useful safe outputs
ideas.original_text:
Shervin and I discussed steering a diffusion model away from unsafe outputs. Can we do that without degrading its performance on the safe region, even if we only have an implicit description of what is safe? A controller could suppress the failures we notice and also eliminate useful outputs. Preserving the average quality of the remaining samples is a weaker demand than preserving all the safe modes of the original model. Which kind of non-degradation matters for the application? I wonder how far stochastic optimal control subject to a safety constraint already takes us.

Related work. Schramowski et al. steer latent diffusion away from specified unsafe concepts [reference in Storage]; Uehara et al. trade off reward against departure from the original model using stochastic control [reference in Storage]. Wu et al. target diffusion conditionals by sequential Monte Carlo [reference in Storage], suggesting a precise benchmark: the original law conditioned on safety preserves the relative frequencies of safe outputs. If safety is only imperfectly observed, which safe modes lose mass relative to that benchmark?

ideas.title: Detecting coordinated misuse across actors
ideas.scope: Control sequential false alarms when suspect user groups and stopping times are selected from correlated benign activity.
ideas.feasibility_reason: This fits sequential inference, but a defensible benign null and dependence-robust power are substantial technical obstacles.
ideas.impact_reason: Could add reliable evidence standards to stateful misuse monitoring rather than another detector score.
ideas.gate: Fix an auditable benign model and prove validity after both group selection and optional stopping.
ideas.rated_version: Control sequential false alarms when suspect user groups and stopping times are selected from correlated benign activity.
ideas.audit_reason: F3/I4 remains reasonable for a real selective sequential-testing contribution. A detector benchmark alone would merit lower impact; benign correlation and selected group membership cannot be assumed away.

audit_evidence.checked_level: primary abstract read in initial pass
audit_evidence.does: Evaluates covert decomposed misuse and stateful defenses.
audit_evidence.does_not: It does not establish selective sequential error control for unknown adaptively chosen user groups.

ideas.F_note: The selected-group sequential guarantee is well defined; defensible benign dependence and useful power remain difficult to establish.
ideas.I_note: Reliable false-alarm standards for coordinated-misuse monitoring could materially improve safety deployment across services, beyond another detector score.
ideas.original_title: B171. Detecting coordinated misuse across actors
ideas.original_text:
Can we build a simple mathematical model of several actors trying to elicit a harmful capability? Each person’s requests might look innocuous on their own. We have to work out which identities belong together, recognize when a new actor has arrived, and decide what evidence of coordination there is across the requests. What probabilistic assumptions on ordinary users are reasonable? Mahdi and Davis’s work prompted the question. A later AI-assisted sketch suggested allowing benign users to have correlated interests, then asking whether we can detect coordination as requests arrive while controlling false alarms, even when the same requests help us pick out the group.

Related work. Brown, Sabbaghi and colleagues benchmark covert misuse through individually innocuous queries that jointly advance an attack [reference in Storage]. Pacheco et al. detect account groups by shared patterns of activity [reference in Storage]. For a live service, what would distinguish deliberate task-splitting from ordinary users pursuing a common interest, when both the membership of the group and the stopping time for raising an alarm are inferred from the same stream?

ideas.title: Strategic entity resolution and synthetic-data calibration
ideas.scope: Analyze entity matching when reported identifiers respond strategically to a bidding rule.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A stylized game is feasible; scarce audited identities make evaluation under changed incentives difficult.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify how matching error and gaming interact, with narrower claims than production identity resolution.
ideas.gate: Identify an incentive effect distinguishable from ordinary covariate shift using available evidence.
ideas.rated_version: Analyze entity matching when reported identifiers respond strategically to a bidding rule.
ideas.audit_reason: The source requires strategic adaptation and scarce ground truth jointly. Ordinary synthetic matching experiments would remove the central difficulty, so F2 remains justified.
ideas.F_note: The strategic matching game is tractable, but audited identities under changed incentives are scarce and synthetic data cannot remove that validation gap.
ideas.I_note: Linking identity error to strategic reporting could improve policy design, with a first stylized result narrower than production identity resolution.
ideas.original_title: B172. Strategic entity resolution and synthetic-data calibration
ideas.original_text:
My friend Tucker works on identity graphs at The Trade Desk. Suppose a company sees many identifiers. It can represent each one by its features, estimate which pairs refer to the same entity, and cluster the weighted graph. What I find interesting is what happens when the entities themselves care about the resulting bid. They might change an identifier or selectively report a feature. Can the company audit this behavior and adjust its bids so that gaming the system becomes less attractive? Ground truth on identity is scarce. Could synthetic data help evaluate the matching rule when the reporting behavior itself is strategic?

Related work. Fellegi and Sunter score candidate matches by how likely their agreements are among true links versus nonlinks [reference in Storage]; Hardt et al. model people changing features in response to a decision rule [reference in Storage]. Here the bid changes the incentive to disclose a feature, so I would want audited matches under different bidding rules before trusting a synthetic benchmark to predict error or gaming after the policy changes.

ideas.title: Algorithmic primitives of jailbreaking and defense
ideas.scope: Study constrained text edits under a fixed semantic-preservation test and adaptive adversarial evaluation.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A bounded editor and benchmarks are accessible; semantic fidelity and advantage over existing attacks remain uncertain.
ideas.impact_reason: Would clarify one intervention primitive; broader influence depends on a reusable guarantee or empirically effective intervention beyond a taxonomy.
ideas.gate: Define permitted semantic change independently of the attacked judge.
ideas.rated_version: Study constrained text edits under a fixed semantic-preservation test and adaptive adversarial evaluation.
ideas.audit_reason: The scoped editor experiment is narrower than the taxonomy and defensible. Semantic preservation cannot be certified by the same embedding optimized by the editor.
ideas.F_note: A bounded text editor is accessible; independent semantic-preservation tests and adaptive adversarial comparisons are the difficult validation work.
ideas.I_note: A sound constrained-edit result would clarify one security primitive, while a taxonomy or optimized embedding distance alone adds limited capability.
ideas.original_title: B174. Algorithmic primitives of jailbreaking and defense
ideas.original_text:
What are the few algorithmic primitives behind the zoo of jailbreaking and defense algorithms? In particular, I want to distinguish changing weights, optimizing a prompt, intervening during generation, and steering internal representations. Hamed suggested looking at Milad Nasr’s talks on prompt injection. Surbhi raised the possibility of learning an adaptive intervention map where a conformal rule is too blunt.

Two examples sharpened the question for me. If chat logs are used to construct a training environment, could misleading material in those logs change what the next model learns there (B257)? And when a text optimizer edits a prompt, can we enforce a restriction on the edit? Its location is easy to check. A small change in meaning is harder to define. I also wondered whether we could require the change in the prompt’s embedding to follow a gradient step. Given such a step, what would it mean for an edit to the actual words to realize it?

Related work. Optimized adversarial suffixes [reference in Storage] and contrastive activation addition [reference in Storage] illustrate two distinct operations: editing discrete input tokens and changing hidden states during generation. Nasr and colleagues show why the defense must also be tested against an attacker who can adapt to it [reference in Storage]. For a restricted prompt editor, I would want to test separately whether the edited words stay within the permitted meaning and whether an adaptive attack still succeeds.

ideas.title: Pseudorandomness assumptions against a model that learns the generator
ideas.scope: Audit one randomness-dependent safety protocol under explicit seed leakage and bounded next-output prediction.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A concrete leakage experiment is possible; recognizing a secure generator family is not a cryptographic break.
ideas.impact_reason: Could uncover an implementation assumption, but standard pseudorandomness theory already handles public generator descriptions.
ideas.gate: Find a realistic side channel or protocol failure beyond predicting weak toy generators.
ideas.rated_version: Audit one randomness-dependent safety protocol under explicit seed leakage and bounded next-output prediction.
ideas.audit_reason: The initial score correctly avoids treating generator-family identification as a cryptographic break. Novelty requires realistic leakage or a protocol-specific computational weakness.
ideas.F_note: Leakage experiments can be run, but a realistic safety protocol weakness beyond known public-generator security must first be identified.
ideas.I_note: An actual implementation failure would be useful; recognizing a generator family adds no new cryptographic insight.
ideas.original_title: B175. Pseudorandomness assumptions against a model that learns the generator
ideas.original_text:
Some cryptographic protocols for safety rely on randomness. Suppose an implementation uses a pseudorandom generator. What if the model can infer which kind of generator is being used? Can it learn anything that helps it predict the next draw, and would that compromise the protocol? Knowing the family and being able to predict its output are two different things. I would like to understand what the safety argument actually requires of an adversary with the model’s computational resources.

Related work. Blum and Micali give a public generator for which an efficient next-bit predictor would yield an efficient algorithm for an assumed-hard problem [reference in Storage]. That distinction suggests a concrete test of the safety argument: specify the hidden seed, the outputs and side information the model sees, and the advantage in prediction that would actually change the protocol’s outcome.

ideas.title: Safety through component contracts
ideas.scope: Prove and test compositional safety contracts for two assistants that mutate shared state.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A finite-state testbed is tractable; the challenge is a useful contract beyond standard interface compatibility.
ideas.impact_reason: Could reveal which local guarantees survive real interaction, informing reliable agent architectures.
ideas.gate: Construct a shared-state failure of naive composition and a nonvacuous repair.
ideas.rated_version: Prove and test compositional safety contracts for two assistants that mutate shared state.
ideas.audit_reason: A new shared-state composition theorem could justify I4. Standard assume-guarantee compatibility alone is not new, and natural-language intent is outside formal guarantees.
ideas.F_note: Finite shared-state examples are accessible; a nonvacuous contract repair beyond standard assume-guarantee compatibility is the core research task.
ideas.I_note: Useful local-to-system safety guarantees could guide interacting-agent design, while familiar compatibility results limit the novelty of routine compositions.
ideas.original_title: B176. Safety through component contracts
ideas.original_text:
Adam Kalai’s talk made me wonder whether we could put together useful AI systems from pieces whose behavior is constrained from the outset. Hamed and I discussed the difficulty with composition. Even if each component does what it promised, one can change the state or the information on which the other’s promise depends. Which restrictions on the interfaces let us conclude something useful about the whole system? There is a prior question here, reminiscent of formalizing a proof. We can check the restriction we actually wrote down. How do we know it captures the behavior we intended to rule out?

Related work. Interface automata give a precise meaning to compatibility: one component’s possible outputs must respect what its partner can accept in the relevant environment [reference in Storage]. Shielding gives a different guarantee by checking or correcting actions against a specified safety property [reference in Storage]. For two interacting assistants, I would ask which assumptions survive a change to shared state and whether the property we can enforce is the one we meant.

ideas.title: Can a many-agent safety problem be reduced to two players?
ideas.scope: Characterize when a two-player reduction preserves monitor information and feasible collusion in a small multiagent game.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Finite counterexamples and a restricted positive theorem are plausible; existing team-coordination reductions create a high novelty bar.
ideas.impact_reason: Would prevent misleading reductions and clarify what oversight loses when agents are aggregated.
ideas.gate: Find a safety-relevant quantity preserved by payoffs but broken by a standard reduction.
ideas.rated_version: Characterize when a two-player reduction preserves monitor information and feasible collusion in a small multiagent game.
ideas.audit_reason: Payoff equivalence is weaker than preservation of information and feasible deviations. A restricted counterexample plus a positive condition is a coherent F3 project; no literature clearance claimed.
ideas.F_note: Finite counterexamples and restricted sufficient conditions are feasible; preserving information and deviations rather than payoffs must supply the new theorem.
ideas.I_note: The result could expose unsafe aggregation assumptions in multiagent oversight, while general team reductions already have a substantial literature.
ideas.original_title: B177. Can a many-agent safety problem be reduced to two players?
ideas.original_text:
At the AIAS workshop, Elad described a primary agent that acts on a user’s behalf while another agent monitors it. I told Ivi that the models I could understand seemed always to have two players, whether they were trying to help each other or evade each other. Maybe a larger system can reduce to a two-player game, she suggested. When can several agents be treated as one player? I’d want to know what happens to the possibility of collusion, and to the information available to the monitor, before trusting that reduction.

Related work. In team-maxmin games, members with identical payoffs need not have the coordination available to a single player [reference in Storage]. Carminati and colleagues obtain a payoff-equivalent two-player representation under an explicit coordination model: the coordinator sees only team-public information and prescribes actions contingent on private states [reference in Storage]. For the monitor, the test is whether the reduction preserves who could communicate or detect a violation, as well as the payoff.

ideas.title: Oversight with limited trusted resources
ideas.scope: Derive trusted-audit budget bounds in a finite model separating detection, truthful reporting, and authority to halt.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The setting fits decision theory, but realistic assumptions and informative bounds are not yet established.
ideas.impact_reason: Could identify which trusted resources actually make oversight possible instead of assuming a reliable monitor.
ideas.gate: Produce a nontrivial lower bound and matching policy under one explicit evidence-access model.
ideas.rated_version: Derive trusted-audit budget bounds in a finite model separating detection, truthful reporting, and authority to halt.
ideas.audit_reason: The finite evidence-access model preserves the question. I4 is conditional on informative bounds and matching procedures; a generic impossibility with no trusted evidence would be too easy.
ideas.F_note: A finite evidence-access model is tractable, but informative lower bounds and a matching useful policy still require a precise assumption set.
ideas.I_note: Identifying the necessary trusted audit and stopping resources could change oversight design across settings if the bounds are nontrivial.
ideas.original_title: B179. Oversight with limited trusted resources
ideas.original_text:
Can a less capable agent control a more capable one? Hamed and I discussed what a monitor would actually have to do. It might fail to recognize a violation, recognize it but have no way to stop the action, or recognize it and choose to conceal it. Those are three different obstacles. It gets stranger if both the agent and its monitor are more capable than the human watching them. What could the human check or authorize in that situation? I would like to understand how much trusted review is needed to keep the agent useful and which decisions someone must be able to halt before they take effect.

Related work. In a coding testbed, Greenblatt and colleagues compare protocols that spend limited trusted review on work produced by a potentially subversive model, including trusted monitoring and untrusted monitoring [reference in Storage]. The distinction I would carry over is between a monitor producing a warning and a trusted party having both time and authority to block the action; one can test each failure separately.

ideas.title: Testing capabilities that a model may try to conceal
ideas.scope: Characterize when paired tests identify hidden capability under restricted strategic response policies.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Impossibility examples are accessible; a useful positive result needs behavioral restrictions the evaluator can justify.
ideas.impact_reason: Could establish meaningful limits on capability elicitation and clarify when evaluation evidence is informative.
ideas.gate: State a restriction preventing arbitrary underperformance and explain how it could be checked.
ideas.rated_version: Characterize when paired tests identify hidden capability under restricted strategic response policies.
ideas.audit_reason: The large conditional payoff remains plausible, but arbitrary underperformance destroys identification. Unverifiable behavioral restrictions cannot be presented as a dependable detection method.
ideas.F_note: Impossibility examples are accessible, but justified and checkable strategic-response restrictions are essential for a useful positive result.
ideas.I_note: Clarifying when concealed capabilities can be identified would address a central evaluation limitation across settings.
ideas.original_title: B262. Testing capabilities that a model may try to conceal
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a model seems unable to do something. How can we tell whether it lacks the capability or has some reason to hide it? I wondered whether we could design two tasks on which it couldn’t plausibly fake alignment at the same time. An answer that made it look harmless on one task would give something away on the other. What would the evaluator have to know about the tasks or the model’s incentives for this to work? Observing what a model can do is already difficult. Inferring why it chose a particular answer asks something further.

Related work. Van der Weij et al. elicited selective underperformance on dangerous-capability evaluations while models continued to do well on harmless evaluations; they also trained models whose strong performance could be unlocked with a password [reference in Storage]. Two benchmarks alone therefore give little leverage. The proposed pair needs a reason that concealing success on one task constrains what the model can do on the other.

ideas.title: Safety rules, abstraction, and abstention
ideas.scope: Test explicit-rule-only abstention against principle induction on cases requiring a new rule, measuring useful-task performance and risk at matched coverage.
ideas.feasibility_reason: SELECT already studies abstention generalization and specificity; the new rule-composition question needs a distinct construction or result.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify the cost of restricting generalization, though the contribution is narrower than general alignment.
ideas.gate: Define direct rule entailment versus underdetermined extrapolation; show a distinction beyond descendant/composite taxonomy and evaluate answer quality, not refusal rate alone.
ideas.rated_version: Test explicit-rule-only abstention against principle induction on cases requiring a new rule, measuring useful-task performance and risk at matched coverage.
ideas.audit_reason: Retain scores but qualify overlap. SELECT covers hierarchical concept abstention, including compositions; it does not equate to refusing to infer an unstated safety principle. Earlier phrasing that SELECT directly covers safety-rule extrapolation was too broad. It covers an important operational baseline, not all meta-level abstraction decisions.

audit_evidence.sections_read: Sections 3.1–3.2, 4.1 and Limitations; PDF pages 3–5 and 9
audit_evidence.findings: SELECT has 394 atomic and 156 composite benign concepts built from YAGO. Composites use templates such as creative works about people and inherit taxonomic relations. Generalization is refusal on descendants; specificity is answering questions about siblings and ancestors. It evaluates prompting, steering and fine-tuning. Refusal detection is largely phrase-based with a length heuristic.
audit_evidence.limits: Its desired behavior is to propagate refusal to descendants. The source idea instead asks about declining uncertain principle induction and its capability cost. Taxonomic compositions are already covered, so adding compositional concept cases alone is insufficient; genuinely underdetermined rules or competing abstractions would distinguish the task.

ideas.F_note: Rule-only abstention can be tested on controlled cases; underdetermined principle induction and matched useful-task coverage need careful construction.
ideas.I_note: A clean capability-cost comparison could clarify safety generalization beyond taxonomic refusal, while remaining narrower than general alignment.
ideas.original_title: B180. Safety rules, abstraction, and abstention
ideas.original_text:
Why do we want a model to infer the general principle behind a set of safety rules? In some cases I would rather it abstained from making that leap. How much would that handicap its capabilities?

Related work. Constitutional AI uses written principles to guide model critiques, revisions and feedback [reference in Storage], while SelectiveNet measures the tradeoff between the risk on accepted cases and the fraction accepted [reference in Storage]. I would use that distinction to ask which cases a rule already settles, which require the model to generalize, and how much useful work is lost if it declines the latter.

ideas.title: Privacy through plausible decoy activity
ideas.scope: Measure trajectory deanonymization under coherent decoy histories in a synthetic or consented browsing benchmark.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A controlled privacy testbed is feasible; realistic attacker side information and coherent decoy generation require careful design.
ideas.impact_reason: Could reveal why plausible individual queries fail to protect a whole behavioral trajectory.
ideas.gate: Show benefit against an adaptive sequence-level observer, not only a query classifier.
ideas.rated_version: Measure trajectory deanonymization under coherent decoy histories in a synthetic or consented browsing benchmark.
ideas.audit_reason: The sequence-level threat model is sensible. Coherent synthetic histories can support a narrow controlled study but do not establish real privacy when side information differs.
ideas.F_note: A synthetic trajectory benchmark is manageable, but coherent decoys and realistic sequence-level side information need careful threat-model design.
ideas.I_note: Testing whole-history privacy could expose failures missed by query classifiers; decoy search itself is already established.
ideas.original_title: B181. Privacy through plausible decoy activity
ideas.original_text:
Mark Vero gave a reading-group talk about how well LLMs can deanonymize people. I wondered if agents could also help with the other side of the problem. Imagine browsing the web alongside K agents. Each time I take an action, some follow me while the others take a different but plausible action. After several such decisions there are many search paths. Can an observer still tell which one was mine? A similar idea for an interaction between two people would introduce an extra pair of agents at the point where the interaction occurred. I don’t know what would make those alternatives convincing.

Related work. TrackMeNot already mixes a person’s web searches with machine-generated decoy queries [reference in Storage], and Lermen and colleagues show that LLMs can link identities from online text at scale [reference in Storage]. I would test whether the observer can recover the real path after several branches, including by checking consistency between two people’s histories; plausible individual queries need not make a plausible trajectory.

ideas.title: Interpretable models for public decision-making
ideas.scope: Agenda reflection on why interpretable models remain useful in public decision-making.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The source gives motivation and examples, without a standalone proposed experiment, theorem, or new modeling problem.
ideas.impact_reason: No conference-paper impact is assigned to a general research motivation.
ideas.gate: Choose a concrete unresolved public-decision problem before assigning paper scores.
ideas.rated_version: Agenda reflection on why interpretable models remain useful in public decision-making.
ideas.audit_reason: The original is a motivation for interpretable public models, not a specified experiment comparing explanations. The prior scored scope invents a study; classify as agenda rather than score it.
ideas.original_title: B182. Interpretable models for public decision-making
ideas.original_text:
An elected representative may have a perfectly good prediction and still owe constituents an explanation for a decision. That’s one reason I think interpretable mathematical models will continue to matter in economics and political science, however good our black-box predictors become. Should more applied mathematicians work on formulating such models? Tom Sargent is someone I read for inspiration. Bayesian statistics, robust control, and differential games all have a place in his work, because of the economic questions he is trying to answer.

Related work. Jung and colleagues develop simple scoring rules for decisions such as pretrial release and make explicit the assumptions needed to evaluate them on historical decisions [reference in Storage]. Hansen and Sargent put uncertainty about the economic model itself into a decision maker’s optimization problem [reference in Storage]. Those examples suggest two different things an explanation might owe the public: which features changed the recommendation and which assumptions about the economy made it defensible.

ideas.title: When would governments direct frontier AI development?
ideas.scope: Model when public R&D contracts, equity stakes, or direct control are preferred under a specified strategic objective.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The current question is broad policy research; a novel empirically credible ML paper is not yet defined.
ideas.impact_reason: A stylized framework could organize a policy discussion, but predictive implications would be limited.
ideas.gate: Specify a falsifiable mechanism and suitable evidence before treating this as an ML submission.
ideas.rated_version: Model when public R&D contracts, equity stakes, or direct control are preferred under a specified strategic objective.
ideas.audit_reason: The government-control question is substantive but remains a political-economy research question with weak ML-paper fit. The low scores concern this scope, not the importance of governance.
ideas.F_note: The strategic objective, falsifiable mechanism and suitable evidence are undefined, and a credible ML-conference contribution is particularly uncertain.
ideas.I_note: A stylized state-direction framework could organize policy thinking, but its predictive reach would remain limited.
ideas.original_title: B280. When would governments direct frontier AI development?
ideas.original_text:
I asked Behrad what could trigger a US government program for frontier AI on the scale of the Manhattan Project. The analogy is awkward because the labs I had in mind were private companies. Export controls are one way for the government to influence the race. What would move it from restricting what companies can sell to directing what the labs build?

Behrad suggested looking at government ownership stakes in strategically important companies. That gives me an intermediate case to think about. How much direction could the government exercise through a stake in an existing lab, and under what circumstances would it want to run a program itself?

Related work. Gross and Sampat trace the persistent effects of US wartime R&D contracts on the geography and direction of invention [reference in Storage]. That history gives a concrete form of state direction in which firms and universities still perform much of the research. For AI, what would make contracts of that sort insufficient and lead a government to seek direct control of training decisions?

ideas.title: Location privacy under public-data aggregation
ideas.scope: Estimate incremental location leakage when consented or synthetic image and trajectory clues are linked.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Existing geolocation tools enable an audit; realistic cross-source matching and defensible privacy evaluation remain nontrivial.
ideas.impact_reason: Could identify which combinations of clues create disproportionate leakage and which interventions reduce it.
ideas.gate: Define an attacker and measure gain from linkage over each isolated source.
ideas.rated_version: Estimate incremental location leakage when consented or synthetic image and trajectory clues are linked.
ideas.audit_reason: An incremental-linkage audit is coherent if data are consented or synthetic. I3 assumes a generalizable leakage mechanism; combining familiar tools alone is weaker.
ideas.F_note: Existing geolocation methods support an audit; realistic consented cross-source linkage and fair attacker baselines need construction.
ideas.I_note: A generalizable amplification mechanism would improve privacy evaluation, while merely combining available tools is less distinctive.
ideas.original_title: B183. Location privacy under public-data aggregation
ideas.original_text:
How much can someone infer about a person’s location by combining public information from social media, photographs, video feeds, and device traces? Pieces of information that reveal little separately might be quite revealing together. Conversely, what would help someone protect their location?

Related work. PlaNet estimates location from the visual contents of a photograph [reference in Storage], while de Montjoye and colleagues show how a few time-stamped locations can single out a trajectory in a mobility dataset [reference in Storage]. The question here is how much an observer gains by linking such clues across sources, and which of those links a proposed protection actually breaks.

ideas.title: Compiling repeated AI work into programs
ideas.scope: Replace repeated model calls with synthesized programs, using independent task specifications and a calibrated fallback to the original workflow.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The system is buildable, but EVAPORATE already establishes reusable extraction code; the research gap must be certification or transfer across workflows.
ideas.impact_reason: A reliable criterion for when to compile could reduce inference cost without faithfully reproducing systematic errors.
ideas.gate: Demonstrate a new guarantee or robust cost-quality frontier beyond code-generation and cascade baselines.
ideas.rated_version: Replace repeated model calls with synthesized programs, using independent task specifications and a calibrated fallback to the original workflow.
ideas.audit_reason: EVAPORATE already demonstrates reusable generated extraction code. Program replacement plus calibrated fallback is plausible but requires an explicit advantage beyond existing selective prediction and cascades.

audit_evidence.checked_level: primary abstract read in initial pass
audit_evidence.does: EVAPORATE synthesizes reusable extraction code and combines candidate functions for better cost-quality tradeoffs.
audit_evidence.does_not: It does not by itself establish a general independent-specification guarantee for arbitrary workflows.

ideas.F_note: Program synthesis and fallback systems are buildable; independent-specification certification or cross-workflow transfer must distinguish the result from extraction-code precedents.
ideas.I_note: A justified compilation criterion could reduce repeated inference cost across workflows without preserving systematic errors of the original model.
ideas.original_title: B245. Compiling repeated AI work into programs
ideas.original_text:
Can we “derandomize” an AI application by having it learn a deterministic rule for something it does over and over? I had a company in mind that would “de-AI-ify” parts of an existing workflow. Once we have a program, we can inspect it and check what it does on a particular input, and repeated calls might be cheaper. The question is which behavior we actually want to reproduce. If the original workflow makes the same mistake often enough, a faithful copy of that behavior would be a rather poor improvement.

Related work. EVAPORATE compared asking a language model to extract each record with asking it to write reusable extraction code, measuring both cost and accuracy [reference in Storage]. DSPy compiles pipelines that can continue to call a model [reference in Storage], whereas program sketching can fill in a program subject to a supplied specification [reference in Storage]. For a workflow I want to replace, the consequential choice is the specification: copying prior answers and meeting an independent task requirement can favor different programs.

ideas.scope: Clarify the existing electron-attention model and its physical symmetry assumptions with Amir.
ideas.feasibility_reason: This is a reference-recovery and learning question; no new quantum-modeling problem is specified.
ideas.impact_reason: No standalone paper impact is assigned.
ideas.gate: Identify a limitation of the established wavefunction ansatz before proposing a project.
ideas.rated_version: Clarify the existing electron-attention model and its physical symmetry assumptions with Amir.
ideas.audit_reason: Correctly unrated: the source seeks clarification of an existing electron-attention model and its physics, without a proposed new contribution.
ideas.original_title: B184. Electrons as transformer tokens in many-body quantum systems
ideas.original_text:
I remember Amir Shapour describing a model of a many-electron system in which the electrons are tokens and interact through self-attention. I think twisted bilayer graphene was the application. Is there a useful analogy to physics-informed networks for weather forecasting? I’d like to ask Amir what physical structure actually enters the model.

Related work. PsiFormer uses self-attention between electrons in a wavefunction ansatz for molecules [reference in Storage]. Geier et al. apply a related construction to a moiré heterobilayer made from tungsten diselenide and tungsten disulfide [reference in Storage]. In both, I would distinguish the exchange symmetry built into the wavefunction from the correlations learned by attention. I would ask Amir whether he had this material or a graphene calculation in mind.

ideas.title: Auditing clinical-LLM reasoning
ideas.scope: Audit stated clinical inference steps and test whether correcting an invalid step changes the diagnosis.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Public case benchmarks permit a pilot, but credible labels and medical review cannot be assumed.
ideas.impact_reason: Could distinguish defensible explanations from effective interventions; it would not establish actual deployed-model reasoning faithfulness.
ideas.gate: Confirm access to validated reasoning labels and predefine clinically meaningful error categories.
ideas.rated_version: Audit stated clinical inference steps and test whether correcting an invalid step changes the diagnosis.
ideas.audit_reason: Stated-step defensibility and causal influence on diagnosis are distinct estimands. Text correction experiments can test influence, but not verify faithful internal reasoning or clinical utility.
ideas.F_note: Public clinical cases permit experiments, but credible step labels and independent medical review remain uncommitted resources.
ideas.I_note: Separating defensible stated reasoning from diagnosis-changing interventions would aid evaluation, without proving internal faithfulness or clinical benefit.
ideas.original_title: B185. Auditing clinical-LLM reasoning
ideas.original_text:
Do any clinical deployments give us annotated reasoning traces we could study? Could we use those traces to tell when a model arrives at a plausible diagnosis by reasoning we wouldn’t trust? This seems connected to the problem of reward hacking in reasoning models, except here there may be data to work with. If a clinician cannot retrain the deployed system, I’d like to know what other options they have. What can we learn from an audit, or change through a text-level intervention? I wanted to ask Ahmed Alaa’s group and people working on AI in medicine at Penn and Columbia what they would actually want such an audit to find.

Related work. MedR-Bench derives reference reasoning from clinical case reports and evaluates intermediate reasoning as well as diagnoses [reference in Storage]. Experiments outside medicine show that an LLM can omit an influence on its answer from the explanation it gives [reference in Storage]. I would therefore score whether a stated clinical inference is defensible, then separately test whether correcting that inference through text changes the diagnosis.

ideas.title: Anatomically structured synthetic medical images
ideas.scope: Evaluate anatomical boundary consistency in regionwise synthetic MRI generation.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Training and data preparation are significant; expert validation and gains over label-conditioned generation are unverified.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve synthetic-data quality if it finds failures missed by downstream segmentation metrics.
ideas.gate: Demonstrate a measurable seam or topology failure on accessible scans before training a new generator.
ideas.rated_version: Evaluate anatomical boundary consistency in regionwise synthetic MRI generation.
ideas.audit_reason: The proposed anatomical-seam audit is faithful. Regionwise generation could increase inconsistency, and downstream segmentation gains do not validate anatomical realism.
ideas.F_note: Anatomical seam failures are measurable in principle; generator training, scan preparation and independent anatomical validation are sizable dependencies.
ideas.I_note: Detecting realism failures missed by segmentation could improve synthetic imaging, though one regional-generation study has bounded reach.
ideas.original_title: B186. Anatomically structured synthetic medical images
ideas.original_text:
Suppose I train a diffusion model on good MRI scans and use its samples for data augmentation. What keeps it from inventing anatomy? Even if the validation score improves, I would want to know what it means that some of the synthetic scans contain things we would never see in a patient. I emailed Shervin and Thomas an idea. Could we generate small regions of the brain separately and stitch them together in a more programmatic way? Of course the regions have to agree where they meet. I wondered whether a similar use of structure might help with scientific diagrams (B191).

Related work. SynthSeg generates MRI appearances from whole-brain anatomical labels [reference in Storage]. Peng et al. generate a brain volume progressively, conditioning new slices on previously generated ones [reference in Storage]. For region-by-region generation I would compare these ways of sharing anatomical information: do the structures on either side of a join remain plausible even when the downstream segmentation score improves?
ideas.original_html:
Suppose I train a diffusion model on good MRI scans and use its samples for data augmentation. What keeps it from inventing anatomy? Even if the validation score improves, I would want to know what it means that some of the synthetic scans contain things we would never see in a patient. I emailed Shervin and Thomas an idea. Could we generate small regions of the brain separately and stitch them together in a more programmatic way? Of course the regions have to agree where they meet. I wondered whether a similar use of structure might help with scientific diagrams (B191).

Related work. SynthSeg generates MRI appearances from whole-brain anatomical labels [reference in Storage]. Peng et al. generate a brain volume progressively, conditioning new slices on previously generated ones [reference in Storage]. For region-by-region generation I would compare these ways of sharing anatomical information: do the structures on either side of a join remain plausible even when the downstream segmentation score improves?

ideas.title: Geometric methods for medical imaging
ideas.scope: Benchmark when topology-preserving registration incorrectly suppresses true anatomical changes.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The geometric question is clear, but choosing pathology data and defensible correspondence ground truth requires domain expertise.
ideas.impact_reason: Could expose important failure modes in otherwise accurate registration methods.
ideas.gate: Find a public dataset or controlled deformation family with independently known structural changes.
ideas.rated_version: Benchmark when topology-preserving registration incorrectly suppresses true anatomical changes.
ideas.audit_reason: Topology preservation may be wrong in pathology. Without known correspondence ground truth, a registration score cannot establish suppression of true anatomical changes.
ideas.F_note: The topology failure target is clear, but independent structural-change and correspondence ground truth are the scarce resources.
ideas.I_note: Detecting suppressed real anatomical changes could be important within imaging, though the first benchmark remains specialized.
ideas.original_title: B187. Geometric methods for medical imaging
ideas.original_text:
Pratik’s group’s FireANTs work got me interested in image registration. A conversation with a control theorist brought up diffeomorphisms, optimal transport, Riemannian optimization, and equivariant specialist models. Where in medical imaging do we know enough about the geometry to build it into a model? I’d like to find a particular problem where that matters.

Related work. FireANTs fits a dense, invertible spatial transformation by multiscale Riemannian optimization, without training a registration network [reference in Storage]. It gives me a concrete criterion for choosing a problem: when are correspondences expected to preserve topology, and where would enforcing that geometry hide a real anatomical change?
