ideas.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics
ideas.scope: Characterize identifiability of spatial expression when only a subset of genes anchors the alignment.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The statistical question fits existing strengths; biological assumptions and a bounded model remain to be chosen.
ideas.impact_reason: Could distinguish measured spatial structure from structure imposed by matching assumptions.
ideas.gate: Specify one observation model and exhibit two indistinguishable alignments with different scientific conclusions.
ideas.rated_version: Characterize identifiability of spatial expression when only a subset of genes anchors the alignment.
ideas.audit_reason: An identifiability example is feasible after choosing a model; a generic nonidentifiability construction would not itself be a publishable biological contribution.
ideas.F_note: Statistical identifiability fits current skills, but the observation model and biologically credible assumptions still need domain grounding.
ideas.I_note: Distinguishing measured spatial patterns from matching assumptions could improve scientific interpretation, provided the example is biologically consequential.
ideas.original_title: B188. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics
ideas.original_text:
Thomas and I got to reminiscing about denoising single-cell RNA measurements. Normalizing Poisson counts already gives an interesting random-matrix problem. Edgar’s ePCA work asks how to recover structure when the observation model belongs to an exponential family. I wonder what statistical questions are coming from spatial transcriptomics now. Missing data, trajectory inference, and optimal transport all came up in my reading. I’d like to ask Afnan, Henri, and Peter which of those problems the new measurements have actually made it possible to address.

Related work. ePCA estimates latent covariance structure from exponential-family observations, including noisy counts [reference in Storage]; Tangram instead aligns single-cell expression measurements to spatial measurements and uses the alignment to map genes or cell types [reference in Storage]. A useful first question is whether an apparent spatial pattern is identifiable from the measured genes and locations, or is supplied mainly by the matching assumptions.

ideas.title: Low-frequency gravitational-wave inference
ideas.scope: Compare anomaly detection and template matching on simulated multichannel LISA bursts and glitches.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Public simulation is plausible, but instrument-specific noise, channel construction, and baseline expertise impose substantial setup costs.
ideas.impact_reason: A calibrated comparison could improve robustness to unfamiliar signals within the simulated regime.
ideas.gate: Secure a validated simulator and a domain-appropriate glitch model before developing the detector.
ideas.rated_version: Compare anomaly detection and template matching on simulated multichannel LISA bursts and glitches.
ideas.audit_reason: The instrument-specific dependency is real. Simulated anomaly gains must compare against validated burst/glitch baselines rather than just a weak template matcher.
ideas.F_note: LISA simulation, channel construction and realistic glitch baselines require domain setup before detector work can be evaluated credibly.
ideas.I_note: Robustness to unfamiliar signals could matter for the chosen instrument, but anomaly-versus-template comparisons have existing precedents.
ideas.original_title: B189. Low-frequency gravitational-wave inference
ideas.original_text:
Suchindram and I talked about the statistical work that can be done before an instrument starts collecting data. For low-frequency gravitational waves, people are already modeling the waveforms and building ways to search for them. A binary black hole merger, for example, gives a characteristic chirp that one can try to match with a template. But what if the signal doesn’t look much like a template we thought to include? I would like to understand how people distinguish an unfamiliar waveform from noise, and when an anomaly detector can tell us something template matching would miss.

Related work. Robson and Cornish study how an unmodeled gravitational-wave burst and an instrumental glitch would differ across channels in simulated LISA data [reference in Storage]. There is also an observational precedent: short-duration transient searches first identified GW150914 in ground-based LIGO data using coherence across detectors and few assumptions about the waveform [reference in Storage]. For LISA, which signals would remain hard to distinguish from glitches once we account for how its channels are constructed?

ideas.title: Infinite-horizon monitoring of treatments and subpopulations
ideas.scope: Build sequential subgroup surveillance with explicit control of repeated selection and a clearly separated causal estimand.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Causal identification, adaptively selected subgroups, and indefinite monitoring introduce several unresolved dependencies in the current scope.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve evidence discipline in ongoing surveillance, without treating an alert as proof of treatment harm.
ideas.gate: Fix a causal estimand and observation regime, then isolate one new sequential-selection issue relative to established subgroup and confidence-sequence methods.
ideas.rated_version: Build sequential subgroup surveillance with explicit control of repeated selection and a clearly separated causal estimand.
ideas.audit_reason: The initial scope combines causal identification, adaptive subgroup discovery, and indefinite monitoring. That is multiple unresolved problems, not one major uncertainty; narrow the scope or reduce feasibility.

audit_uncertainty.status: Search result suggests finite-sample subgroup FDR in matched observational studies; direct fetch failed. Specific theorem comparison unverified.

ideas.F_note: Causal identification, adaptive subgroup selection and indefinite monitoring remain several coupled unresolved tasks rather than one clean extension.
ideas.I_note: Sound sequential subgroup surveillance could improve postmarketing evidence across treatments, provided alerts remain distinct from causal conclusions.
ideas.original_title: B190. Infinite-horizon monitoring of treatments and subpopulations
ideas.original_text:
Could there be a Moody’s for pharmaceuticals after FDA approval? I have in mind something like an infinite-horizon clinical trial. As evidence comes in, someone would keep asking what a given drug does in a given subpopulation, even years after the initial trial has ended. Hearing my mother’s account of possible GLP-1 side effects got me thinking about the question. An account like that might tell us what to investigate. It can’t by itself tell us whether the drug caused the effect. What evidence would let us distinguish the two?

Related work. Sequential postmarketing surveillance already tests accumulating safety signals [reference in Storage], and confidence sequences address repeated looks at an estimand under stated assumptions [reference in Storage]. Neither resolves confounding: emulating a target trial requires specifying eligibility, treatment strategies, follow-up and a comparison group [reference in Storage]. For an unexpected subgroup signal I would distinguish the rule that raises the alert from the design that could establish a treatment effect.

ideas.title: Structured generation of scientific diagrams
ideas.scope: Generate executable diagrams through caption-derived relation constraints and test whether verification reduces explicit relation errors on held-out scientific diagrams.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Public diagram tasks and program rendering make a narrow method study plausible; useful novelty beyond graph-conditioned generation remains its main uncertainty.
ideas.impact_reason: A demonstrated reduction in caption-relation errors would be a substantive scientific-generation contribution; another metric-only benchmark is nearer I2.
ideas.gate: Show a specific constraint-preserving generation improvement over existing caption-to-code methods; separate extraction errors, program constraints and rendered-image errors.
ideas.rated_version: Generate executable diagrams through caption-derived relation constraints and test whether verification reduces explicit relation errors on held-out scientific diagrams.
ideas.audit_reason: Revise prior audit upward to 3/3 for a generation-method scope. The 2/2 audit incorrectly reduced the source proposal to another structural evaluation benchmark. Retain the strong prior-art warning for evaluation; retract the inference that evaluation overlap by itself makes the actual generation proposal only a 2/2.

audit_evidence.sections_read: Sections 3, 4.1–4.2 and Limitations; PDF pages 2–4 and 9
audit_evidence.findings: DiagramEval builds text-attributed graphs using SVG parsing plus a VLM inspecting rendered images. Node scores use thresholded textual matches; path scores compare directed reachability among matched nodes, after inducing corresponding subgraphs. It therefore detects many relation errors but need not distinguish every exact-edge difference. Evaluation uses a reference diagram, while inputs include paper text, captions and a reference-derived layout caption.
audit_evidence.limits: It is an evaluation method, not a caption-grounded constraint-preserving generator. Edge extraction is fallible, acknowledged by the authors. Calling it purely symbolic and saying it bypasses rendered-image inspection would be inaccurate.

audit_evidence.sections_read: Section 3.3, 4.2–4.3, Appendix A.1–A.2; PDF pages 4–6 and 13
audit_evidence.findings: SciFlow-Bench compares inverse-parsed image graphs to canonical source-figure graphs. Nodes are matched semantically; edge correctness permits canonical-graph reachability, allowing skipped intermediate nodes. Reversed, unsupported or hallucinated relations are penalized. Graph scoring weights node F1 40% and edge F1 60%. Human validation reports imperfect edge recovery, rather than a sound correctness certificate.
audit_evidence.limits: Strong overlap with a new graph-error benchmark, but neither the metric nor its benchmark establishes faithful caption-to-constraint extraction or a verified generation intervention. Canonical-image recoverability differs from satisfaction of explicit caption claims.

audit_uncertainty.status: Search result only; direct abstract and HTML fetch failed. Not used as verified evidence.

ideas.F_note: Program rendering and public diagram tasks enable a narrow method experiment; caption extraction errors must be separated from generation errors.
ideas.I_note: Constraint-preserving generation addresses a substantive gap beyond graph evaluation, with reuse across scientific figures.
ideas.original_title: B191. Structured generation of scientific diagrams
ideas.original_text:
Xiaohan and I discussed using captions from papers as a source of supervision for generating scientific diagrams. What structure do diagrams have in common that a model could learn from the diagram–caption pairs? I’d love to be able to release a tool that makes a genuinely useful figure from a caption. There may be a shared idea here with the MRI question in B186. For the diagram, the pieces need to express the relationships the caption describes. For the scan, they have to fit together anatomically.

Related work. AutomaTikZ learns to turn captions into executable graphics programs [reference in Storage], and SciDoc2Diagrammer generates diagrams from a paper and a reader’s stated intent [reference in Storage]. A more specific target would be to check the relationships the caption asserts: can a figure compile and look convincing while attaching a label to the wrong object or reversing an arrow?

ideas.title: Routing among multiple energy sources
ideas.scope: Study calibrated dispatch among a few energy sources in a fixed power-system simulator.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Simulation is accessible in principle, but dispatch constraints and a distinct contribution require substantial domain work.
ideas.impact_reason: A validated uncertainty-aware dispatch result could matter; transferring a routing threshold alone would be narrow.
ideas.gate: Specify physical dispatch versus procurement, then reproduce one feasible baseline.
ideas.rated_version: Study calibrated dispatch among a few energy sources in a fixed power-system simulator.
ideas.audit_reason: The physical-dispatch versus procurement distinction is essential. Static calibrated routing is not sufficient for coupled network dynamics; the domain-dependent F2 is appropriate.
ideas.F_note: A simulator is potentially accessible; physical dispatch constraints and a contribution beyond static routing require substantial domain work.
ideas.I_note: A valid uncertainty-aware dispatch improvement could matter in energy systems, but a transferred threshold alone would be a narrow application.
ideas.original_title: B192. Routing among multiple energy sources
ideas.original_text:
I saw an ESE senior poster on the energy grid and wondered whether routing among several energy sources could be modeled along the lines of our routing paper. How do power-system stability and control enter that decision? Kundur’s book and the work of Carmona and Sircar are where I wanted to start.

Related work. Carmona, Coulon and Schwarz model how demand and fuel prices determine electricity prices through the generation bid stack [reference in Storage]; Gan, Thomas and Zimmerman instead put system stability constraints into an optimal power-flow problem [reference in Storage]. Before borrowing a routing rule I would ask whether the choice concerns buying power or physically dispatching it, since the latter can be infeasible even when the selected source is cheap.

ideas.title: Mechanistic biological digital twins
ideas.scope: Characterize when two cell models matching perturbation marginals make distinguishable trajectory predictions.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A credible biological example needs mechanistic expertise and trajectory evidence not established in the notes.
ideas.impact_reason: A precise identifiability result could guide one class of cell models; the full biological-digital-twin ambition lies well beyond this scope.
ideas.gate: Find a public system with both perturbation observations and independently checkable dynamics.
ideas.rated_version: Characterize when two cell models matching perturbation marginals make distinguishable trajectory predictions.
ideas.audit_reason: The original asks about individual biological paths. Marginally equivalent toy Markov models are easy to construct; meaningful biological constraints and observations are the hard part.
ideas.F_note: Marginally equivalent toy models are easy; a biologically credible pair with independently checked trajectories lacks both data and mechanistic groundwork.
ideas.I_note: A meaningful trajectory-identification result could guide cell-model validation, with far less scope than a complete biological digital twin.
ideas.original_title: B193. Mechanistic biological digital twins
ideas.original_text:
Behrad made a point I keep thinking about. Statistical learning can tell us a lot in the aggregate, but if we want to understand one biological system, perhaps we need its mechanism. The Arc Institute’s virtual-cell project made the idea of a digital twin concrete for me. I also met a student in Li Shen’s group working on protein–ligand binding. We discussed what one might learn by following a trajectory inside a synthetic cell. That’s a different question from inferring a trajectory from a collection of single-cell measurements. What would an individual cell model have to get right for the distinction to matter?

Related work. Karr and colleagues coupled models of cellular processes to simulate a bacterium over its life cycle [reference in Storage], while Arc’s State predicts transcriptomic responses to perturbations across cellular contexts [reference in Storage]. The distinction matters for a digital twin: two models could agree on the distribution of measured responses but disagree about the path taken inside a particular cell.

ideas.title: Public hazards, responsibility, and resolution
ideas.scope: Learn hazard-prioritization policies under neighborhood-dependent reporting and limited repair capacity.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Reports alone cannot measure unreported hazards or completed repairs; independent inspections are the main dependency.
ideas.impact_reason: Correcting reporting bias could improve municipal allocation, with wider value if the missingness model transfers.
ideas.gate: Obtain independent condition assessments; otherwise restrict claims to a transparent missingness model.
ideas.rated_version: Learn hazard-prioritization policies under neighborhood-dependent reporting and limited repair capacity.
ideas.audit_reason: The rating appropriately requires independent inspections. Learning only from reports can reproduce reporting inequity and cannot establish that hazards were removed.
ideas.F_note: Prioritization methods are tractable, but independent inspections and repair verification are unavailable and cannot be recovered from reports alone.
ideas.I_note: Correcting unequal reporting could improve municipal allocation, with reuse depending on whether the missingness model transfers.
ideas.original_title: B194. Public hazards, responsibility, and resolution
ideas.original_text:
There is a broken fence that sticks out near Walnut and 22nd in Philadelphia. Why hasn’t someone fixed it? Suppose anyone who walks past can send in a picture. An AI could recognize duplicate reports and forward the most urgent hazards to the responsible civic authorities. But somebody still has to take responsibility, and somebody has to check whether the fence was fixed. With limited repair crews, how do we decide which hazards need attention first, including ones in neighborhoods that rarely report them?

I also wondered whether a camera might anticipate a danger, such as a branch in the path of a cyclist, and whether something like “see something, say something” could work online. Predicting a hazard (B250) and getting it resolved are two different problems.

Related work. Kontokosta and Hong compared 311 street complaints with independent street-condition assessments and found that neighborhoods differed in their propensity to report a problem [reference in Storage]. An evaluation of a repair service could use independent inspections twice: to look for hazards that never generated a report, and to check whether a reported hazard was actually removed.

ideas.title: Discovering and checking hazards in physical scenes
ideas.scope: Separate hazard discovery from conditional verification in a small simulated-home benchmark with uncertain perception.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A constrained simulator study is plausible; reliable ground truth and novelty beyond existing hazard categories remain unresolved.
ideas.impact_reason: A conditional verification study could improve embodied evaluation, but one hazard family does not establish open-ended discovery or broad safety guarantees.
ideas.gate: Separate a new conditional-verification target from HomeSafeBench active inspection and cue-confirmation baselines, with explicit perception-error assumptions.
ideas.rated_version: Separate hazard discovery from conditional verification in a small simulated-home benchmark with uncertain perception.
ideas.audit_reason: HomeSafeBench already studies active hazard inspection and cue-to-confirmation behavior. A one-family occlusion benchmark supports a useful community result, not yet I4-level general safety impact.

audit_evidence.does: Benchmarks active free-exploration household hazard inspection and proposes cue-to-confirmation supervision.
audit_evidence.does_not: It does not establish open-ended hazard completeness or formal verification under bounded perception error.

ideas.F_note: A constrained simulator is plausible, but perception-error ground truth and a verification target beyond active hazard inspection are unresolved.
ideas.I_note: One conditional-verification study could aid embodied evaluation without establishing open-ended hazard completeness.
ideas.original_title: B250. Discovering and checking hazards in physical scenes
ideas.original_text:
I was thinking about how to make my home safe when I have a child. I can spot a sharp corner or an unstable pile of books. What I can’t do is mentally roll out all the ways an ordinary arrangement of objects might become dangerous. Could I take pictures, build a model of the room, and have a system propose things that could go wrong?

This grew out of a conversation with Maya about using formal verification outside mathematics. Ivi pointed out that a verifier can check for bad actions if we have specified what counts as bad. That leaves two problems in the home example. How do we discover the hazards we didn’t think to list, and how much can we check about a particular one from what the pictures show?

Related work. HomeSafeBench lets a model move through a simulated home and report hazards from five specified categories, including falling objects and child safety [reference in Storage]. Dean and colleagues give safety conditions for a controller operating with bounded perception error [reference in Storage]. The two approaches clarify different limits: a room model can suggest a danger I did not name, while a formal check only applies to the danger, dynamics, and uncertainty I have specified.

ideas.original_title: B195. Statistical contributions to experimental physics
ideas.original_text:
Watching the physics Nobel announcement made me want to write about doing statistics for physics. I had Efron in mind. What can a statistician contribute to the experimental work? The gravitational-wave discussion in B189 gives me one concrete place to start.

Related work. Efron and Petrosian designed a test of independence for redshift surveys in which some combinations of measurements never enter the sample [reference in Storage]. Robson and Cornish ask how LISA’s channels would distinguish a transient from an instrument glitch [reference in Storage]. Both give the essay a concrete starting point: an inference changes once one takes seriously how an instrument selects or records its observations.

ideas.title: Real versus depicted objects and inheritance rules
ideas.scope: Benchmark whether depicted status propagates through nested scenes, with controlled image composition and a relation-aware baseline.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Nested status propagation goes beyond RoLA image-level classification, but realistic transfer and a nontrivial compositional contribution remain unverified.
ideas.impact_reason: Would expose a specific compositional failure relevant to physical grounding, though its reach is narrower than general visual reasoning.
ideas.gate: Establish nested object-level failures beyond RoLA, screen masking, and a simple scene-graph baseline on real as well as composited scenes.
ideas.rated_version: Benchmark whether depicted status propagates through nested scenes, with controlled image composition and a relation-aware baseline.
ideas.audit_reason: RoLA establishes real/look-alike classification. Nested object-level status propagation is a genuine distinction, but exact-label compositing alone does not establish a sufficiently novel conference result.

audit_evidence.checked_level: primary article abstract and methods summary
audit_evidence.does: RoLA evaluates real versus look-alike exemplars and a CLIP embedding-direction classifier.
audit_evidence.does_not: The reported image-level classifier does not settle object-level inheritance through nested displayed scenes.

ideas.F_note: Nested scenes offer a concrete construction; real-image transfer and comparisons with masking and scene graphs remain to be demonstrated.
ideas.I_note: Object-level depicted-status inheritance is distinct from image-level real/look-alike classification, but addresses a specific grounding failure.
ideas.original_title: B196. Real versus depicted objects and inheritance rules
ideas.original_text:
A bowl on a table is one thing. A bowl on a table on television is another. Do object detectors such as DETR or YOLO recognize the difference? If the table is depicted on a screen, the objects resting on it inherit that status. Would we have to label that distinction explicitly in the training data, or do detectors learn it already? More generally, I wonder what object-detection problems force a model to reason through a sequence of such relationships. How would we implement one of those tasks?

Related work. Cohen, Fetaya and Rosenfeld test whether vision-language representations distinguish real instances from look-alikes such as toys and drawings [reference in Storage]. The screen example adds a relation that their image-level distinction does not settle: can the detector assign depicted status to the bowl because it belongs to a scene on the screen, while recognizing that the screen itself is present?

ideas.title: Assistive robots for older adults
ideas.scope: Test whether one robot interaction policy improves both companionship and physical activity.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Hardware access, participant recruitment, longitudinal outcomes, and study approvals are unestablished.
ideas.impact_reason: Jointly measuring social benefit and activity could guide assistive design; a small trial has limited generality.
ideas.gate: Establish a clinical or care-site collaboration and feasible outcome collection.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether one robot interaction policy improves both companionship and physical activity.
ideas.audit_reason: Hardware, care-site access, recruitment, and longitudinal outcomes are all absent. A simulator or conversational demo would not answer the original companionship/activity question.
ideas.F_note: Hardware, care-site access, participants and longitudinal outcomes are all unestablished; a conversational demonstration cannot answer the scoped question.
ideas.I_note: Joint social and activity outcomes could improve assistive-robot evaluation, but a small trial would generalize only cautiously.
ideas.original_title: B197. Assistive robots for older adults
ideas.original_text:
Could an interactive robot help an older person who is lonely or physically inactive? This is one use I had in mind when asking what a specialist model can contribute to a physical task (B110).

Related work. A randomized study of the companion robot PARO examined loneliness in residential care [reference in Storage]. In a separate cluster-randomized trial involving residents with dementia, daytime step counts fell more over ten weeks with PARO than with usual care [reference in Storage]. Those are different outcomes. If the aim is both companionship and movement, I would measure both in the same trial.

ideas.title: Monitoring invisible and chronic medical conditions
ideas.scope: Evaluate within-person symptom forecasting from motion and repeated self-reports, with uncertainty and missingness analysis.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Useful sensor-and-symptom data access is unverified, and the target remains broad.
ideas.impact_reason: A careful forecast and uncertainty study could help monitoring without claiming sensors directly measure subjective pain.
ideas.gate: Find a usable longitudinal dataset and define the forecast horizon and intervention it could inform.
ideas.rated_version: Evaluate within-person symptom forecasting from motion and repeated self-reports, with uncertainty and missingness analysis.
ideas.audit_reason: Sensor prediction of self-reports is a faithful narrowing. It must remain prediction of reported symptoms, not an objective pain measurement or diagnosis.
ideas.F_note: The longitudinal dataset, forecast horizon and useful monitoring decision are not established; sensor modeling is not the only dependency.
ideas.I_note: A careful within-person symptom forecast could support monitoring, without establishing an objective pain measure or diagnostic method.
ideas.original_title: B198. Monitoring invisible and chronic medical conditions
ideas.original_text:
What can we monitor in real time for conditions that afflict many people but aren’t covered by routine blood tests? I was thinking of back pain and other invisible or chronic symptoms. I’d like to know what can actually be measured today.

Related work. Bell and colleagues paired repeated real-time reports of pain and interference with wrist, waist and lower-back motion sensors during daily life [reference in Storage]. That design gives us a way to ask when movement helps predict changes in a person’s own pain reports; the sensor measures movement, so it cannot by itself tell us what pain felt like.

ideas.title: Preserving endangered and ancient languages with LLMs
ideas.scope: Compare grammar tests, unseen translation, and controlled production on one documented low-resource language.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A usable uncontaminated corpus, specialist production judgments, and a distinct competence comparison are not yet established.
ideas.impact_reason: Would clarify when grammatical test success overstates usable language competence, but cannot establish preservation by itself.
ideas.gate: Confirm data permissions and specialist judgments before choosing the language and claiming a production-capability result.
ideas.rated_version: Compare grammar tests, unseen translation, and controlled production on one documented low-resource language.
ideas.audit_reason: Grammar tests, translation, and production are meaningfully different. With expert judgment and data access still unverified, the project has several dependencies rather than one; F2 is safer.
ideas.F_note: Grammar-versus-production comparisons are clear, but uncontaminated data and specialist judgments are still unverified bottlenecks.
ideas.I_note: A competence mismatch would clarify language-model evaluation; one language study cannot establish preservation.
ideas.original_title: B199. Preserving endangered and ancient languages with LLMs
ideas.original_text:
Could an LLM be a reliable store of a dying or ancient language? If I give it a grammar test and it passes, what have I learned about its ability to generate the language? I worry that a model could know how to answer questions about the grammar while struggling to say what a speaker would have said.

Related work. The Kalamang translation benchmark gives a model a grammar, vocabulary and examples and asks it to translate material in both directions [reference in Storage]. Aycock and colleagues found that most of the translation gain in their experiments came from parallel examples rather than grammatical explanations [reference in Storage]. I would therefore keep grammatical judgments, translation of unseen material and free production as distinct tests, and seek speaker judgments where these are available.

ideas.title: AI for legacy semiconductor simulation tools
ideas.scope: Classify and repair agent failures on one open electronic-design workflow, separating planning from interface errors.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A small open toolchain is possible, but engineering expertise and realistic tasks are not yet secured.
ideas.impact_reason: Separating interface from engineering failures could improve specialized agents; value depends on transfer beyond one wrapper.
ideas.gate: Run a reproducible public toolchain end to end and identify failures beyond ChatEDA-style automation.
ideas.rated_version: Classify and repair agent failures on one open electronic-design workflow, separating planning from interface errors.
ideas.audit_reason: An open EDA workflow is an appropriate tractable surrogate. Benefits on it cannot substantiate claims about proprietary legacy tools without access and transfer evidence.
ideas.F_note: An open EDA task is a tractable surrogate, yet engineering expertise and a realistic end-to-end workflow are not secured.
ideas.I_note: Separating planning from interface failures could improve specialized agents, with limited evidence of transfer to proprietary legacy tools.
ideas.original_title: B200. AI for legacy semiconductor simulation tools
ideas.original_text:
My friend Chris told me that several stages of semiconductor design and manufacturing already take place entirely in simulation. I would have expected those stages to be relatively easy to accelerate with AI. To my surprise, one obstacle comes much earlier than transferring a design to the physical world. Can an agent even use the industry’s legacy design tools successfully inside the simulator?

Related work. ChatEDA turns natural-language requests into plans and code that manipulate electronic-design-automation tools [reference in Storage]. That makes tool use in a simulator a testable bottleneck: which failures come from choosing the wrong engineering operation, and which from expressing or executing the right operation in a particular legacy interface?

ideas.title: When should I drink coffee?
ideas.scope: Study an individually adapted alertness-versus-sleep objective in a small caffeine-scheduling model.
ideas.feasibility_reason: An app is easy; causal personalization and credible prospective validation are not available from a diary alone.
ideas.impact_reason: The scoped contribution is a narrow personalization extension in an already studied scheduling problem.
ideas.gate: Choose an identifiable objective and data design before recommending individual schedules.
ideas.rated_version: Study an individually adapted alertness-versus-sleep objective in a small caffeine-scheduling model.
ideas.audit_reason: The source is a product idea with a causal personalization question. Scores should concern a validated scheduling contribution, not merely displaying correlations from a diary.
ideas.F_note: A scheduling model is simple, but identifiable personal effects and prospective sleep/alertness validation are unavailable from a diary alone.
ideas.I_note: Combining personal alertness and sleep objectives is useful, though personalized caffeine scheduling already has direct precedents.
ideas.original_title: B243. When should I drink coffee?
ideas.original_text:
I had in mind an app that displays personal time series to explain when it’s optimal for me to drink coffee. But optimal for what? Being alert during work and getting to sleep afterward may favor different schedules. I’d like to be able to see that tradeoff. If I tend to drink coffee after a bad night’s sleep, the pattern in the display won’t by itself tell me what would happen if I changed the time.

Related work. 2B-Alert already used individual responses to sleep loss to recommend caffeine schedules for a target level of alertness [reference in Storage]. Gardiner and colleagues varied dose and timing in a randomized crossover trial and measured subsequent sleep [reference in Storage]. I would like to see those two outcomes together for one person; a diary alone cannot separate the effect of coffee from the effect of the bad night that prompted it.

ideas.title: A textbook that expands where understanding fails
ideas.scope: Compare targeted proof-step explanations with full explanations on later unaided transfer problems.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The interface is straightforward, but meaningful learning evaluation needs recruited participants and carefully matched tasks.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve mathematical tutoring by distinguishing immediate assistance from retained understanding.
ideas.gate: Arrange a feasible participant study with preregistered unaided-transfer outcomes.
ideas.rated_version: Compare targeted proof-step explanations with full explanations on later unaided transfer problems.
ideas.audit_reason: Unaided transfer is the right endpoint. The existing F2 correctly reflects participant and task-design dependencies rather than interface-development difficulty.
ideas.F_note: Targeted explanations are straightforward to deliver; recruiting learners and constructing matched unaided-transfer tasks are the paper bottlenecks.
ideas.I_note: Evidence about retained mathematical understanding could improve tutoring, though the targeted-help interface itself has close precedents.
ideas.original_title: B201. A textbook that expands where understanding fails
ideas.original_text:
Reading Ramdas and Wang’s book on e-values with ChatGPT, I found that what I wanted was quite terse. Give me the definitions, brief intuitions, theorem statements, and sketches of the proofs. I can try to fill in the gaps. When I get stuck, though, I’d like to point to precisely that passage and ask for a clarifying note in the margin. Why should the whole chapter get longer because I didn’t understand one step?

Another way to use such a textbook would be to read the overview, open the actual chapter, and call on the model as needed. Behrad and I discussed whether personalized lessons could have the coherence of the Stein–Shakarchi books. The reason I want to try this is to see whether it helps me learn the material faster. I can finish more projects using mathematics I already know without learning new mathematics any faster. Davis pointed out that the tool can improve and I can get better at using it. Could I track the pace at which I come to understand unfamiliar material alongside the amount of work I finish? If AI doesn’t meaningfully accelerate human learning, I’m not sure how we will stay in control of research.

Related work. ScholarPhi places definitions of terms and symbols at the point where a reader encounters them [reference in Storage], and IRead tests how much visual and textual assistance to give someone reading a textbook [reference in Storage]. For a terse mathematics chapter I would ask whether expanding one stuck proof step leads to faster independent work on a new problem after the notes are closed.

ideas.title: A conformal reviewer, with complementary proof assistance
ideas.scope: Calibrate the false-criticism rate for one class of verifiable mathematical review comments.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Sunay has the calibration expertise; independently validating criticisms and constructing representative evaluation data are the hard parts.
ideas.impact_reason: A narrowly validated criticism-calibration study could improve mathematical reviewing; broad reliable-review impact depends on labels and transfer not yet established.
ideas.gate: Label correctness independently of whether authors accepted an edit; start with checkable local claims.
ideas.rated_version: Calibrate the false-criticism rate for one class of verifiable mathematical review comments.
ideas.audit_reason: Author edits are selective noisy labels, not correctness labels. A small calibrated criticism study is plausible, but its realistic contribution has community-level rather than already transferable I4 impact.
ideas.F_note: Calibration methods fit existing expertise; independent correctness labels and representative review comments require substantial curation.
ideas.I_note: Reliable criticism could improve mathematical review, but the narrow labeled class limits claims of broad reviewer reliability.
ideas.original_title: B202. A conformal reviewer, with complementary proof assistance
ideas.original_text:
Could we train a conformal reviewer from the successive versions of arXiv papers? GoodPoint made me wonder what constructive feedback we might be able to calibrate. Is the final diff enough, or does it help to see how the authors got there? Papers that go through many revisions might differ from the papers we eventually want to review. Sima raised a more fundamental objection. If the target is to reproduce the human’s changes, how will we reward the model for catching something everyone missed? Conversely, several models can take the same wrong turn that a human spots immediately.

Riley would welcome a reviewer that simply points out unclear passages. He still wants to check his proofs himself, whereas Hari would value help with verification. Riley also suggested giving an assistant a proof sketch with several lemmas left open. Let it choose the ones it can handle and hand the argument back when it gets stuck.

Shayan suggested using weak and strong verification when there are more submissions than human reviewers can read closely. Behrad raised a different constraint. He’d let a model check the algebra but would want a human to decide independently whether the question was interesting and well motivated. Could the reviewer record that judgment before seeing the model’s report?

Related work. GoodPoint labels constructive feedback from author responses [reference in Storage], while arXivEdits aligns successive drafts and annotates why passages changed [reference in Storage]. Conformal risk control bounds a specified monotone loss under exchangeability [reference in Storage]. What loss would give credit for a correct criticism that no author acted on, and would heavily revised papers represent the intended submissions? Bansal et al. found that explanations increased acceptance of AI advice even when it was wrong [reference in Storage], which makes me want to compare a reviewer who records an independent judgment first with one who sees the model’s report immediately.

ideas.title: Fixed points of repeated AI peer review
ideas.scope: Test whether review-loop stabilization predicts independently checked mathematical correctness, then calibrate a stopping or escalation rule.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Revision trajectories are easy to collect; authentic error labels and a stopping signal beyond existing diagnostics remain substantial dependencies.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve mathematical-review stopping decisions, but a bounded diagnostic study is a community contribution rather than a general oversight advance.
ideas.gate: Improve verification cost at fixed residual error against confidence, edit distance, fixed-round review, and independent-review baselines.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether review-loop stabilization predicts independently checked mathematical correctness, then calibrate a stopping or escalation rule.
ideas.audit_reason: Stabilization cannot certify correctness. The revised scope is defensible because it requires independent errors and comparison with simple stopping baselines.
ideas.F_note: Revision loops are inexpensive to collect; independent mathematical error labels and a stopping advantage over simple diagnostics constrain readiness.
ideas.I_note: A reliable stabilization diagnostic could improve mathematical-review workflows, but self-refinement and agreement themselves are established.
ideas.original_title: B274. Fixed points of repeated AI peer review
ideas.original_text:
Suppose I send a manuscript to Refine, have an agent revise it in light of the review, and send the result straight back. Where does the manuscript go after many rounds? It could settle on a version that attracts no further substantive change. I’d want to know whether the arguments had improved along the way, and whether the same errors survived every round.

I later wondered about using approximate stability under a frontier model’s revisions as a desk-rejection criterion. What counts as a consequential change here? A reviewer that keeps rewriting a sound proof for style and one that keeps finding genuine gaps would give very different meanings to the same failure to settle down.

Related work. Self-Refine repeatedly asks a language model for feedback and a revision [reference in Storage]. Liang et al. compare model-generated comments on real research papers with human feedback [reference in Storage]. Taken together, these suggest a way to test the fixed-point proposal: track independently checked errors through several rounds and ask whether they disappear before the wording stops changing.

ideas.title: Keeping a web of research consistent as it changes
ideas.scope: Detect which informal proof claims become unsupported after an assumption or lemma changes.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A curated set of controlled corrections is feasible; dependable labels for real informal dependencies require expert work.
ideas.impact_reason: Claim-level correction propagation addresses a growing bottleneck in maintaining AI-assisted mathematical research.
ideas.gate: Separate true logical dependencies from contextual citations using blinded expert labels.
ideas.rated_version: Detect which informal proof claims become unsupported after an assumption or lemma changes.
ideas.audit_reason: The correction-propagation target is specific and consequential. I4 remains conditional on real assumption changes and useful claims beyond synthetic citation matching; expert labels are the major uncertainty.
ideas.F_note: Controlled assumption changes provide a concrete benchmark route; expert labels separating logical dependence from contextual citation remain the bottleneck.
ideas.I_note: Reliable propagation of corrections through informal research would address a reusable bottleneck that formal dependency tools do not directly solve.
ideas.original_title: B204. Keeping a web of research consistent as it changes
ideas.original_text:
I ran into this while revising the routing paper. We had already generated extensions, and now a correction to the base paper could change an argument in an extension that still read perfectly well. Could a system tell me which claims actually depended on the part I had changed? Could the agent then make the corresponding edits to the follow-up papers as I revise the base? As the collection grows, I would also like a short trail of prerequisites into an unfamiliar idea and a way to see when a newer paper supersedes an older one. Amir suggested visualizing the web of research. If models generate more mathematics than anyone can read, could we group the results into subfields well enough for a person to decide which direction to pursue? I thought of starting by extracting open problems from Weijie’s high-dimensional statistics survey. Behrad pointed out that the choice of problems is subjective and that the survey leaves out much of deep-learning theory.

There is a related problem with the shape of a conversation. A linear chat makes it hard to follow a side idea or recover from a wrong turn without starting over. Could I branch it, or give a model a Google Doc along with the discussion in its margins? I also tried to recover a paper’s exposition from a sketch and a compact style guide. That attempt failed. I hadn’t even settled what would count as reproducing the style.

Related work. Alama, Mamane and Urban extract statement-level dependencies from formal Coq and Mizar libraries [reference in Storage]; the oai-math-revised project instead invites people to repair exposition and citations in informal write-ups [reference in Storage]. For an informal extension of a paper, can the system point to the exact step that uses a changed assumption and distinguish that dependence from a citation included only for context?

ideas.title: Citation rules for provisional and verified mathematics
ideas.scope: Analyze error propagation and verification scheduling on a dependency graph of provisional mathematical claims.
ideas.feasibility_reason: A stylized graph model is tractable, but the per-claim error semantics and relation to real citation practices need care.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify speed-versus-repair tradeoffs in one decision setting; broader institutional consequences would require further evidence.
ideas.gate: Define a falsifiable error event and compare against existing online testing and verification scheduling.
ideas.rated_version: Analyze error propagation and verification scheduling on a dependency graph of provisional mathematical claims.
ideas.audit_reason: A graph error model must distinguish invalid dependency use from a benign citation to a false paper. Generic branching-process propagation plus standard online testing would be incremental.
ideas.F_note: A stylized dependency graph is easy to study, but falsifiable claim-error semantics and an advance beyond existing verification scheduling remain unresolved.
ideas.I_note: A speed-versus-repair result would clarify one research-maintenance setting, not by itself justify an institutional publication policy.
ideas.original_title: B268. Citation rules for provisional and verified mathematics
ideas.original_text:
What if mathematicians could publish on two tracks? A provisional paper would be labeled as such and could cite work on either track. A formally verified paper could cite only other formally verified papers. Even if an AI could formalize my proof quickly, I’d have to wait for its dependencies before putting it on the verified track.

The provisional track could move very fast. If a result turned out to be false, though, someone would have to trace which later arguments relied on it and propagate the correction. How much of the initial gain in speed survives that repair work? Could we impose some statistical error-rate control on each provisional paper? I hadn’t worked out what error to control.

Related work. The Lean mathlib community describes how a library of checked mathematics shares definitions, proofs and dependencies [reference in Storage]. A formally verified paper could cite only other formally verified papers. ideas.title: Problem formulation as a credited research artifact
ideas.scope: Evaluate a small corpus of problem formulations through reproducible solver attempts and expert assessment of missed requirements.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Collecting formulations is possible; defining and validating formulation quality remains open.
ideas.impact_reason: Could make problem specification measurable and reusable, but a publishing platform alone adds little scientific evidence.
ideas.gate: Choose one problem domain and an independent criterion for fidelity to the motivating task.
ideas.rated_version: Evaluate a small corpus of problem formulations through reproducible solver attempts and expert assessment of missed requirements.
ideas.audit_reason: Solver mismatch can make formulation quality measurable, but a product or credit proposal alone does not. F2 is appropriate until one domain supplies independently judged requirements.
ideas.F_note: Collecting solver attempts is straightforward; independently judging whether a formulation matches its motivating problem is not yet operational.
ideas.I_note: Reusable evidence about formulation quality could support research practice, whereas a credit platform alone supplies no new scientific result.
ideas.original_title: B205. Problem formulation as a credited research artifact
ideas.original_text:
Suppose someone notices a real-world problem, someone else finds the mathematical formulation that makes it tractable, and a third person solves it. Why should only the solution count as a research contribution? I’d like a place to publish a good problem formulation on its own. With AI there to attempt solutions, we could try this locally: put a problem up, see what a few inexpensive attempts get wrong, and go back to the person who framed it. Sometimes the interesting work would be recognizing that what was solved wasn’t quite what the original observation called for.

Behrad suggested posting formulations publicly for comment. I’d like the author to be able to attach the model and its deterministic settings, so someone else can rerun the solver and see the intended solution. If submissions grew, could a small group of people use models to sort them by subject and judge which formulations deserve attention?

Related work. The Conference on Learning Theory already publishes authored open problems; the direct-sums paper is one concrete example of a formulation receiving credit before a full solution [reference in Storage]. The extra artifact I have in mind would show how a solver interpreted the formulation and let the original observer explain where that interpretation departed from the motivating problem.

ideas.title: Helping researchers move between fields, and bringing problems to new solvers
ideas.scope: Test whether structured prerequisite bridges help mathematically trained users solve one unfamiliar technical task.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Needs destination-domain expertise, matched tasks, and participant access; broad career transition is outside twelve weeks.
ideas.impact_reason: A successful bridge could improve cross-field learning, but one task would support only limited conclusions.
ideas.gate: Identify a destination task and a measurable transfer outcome beyond self-reported familiarity.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether structured prerequisite bridges help mathematically trained users solve one unfamiliar technical task.
ideas.audit_reason: A specific prerequisite bridge is faithful to the transfer-learning question. Participant access and destination-domain evaluation remain separate dependencies.
ideas.F_note: A prerequisite bridge can be bounded to one task, but participants and destination-domain expertise are unverified dependencies.
ideas.I_note: Demonstrated transfer would inform cross-field teaching, while a single task supports limited conclusions about research or career transitions.
ideas.original_title: B206. Helping researchers move between fields, and bringing problems to new solvers
ideas.original_text:
What will mathematicians do if AI displaces some of the work they trained for? I imagine people in materials science, hardware design, or computational biology helping build a path into their field for a particular mathematician. What carries over? Perhaps the willingness, sometimes even the enjoyment, of following a difficult logical or algorithmic argument for a long time. The people already working in the destination field would know where that ability is useful and what else the newcomer needs to learn. Take the design of a new kernel for an ML system. Which parts could a mathematician pick up quickly and which require practice building systems? Xinmeng emphasized the qualitative mathematical intuition behind inventing an architecture. I’d like to know how someone acquires that intuition.

There is another way to make the connection. Could we take a frontier problem and expose its essential puzzle in terms someone outside the field can understand? I would like to give that person a shot at the central difficulty. Dividing the specialist’s work into small errands for other people would miss the point. Could we do this at a scale that puts many more eyes on a problem, including digital ones?

Related work. Jeppesen and Lakhani studied broadcast scientific challenges and found that solvers from less closely related technical fields could have an advantage [reference in Storage]. Their result concerns self-selected entrants to discrete contests; it leaves open how to explain a field’s central puzzle to a newcomer and how to tell which skills transfer to sustained work there.

ideas.title: Personalization without overfitting to the individual
ideas.scope: Design a user-memory representation that preserves explanatory personalization while resisting belief-induced factual errors.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Paired tests and existing memory benchmarks are accessible, but direct prior work substantially narrows novelty.
ideas.impact_reason: Useful personalization with factual invariance matters, yet a small benchmark or generic anti-sycophancy prompt would be incremental.
ideas.gate: Beat memory-specific mitigations while measuring both personalization benefit and factual consistency.
ideas.rated_version: Design a user-memory representation that preserves explanatory personalization while resisting belief-induced factual errors.
ideas.audit_reason: The source focuses personalization-induced agreement. Require a measurable explanation benefit as well as factual invariance; removing all user context is not a successful personalization solution.
ideas.F_note: Paired belief interventions and memory benchmarks are accessible; a representation must preserve personalization benefits while beating direct anti-sycophancy baselines.
ideas.I_note: Factual invariance with useful personalization has broad assistant relevance, but generic prompting and benchmark-only gains would be incremental.
ideas.original_title: B207. Personalization without overfitting to the individual
ideas.original_text:
How do we navigate the tradeoff between personalization and objectivity? In my experience ChatGPT sometimes gets too good at answering in my terms. I would like an assistant to know enough about me to explain something well, and still be able to tell me when I’ve got it wrong.

Related work. Sharma and colleagues show that assistants trained with human feedback can shift an answer toward an expressed user view, including when that view is wrong [reference in Storage]. A useful paired test would keep the question fixed and vary only the stated belief: the explanation may adapt to the reader, but contradictory beliefs should not reverse a well-supported conclusion.

ideas.original_title: B208. A personalized monitor of relevant research
ideas.original_text:
Could a monitor pick out new research relevant to me and explain why it matters in terms I understand? I had industry practitioners in mind in particular. A paper can be directly relevant to someone’s work even when its title and abstract give them little reason to open it.

Related work. Scholar Inbox uses readers’ paper ratings to learn personalized rankings and suggests papers for users to rate when their interests are still unclear [reference in Storage]. For a practitioner, I would test the proposed explanation separately from the ranking: can the reader identify a decision the paper bears on, even when its title uses unfamiliar terminology?

ideas.original_title: B210. Attributing mathematical ideas in generated proofs
ideas.original_text:
When a model writes a proof, it can pull in an idea from earlier work without naming the people who developed it. Could we encourage appropriate attribution during training? Or could we give a separate system the completed argument and ask which steps owe the reader a reference? A useful answer would tell me what prior idea the citation explains. We may be able to recognize the argument in the literature even when we cannot know what the model actually relied on to generate it.

Related work. CiteWorth studies which sentences in scientific papers carry citations [reference in Storage], and DeepMath learns to select premises for formal proofs [reference in Storage]. For an informal proof, neither a citation-shaped sentence nor a useful premise settles attribution: the reference should explain the particular idea at that step without claiming to reveal what the generating model consulted.

ideas.title: Doctor--AI collaboration and evidence-backed diagnosis
ideas.scope: Test evidence-seeking diagnostic critiques against initial diagnoses on public clinical vignettes and a small clinician study.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Automated vignette evaluation is feasible; demonstrating human-AI complementarity requires clinician access and careful study design.
ideas.impact_reason: A workflow that improves on both doctor and AI could matter widely; vignette-only gains would support a weaker claim.
ideas.gate: Secure clinical expertise and compare against AI alone, doctor alone, and structured second opinions.
ideas.rated_version: Test evidence-seeking diagnostic critiques against initial diagnoses on public clinical vignettes and a small clinician study.
ideas.audit_reason: The proposed human-AI comparison preserves the source. I4 requires improvement over both parties and structured second opinions; automated vignette gains alone merit lower impact.
ideas.F_note: Vignette automation is feasible; clinician access and a study capable of testing human-AI complementarity are the main bottlenecks.
ideas.I_note: Improvement over both doctors and AI could transfer widely in diagnosis, but must exceed existing structured-opinion workflows.
ideas.original_title: B213. Doctor--AI collaboration and evidence-backed diagnosis
ideas.original_text:
What kind of interaction would let a doctor and an LLM diagnose a case better together than either could alone? A study comparing doctors with and without access to an LLM made me wonder whether having the model there can make it too easy to stop thinking through a case. What if the model could play devil’s advocate, offering objections to a proposed diagnosis? I also wondered whether an agent could retrieve the data and studies supporting each step of the argument. How do we keep it from searching until it finds support for the diagnosis it has already chosen?

Related work. Goh and colleagues found no significant benefit from giving physicians ordinary LLM access on clinical vignettes [reference in Storage]. In a later trial, Everett and colleagues found that structured first- and second-opinion workflows improved scores over conventional resources, without a significant difference from the AI alone [reference in Storage]. I would ask whether a devil’s advocate can improve on both baselines by retrieving evidence against the initial diagnosis as well as evidence for it.

ideas.title: Identifying musical taste through experiments
ideas.scope: Use controlled stem interventions and adaptive comparisons to identify one listener-relevant musical feature.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Stimuli can be generated, but isolating the intended feature and collecting reliable preferences are substantial uncertainties.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve causal preference elicitation if effects survive collateral acoustic changes.
ideas.gate: Verify intervention specificity and compare adaptive selection against random paired listening trials.
ideas.rated_version: Use controlled stem interventions and adaptive comparisons to identify one listener-relevant musical feature.
ideas.audit_reason: Changing one audio stem can alter timbre, harmony, rhythm, and perceived balance. The stated gate correctly requires intervention specificity rather than assuming it.
ideas.F_note: Audio stems permit interventions, but isolating one perceptual feature and obtaining stable listener preferences are substantial experimental dependencies.
ideas.I_note: Feature-specific causal preference elicitation would be informative, with first-listener results and collateral acoustic changes limiting reach.
ideas.original_title: B214. Identifying musical taste through experiments
ideas.original_text:
If someone says they like a song because of the bass line, could we find out whether that’s really the feature driving their taste? An automated experimenter could suggest candidate features, vary one, and ask the listener again. The difficulty is getting enough genuine variation in that feature while holding the rest of the music reasonably fixed. I don’t even know how one would turn up or down a feature that is itself a nonlinear function of an entire time series.

Related work. Witek and colleagues varied the syncopation of drum breaks and measured pleasure and the desire to move [reference in Storage]. MusicGen-Stem can replace a bass part while conditioning on the remaining stems [reference in Storage]. That makes a useful pair of listening trials possible, although I would still need to check whether changing the bass also changed other things the listener noticed.

ideas.title: First impressions and AI model adoption
ideas.scope: Randomize chatbot style at first exposure and measure later choice after matched-quality interactions.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The faithful question needs participant access and repeated model-choice opportunities; a single-session preference test would answer less.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify a concrete human-AI adoption mechanism and inform the design of learning tools.
ideas.gate: Separate initial style from answer quality and include an opportunity to return to the rejected model.
ideas.rated_version: Randomize chatbot style at first exposure and measure later choice after matched-quality interactions.
ideas.audit_reason: Recruitment and longitudinal adoption outcomes are unestablished; a one-session preference experiment would answer a weaker question. F2 better reflects the faithful scope.
ideas.F_note: A style manipulation is clear, but recruitment and repeated opportunities to revisit a rejected model are not secured.
ideas.I_note: A demonstrated adoption mechanism could improve human-AI design, while first-impression effects have substantial behavioral precedents.
ideas.original_title: B215. First impressions and AI model adoption
ideas.original_text:
My first impression of GPT-5 was that it was verbose and sycophantic, and after that I stopped using it. How much does a bad first impression shape which model a person keeps using? I wondered whether we could learn something about that from surveys or from people’s subsequent choices in their chat histories.

Related work. After seeing a forecasting algorithm make a mistake, people sometimes abandoned it even when it outperformed them [reference in Storage]. In a later experiment an early error reduced reliance more persistently than a late one when people had to choose between their own prediction and the algorithm’s; the timing effect disappeared when they could adjust how they used the prediction [reference in Storage]. I would like to know whether disliking a chatbot’s style on the first encounter likewise changes later model choice, including whether a user ever returns.

ideas.title: A personal mathematical knowledge and cognition archive
ideas.scope: Test whether a small personal mathematics archive improves explanation transfer to held-out concepts.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Recording is easy; validating captured intuition and effects on actual learning needs careful self-study or participant design.
ideas.impact_reason: A single-person archive offers limited generality without a transferable method and independent learning outcomes.
ideas.gate: Compare archive-conditioned explanations with standard personalization and later unaided problem solving.
ideas.rated_version: Test whether a small personal mathematics archive improves explanation transfer to held-out concepts.
ideas.audit_reason: A personal archive can be built quickly, but capturing unspoken intuition is not validated by retrieval success. Narrow impact and the need for unaided learning outcomes are appropriate.
ideas.F_note: A personal archive is easy to assemble; unaided learning outcomes and evidence that unspoken intuition was captured are much less ready.
ideas.I_note: A one-person archive has narrow scientific reach unless a transferable learning benefit is independently demonstrated.
ideas.original_title: B216. A personal mathematical knowledge and cognition archive
ideas.original_text:
What if I did a day’s worth of mathematics out loud? Andrej Karpathy’s personal knowledge wiki could include the recording. An assistant might then pick up some of the language and nonvisual intuitions I actually use when I think, and translate a collaborator’s idea into those terms. Would recording change the very habits I wanted to study? Even recordings confined to research would raise questions about privacy.

I would also like to listen for strategies we might try in a reasoning model. Coming back from the gym, I thought to wash my hands, then remembered I still had to take out the trash. That little look ahead changed the order of my actions. How often do I explicitly roll things out, and when do I just use a judgment built up from earlier experience?

There is another habit I’d like to listen for. When I first learn a concept like a group action, I try using it in conversation before I fully understand it. Does using the language help me learn the mathematics?

Related work. Karpathy’s LLM Wiki describes a model maintaining a personal knowledge base [reference in Storage]; MyLifeBits explored collecting and retrieving records from one person’s life [reference in Storage]. For the mathematical recordings, a useful distinction is between saying what already comes to mind and being asked to explain why: think-aloud studies found little average change in accuracy for the former, unlike directed explanations [reference in Storage]. Neither result tells me whether a recording captures the intuitions I never verbalize.

ideas.original_title: B218. A hypothesis-testing teaching story
ideas.original_text: One morning before the gym I couldn’t find my wallet. On the treadmill I retraced my steps. Either the wallet was in my room or I’d left it somewhere else in the building. It occurred to me that I could turn this into a hypothesis test simply by waiting. If someone used my card, I’d have evidence for the second possibility. Of course, the power of my test depended on somebody finding the wallet and deciding to use it. Feeling rather pleased with this statistical solution, I opened my sock drawer. There was my wallet.

ideas.original_title: B261. Teaching AI as a unified subject
ideas.original_text:
The preface to the Stein–Shakarchi books talks about making plain the unity between different parts of a subject. I’d love to see someone try that for AI. Statistics, computer science, information theory, and neuroscience all have something to say about it, but a student could take courses in all four and still wonder how their accounts fit together. Is there already a course that presents AI as a unified subject in this sense? If it doesn’t exist, I wonder who could teach it. I don’t know one person with the necessary range, but perhaps a duo could do it.

Related work. Russell and Norvig organize search, uncertainty, learning and decision-making around the intelligent agent [reference in Storage]. That gives a concrete answer to the question of how one course might unify much of AI. I would compare how far that organizing principle takes a student when the same phenomenon also has a statistical, information-theoretic or neuroscientific account.

ideas.original_title: B238. Automated discovery of webpage bugs and edge cases
ideas.original_text:
Why aren’t webpages technically flawless by now? I’d like an automated way to find the bugs and edge cases a developer missed and show how to reproduce them.

Related work. Mesbah and van Deursen already crawled interactive pages, checked conditions on the states they reached, and generated test cases from the paths they traversed [reference in Storage]. Those paths are a useful model for reproducible bug reports. The harder cases are states a crawler never reaches and failures for which nobody has written down what correct behavior looks like.

ideas.original_title: B239. Webpages that adapt their presentation to the user
ideas.original_text:
Why can’t I regenerate a webpage on the fly to suit my own needs? I might prefer a different layout for aesthetic reasons, or need one that makes the site easier to read or navigate.

Related work. Supple generated interfaces adapted to a user’s abilities and preferences, improving speed and accuracy for participants with motor impairments [reference in Storage]. Chickenfoot let users change rendered pages from within their browsers [reference in Storage]. The combination I have in mind would let someone ask for a different presentation of an existing page and still complete the same task on it.

ideas.original_title: B241. An evidence-based explanation of why a computer is slow
ideas.original_text:
I’d like an app that explains why my computer is slow. When several things are running, can it tell me which one is holding up what I’m trying to do?

Related work. Basu, Dunagan, and Smith built a tool that ranked anomalous processes and resources at the moment someone reported a slowdown [reference in Storage]. Coz asked a different question inside a program: would speeding up a particular piece of code improve the performance measure the developer cares about [reference in Storage]? For a desktop explanation, I would like to distinguish a process that happens to be busy from one whose activity delays the action I am waiting for.

ideas.original_title: B246. Affordable creative tools and science through art
ideas.original_text:
I’d like to put inexpensive tools in people’s hands to make good music and videos, especially music videos. I also love educational materials that bring science and art together. Animation lets a scientist and an artist show something that can be quite hard to get across in prose. BrainPOP and the illustrated stories of scientists by Villani and Edmond Baudoin come to mind. I’d love to see more collaborations of that kind.

Related work. Scratch is one example of putting the means to create and share animations into the hands of beginners [reference in Storage]. Villani and Baudoin’s illustrated portraits of four scientists offer a different precedent: the scientific storytelling itself is shared between a mathematician and an artist [reference in Storage]. I am interested in making collaborations of that kind easier for people who want to work in music and moving images.

ideas.original_title: B220. A science of safety begins with understandable systems
ideas.original_text:
Sara asked why Mahdi thought AI safety had become an engineering problem. He had spent a long time trying to bring ideas from optimization and learning theory to defenses and to getting a model to follow a constitution. My sense is that to develop a science we first need a system simple enough that we can poke it, perturb something, and see why the output changes. If we go straight to stacking a hundred LLM judges because the stack happens to work, what do we learn about the simplest mechanism? I would like to start with something we can understand well enough to say what we mean by alignment.

Related work. AI Safety Gridworlds made some failures easy to study by giving an agent a reward and separately specifying how its behavior would be evaluated [reference in Storage]. Constitutional AI used written principles to guide critiques, revisions, and model feedback [reference in Storage]. A small example in which changing one principle changes one identifiable behavior would let me ask how the principle produces that change.

ideas.original_title: B221. When theory becomes valuable in a mature engineering pipeline
ideas.original_text:
Sara relayed a thought from Maggi. As long as engineering changes keep improving the models, why would a lab look elsewhere for ideas? When progress levels off, there might be a real demand for theory that tells people what to try next. I found that plausible. I’d like to know who will have something to offer when that happens.

After a separate conversation with Michael Tang, I wondered how much freedom there was to change an established lab’s training pipeline. If a great deal of the work consists of watching and debugging very large runs, perhaps a smaller lab still choosing its architectures would have different problems to work on. That was my impression at the time.

Related work. The maximal-update parametrization offers a case in which theory changed a practical decision: Yang and colleagues tuned hyperparameters on smaller networks and transferred them to larger ones [reference in Storage]. It gives me something concrete to ask a lab about—what made the cost of tuning worth addressing, and when would a result like this actually change its training pipeline?

ideas.original_title: B226. Why a mature applied problem may require distant mathematics
ideas.original_text:
One reason I like coding theory as an example of good applied math is that the engineering question was clear from the outset. People wanted to communicate reliably. After the problem had been worked on for a long time, some of the remaining questions led into mathematics as distant as additive combinatorics. Where else has a practical problem been understood well enough that one can see precisely what is still missing, even if the tool that will settle it comes from somewhere unexpected?

Related work. Guruswami and Velingker needed to bound how much entropy grows when independent copies of a random variable are added. Their sumset inequality gave a polynomial bound on the block length polar codes need to approach capacity over prime alphabets [reference in Storage]. Here the engineering quantity and the mathematical obstacle can both be named.

ideas.original_title: B222. Useful mathematical structure versus decorative abstraction
ideas.original_text:
Sara asked whether neural networks might inspire new mathematics the way physics has. I thought of a connection to statistical physics that I do understand a little. Spin-glass models turn up in high-dimensional matrix denoising and regression, and the physics can help predict something a statistician wants to know, such as the asymptotic risk of an estimator. That’s the kind of payoff I would look for in an analogy between a neural network and a physical system. What quantity does the analogy help us explain or calculate?

Related work. For a symmetric low-rank signal in Gaussian matrix noise, Lelarge and Miolane gave rigorous formulas for the information-theoretic estimation limit [reference in Storage]. In proportional-dimensional robust regression, Donoho and Montanari characterized the asymptotic variance of M-estimators using approximate message passing [reference in Storage]. These are examples of the payoff I have in mind: a quantity and a model precise enough that a prediction inspired by statistical physics can be checked.

ideas.original_title: B267. When notation changes what a mathematician sees
ideas.original_text:
Edgar has often wondered why neighboring fields use different notation for isomorphic objects. I sympathize every time I have to translate a paper. But I’d like to find a problem where an information theorist’s notation makes one move easy to see and a statistician’s notation makes another move easy to see. What disappears when we standardize on either one?

Perhaps good notation compresses an argument. The interesting case would be two descriptions that compress different parts of the very same argument. Then the choice of symbols might influence which step someone discovers first.

Related work. Iverson’s Turing lecture develops examples in which a notation makes a generalization or proof easier to see [reference in Storage]. I would like a paired example: give two groups the same mathematical problem in two isomorphic notations, and ask which intermediate step each group finds first.

ideas.original_title: B223. Important applications should drive the mathematical formulation
ideas.original_text:
I would like to start with a problem whose importance I can explain before I know what mathematics it will take. A delivery worker taking a risk to complete an order, or a financial system becoming unstable, gives me a reason to care about the eventual answer. Then comes the part I find difficult. Which feature of that situation should go into the mathematical problem, and would solving it tell me something about what originally caught my attention?

Related work. Interviews with Sydney delivery riders identified waiting at restaurants and handling several orders at once as sources of time pressure [reference in Storage]. In a different setting, Eisenberg and Noe turned the question of who can pay whom after a financial shock into a clearing problem on a network of obligations [reference in Storage]. The useful question in each case is which details one must retain for the answer to refer back to the people or institutions one started with.
