ideas.original_title: B224. Curiosity, peer incentives, and intellectual equilibria
ideas.original_text:
In my high-school science group I asked why the enjoyment of learning can fade. There are things we once thought about for the sheer pleasure of thinking about them. What happens when the people around us start valuing comfort, money, or the impression we make on someone else? Perhaps we settle into an equilibrium where nobody spends very long thinking about simple things.

I asked Behrad a related question about research funding. Would someone try a genuinely different problem if they had long-term support at an institute, or a grant specifically for an unconventional idea? What kinds of work do the usual incentives leave unexplored?

Hearing about Talagrand’s early CNRS appointment made me wonder about a US pilot offering long-term research positions straight out of college. How would we choose people before they have a publication record that tells us much? For researchers further along, I’d like to compare tenure with a long fixed-term appointment. Behrad asked whether the prospect of having to find another position would itself discourage work that takes years to pay off.

I also asked what would happen if an ML conference held recruiting separately from the scientific meeting. Do good problems get passed over because they interest few recruiters or because they won’t yield a paper by the next deadline? Behrad pointed to the smaller workshops, where it’s easier to have a sustained conversation about the research.

Related work. Bursztyn and Jensen found that making educational effort visible to classmates could change students’ choices [reference in Storage]. In the life sciences, HHMI investigators receiving long, flexible support produced more highly cited work than matched researchers with conventional grants [reference in Storage], while a survey experiment found that marginal changes in grant size or duration did more to change who wanted the grant than what recipients said they would do [reference in Storage]. That distinction matters for the proposed appointments: attracting adventurous people and inducing the same person to try a different problem are different effects.

ideas.original_text: When someone tells me to focus, I want to ask what problem they have in mind. I can see why it pays to stay in one area long enough to produce papers and become known for them. I’m also drawn to wandering across applied questions until I find one I can’t leave alone. What makes a problem interesting enough to keep returning to it? I’d rather have one of those problems than another argument for focus.

ideas.original_title: B228. An AI-enabled transition that preserves academic participation
ideas.original_text:
Reading Tristan Buckmaster’s account of the recent Navier–Stokes episode, I thought there had to be a way for AI developers and academic researchers to do this work together. The people who spent years formulating a problem can have a great deal to contribute once a model makes progress on it. Would involving them in the work, and recognizing what each side brought to it, make it easier for researchers to see a future for themselves using these tools? The way a result is developed and introduced to a community matters to me.

Related work. Buckmaster’s own account distinguishes proposing a line of attack, directing models, checking a proof, and writing an argument others can read [reference in Storage]. Davies and colleagues documented a collaboration in knot theory and representation theory in which machine learning suggested patterns and mathematicians turned them into results [reference in Storage]. These accounts give me concrete contributions to ask about when discussing credit; they do not establish how any particular policy would change researchers’ willingness to participate.

ideas.original_title: B229. Experimental outcomes and architectural details as sources of research value
ideas.original_text:
Thomas made two observations I liked. Even a very capable model hasn’t seen the outcome of an experiment nobody has run. Somebody still has to frame the experiment, spend the compute, and see what happens. And sometimes what gets a method adopted is an apparently small detail that makes it work on the hardware. He gave the examples of Newton–Schulz iteration in Muon and the WY parameterization in DeltaNet.

I asked Ivi about Sepp Hochreiter’s work for much the same reason. Could I learn enough about the details of an architecture to improve one of them mathematically? Ivi pointed out a good reason to keep working on black-box methods, too: the boxes change.

Related work. The Muon authors used a short Newton–Schulz iteration to make approximate orthogonalization of matrix updates feasible during training [reference in Storage]. In DeltaNet, Yang and colleagues used a compact WY representation to parallelize the delta-rule recurrence across a sequence [reference in Storage]. These are two concrete cases where a mathematical implementation detail changed which experiments could be run at scale.

ideas.original_title: B230. Revisiting difficult theory with stronger research tools
ideas.original_text:
Are there problems that a theory community stopped working on because the calculations or proofs were too difficult, and that we ought to revisit now that we have better tools? I was thinking of deep-learning theory in particular. I’ve been away from some of that literature long enough that I’d first have to find out which obstacles people still care about. I’d especially like a problem where doing the mathematics would leave us with an algorithm we could actually run.

Related work. Janzamin, Sedghi, and Anandkumar turned a learnability question for two-layer networks into a tensor-decomposition algorithm with explicit assumptions [reference in Storage]. Outside deep-learning theory, AlphaDev used search to find short sorting routines that were incorporated into a software library [reference in Storage]. Those examples give me a criterion for revisiting an old calculation: what algorithm would I be able to implement if the obstacle were removed?

ideas.original_title: B231. Research workflow and collaboration scaffolding
ideas.original_text:
Dwip, Emre and I are college friends now working in different groups. How quickly can we get familiar enough with one another’s subjects to recognize the few algorithmic ideas that matter? On May 29 we discussed a small Qwen experiment. If a model is stuck on a geometry problem, could moving to an algebraic problem for a while help it see a connection? We had more ideas like this than we could try one by one. Could we run several small independent trials in parallel, then move the promising questions into their own working papers?

Tao reminded me that a principled algorithm can explain a phenomenon even when it doesn’t beat the best empirical method. The AI-generated brainstorm with David offered a useful discipline for a pilot: pick one phenomenon, a mechanism that could explain it, and a small experiment whose outcome could change our minds.

For theory projects, I’d like our group to share the prompts and a small set of tools we actually use. When someone gets a model to make progress on a hard argument, can another person start from that setup and see whether it helps with their problem?

Related work. Analogical prompting asks a model to generate relevant examples before it solves a target problem; Yasunaga and colleagues found gains on several reasoning benchmarks [reference in Storage]. Our geometry-to-algebra detour asks something different: once a model is already stuck, does briefly switching problems help more than using the same number of tokens to continue or restart?

ideas.original_title: B233. Research learning, community, and career notes
ideas.original_text:
Statistical theory must be learned slowly. You must savor it as you read. Theory, by its very nature, will wait. I want a shelf of well-thumbed physical books, like Edgar and Hamed have. Thomas and I also talked about learning by meeting people, finding a problem, and picking up tools as we go. There’s room for both kinds of learning.

I follow Morgane Austern, Francis Bach, Surbhi Goel, Enric Boix-Adsera, Meena Jagadeesan, Tatsunori Hashimoto, and Max Simchowitz to see where statistical ML is going. At STAIX I noted Sitan Chen’s diffusion tutorial, Chengchun Shi’s reinforcement learning course, and Soufiane Hayou and Nikhil Ghosh on scaling. For industry, I wanted to ask Dwip (B236). Jennifer Aaker’s work on human flourishing also made me curious about business schools, and Emre and I wondered where theoretically minded researchers could do work relevant to economics.

ideas.original_title: B234. Research agenda and thesis planning
ideas.original_text: How do I choose the other members of a thesis committee when I don’t yet know which of these directions will last? I can start with reliable AI and distribution-free statistical guarantees. I would also like room for cognition-inspired ways of improving a model, tractable models of autoregressive reasoning, and policies for deciding when a human or a model should generate or verify a result. Test-time search has a control-theoretic side. Evaluation and interpretability might benefit from a causal perspective. And I keep coming back to what education and research themselves could look like when people work alongside these systems. I want the proposal to be forward-looking without pretending that all of this is already one thesis.

ideas.original_title: B235. Mathematical reading and collaborator follow-ups
ideas.original_text:
Ask Jason for his optimization seminar notes. I’d like Evan to explain his state-space-model work with Hazan. I also wanted to talk to Kevin Tan. Look over Elad’s slides and Marko’s papers, and ask Alan about his work with Sellke. One question for Emre concerns Rigollet and Polyanskiy’s continuous-time interpretation of transformers. What does Sameer mean when he says the clustering behavior is evidence for attention sinks?

Related work. Geshkovski, Letrouit, Polyanskiy, and Rigollet proved a clustering result for token representations in an idealized continuous-time model [reference in Storage]. Xiao and colleagues observed that trained language models assign large attention weights to initial tokens even when they carry little information [reference in Storage]. One result concerns where representations go, the other which positions receive weight; I would like to know what connects the two in a single model.

ideas.title: Does a hidden layer need an atlas?
ideas.scope: Characterize reconstruction failures under width reduction on manifolds with different topology, distinguishing coordinate charts from embeddings.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Controlled manifold reconstruction and width pruning are feasible; novelty beyond established topological obstructions remains uncertain.
ideas.impact_reason: The proposed width experiment mainly illustrates known chart-versus-embedding limitations.
ideas.gate: Find a phenomenon not implied by established topological autoencoding obstructions before treating the width sweep as a conference contribution.
ideas.section: Shorter research leads from the Hamed group
ideas.rated_version: Characterize reconstruction failures under width reduction on manifolds with different topology, distinguishing coordinate charts from embeddings.
ideas.audit_reason: Width and reconstruction experiments are feasible, but topology obstruction and multi-chart architectures are already cited; current scope mainly illustrates known distinctions.
ideas.F_note: Manifold reconstruction and width pruning are cheap and controlled; the bottleneck is a phenomenon beyond known topological obstructions and multi-chart models.
ideas.I_note: The current width sweep mainly illustrates the chart-versus-embedding distinction rather than supplying a new general principle.
ideas.original_title: Does a hidden layer need an atlas?
ideas.original_text:
A sphere takes more than one chart to cover. When I think of the last hidden layer as giving intrinsic coordinates for a data manifold, am I asking one chart to do too much? The layer could instead embed the manifold in a larger space. What would let me tell which description fits, and what does its width tell me? Could we start wide at a fixed depth, remove neurons and retrain, and see how far we can reduce the width while keeping the fit about the same?

Related work. Batson et al. show how a mismatch between data topology and latent space can obstruct continuous autoencoding [reference in Storage]. AtlasNet generates surfaces from several learned patches [reference in Storage]. On a sphere, I would test whether a narrow hidden layer maps distant points to the same code, then check whether a wider layer separates them while still allowing reconstruction. Width alone cannot establish that the code is a coordinate chart.

ideas.audit_reason: Controlled prerequisite tasks are explicitly suggested; the contribution must separate prerequisites from scoring artifacts and established skill-acquisition models.

ideas.original_title: How much prior knowledge does a task take?
ideas.original_text:
Watching a scooter recede down the street, I tried to imagine seeing only a shape moving up my field of view and getting smaller. What lets me interpret that scene so easily? I wonder whether we could find language tasks with equally well-hidden prerequisites. Would apparent jumps in model ability look smoother on a scale built around those prerequisites?

Related work. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo show that a scoring rule can make a gradual change in performance look abrupt [reference in Storage]. Michaud et al. model scaling in terms of separately acquired pieces of knowledge [reference in Storage]. I would test each proposed prerequisite on its own, then vary which ones a task requires while holding the scoring rule fixed.

ideas.title: What should a network see when it learns primality?
ideas.scope: Compare raw-digit and limited-divisor inputs on primes and composites outside the supplied sieve, with genuine size extrapolation.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Data and baselines are inexpensive; obtaining a learning insight beyond memorization or known divisibility structure is less certain.
ideas.impact_reason: Useful as a controlled test of algorithmic generalization, but a primality classifier alone would have limited scientific reach.
ideas.gate: Show a robust generalization phenomenon beyond supplied divisibility tests and simple arithmetic baselines.
ideas.section: Shorter research leads from the Hamed group
ideas.rated_version: Compare raw-digit and limited-divisor inputs on primes and composites outside the supplied sieve, with genuine size extrapolation.
ideas.audit_reason: The raw-input versus limited-sieve comparison is concrete; successful or failed size extrapolation is a narrow algorithmic-learning result.
ideas.F_note: Exact primality labels, controlled inputs and cheap baselines make execution ready; a nontrivial extrapolation phenomenon is still needed.
ideas.I_note: The experiment is a useful controlled generalization probe, with limited value from primality classification alone.
ideas.original_title: What should a network see when it learns primality?
ideas.original_text:
Could a neural network learn to tell which integers are prime? My first thought was to give it features derived from the integer’s divisors. A complete factorization already gives away the answer. I’d have to decide which information the network gets before I could say what a successful classification teaches me.

Related work. Egri and Shultz trained a network that could recruit previously learned divisibility tests when deciding primality [reference in Storage]. I would compare an integer’s raw digits with a fixed, limited set of small-divisor indicators, then test larger odd composites whose factors evade every supplied indicator. This would separate learning to use a given sieve from learning a test that works beyond it.

ideas.original_title: Can we translate between PDE and statistical image reconstruction?
ideas.original_text:
When I was thinking about which image pixels count as neighbors, I remembered that people working on PDE-based image reconstruction also talk about nonlocal interactions. Are there cases where a statistical signal-processing method and a PDE method perform the same operation? I wondered whether the two families of methods could even be put in one-to-one correspondence. An explicit pair would give me a place to start.

Related work. Buades, Coll and Morel denoise an image by averaging pixels with similar surrounding patches [reference in Storage]. Gilboa and Osher develop the corresponding language of weighted nonlocal differences [reference in Storage]. For fixed row-normalized weights W, one nonlocal-means update sends u to Wu, exactly one unit Euler step for du/dt = (W − I)u. Recomputing the patch weights after each step would change the flow.

ideas.original_title: What kinds of coverage let a mechanical model extrapolate?
ideas.original_text:
Behrad described universality in terms of a few high-level characteristics that matter. I wondered about an inclined plane. If I see motion in sufficiently many configurations, can I recover a coordinate frame that predicts motion at an unseen inclination? For a deterministic system, I’m still unsure which part of that would deserve to be called universality.

Related work. Brunton, Proctor and Kutz infer sparse dynamical laws in a chosen set of coordinates [reference in Storage]. Champion et al. learn coordinates and a sparse law together [reference in Storage]. For the plane I would hold out entire inclinations and compare the learned acceleration with the gravitational acceleration projected along the slope, stating the friction assumption and what angles and initial conditions the model saw.

ideas.original_title: Is the tensor decomposition gap a search problem?
ideas.original_text:
Behrad suggested looking at the gap between the data needed to recover a tensor decomposition in principle and the data needed by efficient algorithms. He thought finding a way across the gap might itself be a search problem. I suggested asking Lucas Kania. We left open what one would actually search over.

Related work. Montanari and Richard study recovery of a single spike from a noisy tensor [reference in Storage]. In the order-three Gaussian model, Hopkins, Shi and Steurer give both a recovery result and a limit for a degree-four sum-of-squares relaxation [reference in Storage]. That limit applies to the relaxation. A different result for overcomplete order-four decompositions assumes algebraic nondegeneracy of the components [reference in Storage]. For Behrad’s search idea I would first choose the model and specify whether we are searching over factors or over algorithms.

ideas.original_title: Singular learning theory for training-data attribution
ideas.original_text:
I relayed a question Hamed had asked me about mathematics in AI safety. Davis suggested that singular learning theory might help us trace behavior back to training examples more efficiently or identify an interpretable subset of weights. He thought the immediate obstacle was computational. Which quantities could we approximate well enough to use on a model?

Related work. Lau et al. estimate a local learning coefficient that describes the geometry of the loss near fitted weights [reference in Storage]. Wang et al. refine it to study the data and components associated with particular attention-head specializations [reference in Storage], while TRAK scores the influence of training examples on model outputs [reference in Storage]. For one behavior I would compare the rankings with what actually changes after removing examples or ablating weights, recording the cost of each estimate.

ideas.original_title: Let a mathematician's diagnosis guide the next training set
ideas.original_text:
I asked what a mathematician working with a frontier lab might contribute. Behrad suggested letting the mathematician try the model on problems they know well, see where it succeeds and breaks down, and curate examples around those observations. I’d be curious whether the examples help on a fresh problem with the same underlying difficulty.

Related work. AdaTest pairs people with a language model to find failures, propose examples and test repairs [reference in Storage]. Lightman et al. use human judgments of intermediate mathematical steps and study which solutions to send for labeling [reference in Storage]. I would compare examples selected after a mathematician diagnoses a recurring error with an equal-sized ordinary training set, then ask another mathematician for fresh problems that require the same idea.

ideas.original_title: Which industry problems make it back into a professor's lab?
ideas.original_text:
I can imagine a part-time industry appointment exposing a professor to a problem their students would otherwise never see. I’ve also heard students describe their projects and their advisor’s company work as almost entirely separate. Could we trace where a lab’s questions came from, before and after an advisor took an industry role?

Related work. Azoulay, Ding and Stuart trace changes in public research around academic scientists’ entry into patenting [reference in Storage]. Sariri studies changes in machine-learning researchers’ publication agendas after they affiliate with corporate labs [reference in Storage]. For my question I would date the origin of students’ projects relative to the appointment, compare similar labs without a new appointment, and look for evidence that a particular question came through the company.

ideas.title: What did our mistaken picture of rotations get right?
ideas.scope: Identify which tasks tolerate a mistaken sphere representation of rotations and which expose the missing antipodal identification.
ideas.feasibility_reason: The basic mathematical examples are already explained; a new research contribution or ML question is not currently identified.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify a bounded representation error, though the current material is mainly pedagogical.

ideas.rated_version: Identify which tasks tolerate a mistaken sphere representation of rotations and which expose the missing antipodal identification.
ideas.audit_reason: Restored under the source-question criterion: the source asks which tasks reveal the mistaken representation, while known answers sharply limit new-paper feasibility.
ideas.F_note: The available local examples and full-turn counterexample already answer much of the question; accessible calculations do not identify a new paper claim.

ideas.original_title: What did our mistaken picture of rotations get right?
ideas.original_text:
Amir and I were walking to the library when we realized we’d both been picturing the rotation group SO(3) as a sphere. We’d left out the identification of antipodal points on the three-sphere, yet we’d managed the class exercises with that picture. Which questions let us get away with that, and which one would have exposed the mistake?

Related work. Zhou et al. analyze continuity problems that arise when a representation has to choose a single quaternion for each rotation [reference in Storage]. Near the identity one can choose a sign continuously, so a local calculation may work. Tracking a full turn about one axis shows where the pictures differ. The rotation returns to the identity while its continuous quaternion path ends at the antipode of its starting point.

ideas.original_title: Does it help to reach past the front cereal box?
ideas.original_text:
At the CVS I reach past the front box because I think it’s been more exposed. Suppose each shopper swaps it with a randomly chosen box farther back and buys the one they chose. If earlier shoppers did that too, does reaching back still lower my chance of buying a box that was tampered with? Time spent at the front could be one way to model that risk. I’d need a rule for how the shelf gets restocked.

Related work. Jain and Nestoridi study a fixed deck under repeated swaps between its top card and a random card, relating mixing to the time by which the other cards have been selected [reference in Storage]. A shopper removes a box after each swap. With a specified replacement position and timing, I would track each surviving box’s accumulated time at the front and compare that quantity for the front box and a random rear box at purchase.

ideas.audit_reason: Restored as an actual normative problem. Poor venue fit and missing formulation warrant low feasibility, not classification as a personal reflection.
ideas.F_note: The normative question is real, but neither a bounded new argument nor an ML-conference route is presently identified.

ideas.original_title: Who has standing to impose a social sanction?
ideas.original_text:
I was trying to separate my reaction to a social sanction from my reaction to who gets to impose it. Suppose two people have each caused serious but quite different harms. What would give either of them standing to sanction the other? The example left me unsure what rule I actually wanted.

Related work. Wallace grounds the objection to hypocritical blame in people’s equal moral standing [reference in Storage]. Duff separately asks who may call a wrongdoer to account in a criminal trial [reference in Storage]. For two people who have caused different harms, I would distinguish an inconsistency in the standards each accepts from the further question of what authorizes either person to impose a penalty.

ideas.original_title: Can a calibration fixed point suggest an update rule?
ideas.original_text:
While thinking about a model rewriting its own prompts, I wondered about a simpler fixed point. Among cases assigned probability p, a calibrated predictor gets the event frequency p back. Can that identity tell me how to update a predictor when the two values disagree? I had the condition in mind and hadn’t worked out an iteration.

Related work. Zadrozny and Elkan use observed event frequencies within score bins to recalibrate predictions [reference in Storage]. For a fixed population, replacing a score P by its true conditional event frequency E[Y | P] already gives a calibrated score. Hebert-Johnson et al. iteratively correct errors on overlapping groups [reference in Storage], which points to a question about prompt rewriting. After a rewrite, do the cases receiving a given score still have the event frequency estimated before the rewrite?

ideas.title: Does repeated AI help change what a person can later do alone?
ideas.scope: Compare forms of proof assistance on delayed unaided transfer to fresh problems requiring the same idea.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Recruitment, delayed testing, and separating assistance effects from practice remain substantial unresolved dependencies.
ideas.impact_reason: Proof-transfer evidence could inform AI-assisted mathematics education, but a small study would not settle broad cognitive impacts.
ideas.gate: Secure a feasible participant cohort and delayed transfer endpoint; distinguish learning from assisted performance.
ideas.section: AI safety and its mathematical foundations: discussions with Hamed
ideas.rated_version: Compare forms of proof assistance on delayed unaided transfer to fresh problems requiring the same idea.
ideas.audit_reason: Delayed unaided proof transfer is explicit and valuable; recruitment, intervention duration, and existing AI-learning-effect literature limit feasibility and scoped impact.
ideas.F_note: The proof-transfer question is clear, but recruitment, delayed follow-up and separation of assistance from practice are unresolved within twelve weeks.
ideas.I_note: Evidence on delayed unaided proof transfer could improve mathematical education, while a small cohort would not resolve general cognitive effects.
ideas.original_title: B251. Does repeated AI help change what a person can later do alone?
ideas.original_text:
One concern I raised was what using AI all the time might do to our ability to think through a problem on our own. An AI-assisted reply gave a good example. Suppose a student asks for help on a proof whenever they get stuck, and every proof the model supplies is correct. What, exactly, is an output classifier supposed to flag? The consequence we care about might only show up a month later, when the student gets stuck on a fresh problem without the model. Perhaps the earlier proofs taught a useful trick. Perhaps the student has had less practice finding the next step. I’d like to know which.

Behrad asked whether people would still want to understand a phenomenon if a machine could already get the result they needed. I wondered whether handing off the part of the work that takes real concentration could leave someone bored or restless even on a productive day. There’s a measurement problem here too. What could I ask someone to do that would convince me they understood an idea?

Related work. In a randomized high-school math study, students using a standard GPT interface outscored the no-AI group during practice but scored lower on a later unaided exam. Students using a tutor with teacher-designed safeguards also improved during practice, and their unaided scores did not differ significantly from the no-AI group [reference in Storage]. For proof writing, I would compare forms of help on a fresh problem that requires the same trick, with the student working alone.

ideas.original_title: B252. What evidence should change a decision to train the next model?
ideas.original_text:
Given what existing models might already do for science, I suggested taking a year to focus on safety. Hamed thought we could continue improving safeguards as the models scale. I wasn’t convinced, but I’m uncertain about how to weigh the people helped by a new capability against the harms we already see. A GPT response I sent to Amir raised two questions. What could another year of scaling achieve that a year of using today’s models for science could not? If we paused, what evidence would justify restarting?

Related work. Shevlane et al. distinguish evaluations of dangerous capabilities from evaluations of whether a model will use them in harmful ways, and discuss their role in training decisions [reference in Storage]. The GPT response I forwarded to Amir asked what evidence would justify restarting after my proposed pause, and what another year of scaling would achieve compared with using existing models for science. An evaluation could bear on the restart criterion. Answering the second question would also require a way to compare the two uses of the year.

ideas.original_title: Task success, externalities, and incomplete specifications
ideas.original_text:
The whiteboard separates the user’s task from its externalities. An agent may accomplish the requested goal while causing consequences the user or other affected parties would reject. The meeting used the Hugging Face and Navier–Stokes examples to distinguish harmful side effects from useful scientific collaboration. Their role here is conceptual: successful coordination alone does not specify what, if anything, went wrong.

We therefore need to keep several things separate. Task performance concerns the delegated objective. A safety constraint identifies outcomes or actions that are unacceptable. An externality concerns effects outside the narrow task objective, potentially on other people. Faithfulness to the user and acceptability to those other parties can therefore require different conditions. Any formalization must say whose preferences and constraints are represented.

Underspecification concerns information missing from the instruction or objective. If multiple intended goals fit what the user said and recommend different actions, clarification may be necessary. Such a case differs from an actor that understands the intended constraint but violates it. It also differs from an actor that aims at the correct objective but makes an error about the consequences of its action. Observed behavior may not identify which explanation is correct.

ideas.original_title: What would justify trusting an actor or its monitor?
ideas.original_text:
The central oversight question is about an AI acting on a user’s behalf and another AI acting as its “cop.” What exactly are we trusting it to do? Perform the task competently, report accurately, enforce a rule faithfully, or avoid a particular harm? A monitor might recognize a violation and conceal it, miss the violation entirely, or report it correctly without being able to stop it. These failures require different explanations.

Two regimes should guide the discussion. In a near-term setting, the cop may be a sequence of classifiers or other bounded checks. The research questions concern their joint errors, what another check contributes, and when to escalate. The acting agent may still adapt to those checks; the classifiers need not themselves be modeled as strategic agents.

In the more demanding setting, the acting agent and the cop may be comparably superintelligent, while both exceed the human’s capabilities. The cop’s allegiance is now part of the problem. Giving it enough intelligence to detect a violation does not tell us that it will reveal what it detects. Nor does adding another learned monitor settle where reliable evidence ultimately enters the system.

The relative-intelligence description motivates this setting but does not yet define a mathematical model. More precise ingredients include access to evidence, computational resources, timing, permissible communication, control of the execution environment, and authority to intervene. A limitation result would need to state which of these resources are absent. Which asymmetries could make oversight possible? Could particular information restrictions make safe and harmful behavior indistinguishable? These questions remain open.

ideas.original_title: Incentives.
ideas.original_text:
A useful feature of the game-theoretic viewpoint is that the monitor’s behavior is part of the design problem. What makes monitoring worthwhile, and what makes an available deviation unattractive? The corresponding scrutiny should cover the modeled actions and preferences, the source of verdicts, enforceability of rewards, coalitional deviations, and behavior during learning.

The inspected Hazan paper identifies a tension: deterring solver misconduct can weaken incentives to audit. It says the mixed equilibrium need not be a stable attractor or attainable through model weights, and includes noisy resolution. Hazan’s accompanying explanation assumes no collusion and describes a separate resolution process and checks on the auditor. These qualifications should accompany the meeting’s informal account of eventual safe equilibrium.

ideas.original_title: Making the watermarking setting precise.
ideas.original_text:
Hamed suggested this as a promising source of mathematical problems. Mixing the outputs of different models can scramble, rearrange, or dilute the signal used by traditional watermark detectors. I should start with the basic watermarking theorems, then study these more challenging settings, with guarantees in terms of edit distance. Global testing and combination tests come to mind: can weak evidence scattered across several sources still support reliable detection? Talk to Rene, Weijie, and Hamed.

Splicing or rearranging generated text, averaging next-token distributions, and rewriting with another model are different observation models. Ordinary edit distance does not automatically give useful guarantees for arbitrary block permutations. A possible first question is the detection boundary for unknown watermarked fragments within a document, as a function of surviving signal, fragment lengths, possible sources, and edit budget. Compare scanning for a few strong fragments with aggregating weak evidence, while accounting for dependence and the search over locations and keys. Some marked content must survive for detection to be possible.

Useful starting references are A Statistical Framework of Watermarks for Large Language Models and Edit Distance Robust Watermarks via Indexing Pseudorandom Codes. Existing work on Efficiently Identifying Watermarked Segments in Mixed-Source Texts and the preprint Linear Ensembles Wash Away Watermarks should shape any novelty claim; the latter concerns distribution-level ensembles.

ideas.original_title: What should ``curriculum learning for safety'' mean?
ideas.original_text:
Hamed liked the idea of mixing additional data into pretraining so that the model learns ethics alongside the knowledge to which it applies, for example in biosecurity. His interpretation was simpler than the idea Rohan and I originally discussed: we had in mind constructing individual datapoints that require the model to learn both concepts together. Interleaving ethics and biology textbooks may teach something different from examples in which biological understanding and ethical judgment are needed together.

More generally, Hamed saw the proportions and co-occurrence of different kinds of data in the pretraining mix as essential questions for safety. Our intuition was that concepts that “fire together wire together,” and perhaps make one another more robust. This is a conjecture; putting the concepts in the same example does not by itself establish that the model learns them inseparably. I would distinguish data proportions, order during training, and connections within individual examples. Changing the order while holding the mixture fixed isolates another question. Which choices matter for the durability of safety?

ideas.original_title: What should ``curriculum learning for safety'' mean?
ideas.original_text:
We returned to the question of baking safety into an open model’s weights so that an adversary cannot easily undo it. Hamed suggested reading Safety Pretraining, coauthored by Alex Robey and Zico Kolter, and Open Technical Problems in Open-Weight AI Model Risk Management, coauthored by Kolter. A possible small-scale experiment would ask whether teaching ethics alongside scientific knowledge makes the two more deeply connected. The motivating domains were biology, chemistry, cyber, and the broader CBRN setting. Can the model learn the consequences and appropriate uses of a capability as part of learning the capability itself?

Safety Pretraining combines data filtering, recontextualized text, refusal examples, moral education, and harmfulness tags. It finds improved safety retention after benign fine-tuning. Its lowest reported attack success rate after that fine-tuning also uses SafeBeam, a decoding procedure that a recipient of the weights could remove. Resistance to adversarial weight modification remains open. The second paper situates data curation, tamper-resistant training, weight editing, and evaluation under modification within a broader agenda, including whether achievable resistance imposes a meaningful cost on an attacker.

Hamed liked the idea of mixing additional data into pretraining so that the model learns ethics alongside the knowledge to which it applies, for example in biosecurity. His interpretation was simpler than the idea Rohan and I originally discussed: we had in mind constructing individual datapoints that require the model to learn both concepts together. Interleaving ethics and biology textbooks may teach something different from examples in which biological understanding and ethical judgment are needed together.

More generally, Hamed saw the proportions and co-occurrence of different kinds of data in the pretraining mix as essential questions for safety. Our intuition was that concepts that “fire together wire together,” and perhaps make one another more robust. This is a conjecture; putting the concepts in the same example does not by itself establish that the model learns them inseparably. I would distinguish data proportions, order during training, and connections within individual examples. Changing the order while holding the mixture fixed isolates another question. Which choices matter for the durability of safety?

One way to test the October 30 idea would be to train three models on matched data and compute. The first learns safety and reasoning in separate stages, the second sees those examples interleaved, and the third solves problems whose correct solution requires applying the safety rule. Match initial safety and reasoning performance as closely as possible. After the same further fine-tuning, compare retained safety at the same downstream utility, including on an adaptation held out when designing the training tasks. If the third model retains more, what intervention would tell us whether a shared representation accounts for the difference?

October 30 follow-up research note on mathematically trained empiricism. The comparison is a proposed experiment.

ideas.original_title: Representations and the difficulty of unlearning.
ideas.original_text: Hamed was also interested in the question Rohan and I had discussed: why does knowledge of physics seem robust while adherence to applied ethics can seem brittle? Our conjecture was that distributed representations and nonmonosemanticity might have something to do with the difference. We did not get beyond a conceptual discussion, and both the comparison and the proposed explanation need to be made precise. Perhaps the model knows ethics theoretically without reliably applying it. Knowing a principle, acting on it, and retaining it after further training are different properties. Shared representations alone would not establish durability. What data or compute would be needed to change the model’s conduct while preserving useful competence?

ideas.original_title: Unexpected effects of further training.
ideas.original_text:
Read the emergent-misalignment and subliminal-learning work from Owain Evans’s group, and revisit the Mark Vero talk. The concern is that training examples which look narrow or superficially harmless can have unexpected effects on behavior and internal representations. This feels connected to machine unlearning: what determines whether a learned capability or behavior can be removed, and whether it returns after additional training? Talk to Alex and Hamed, and arrange a meeting with Alex about the problems he considers important and tractable.

The likely Thinking Machines post is A Safe Path to Open Weights. Alex coauthored Safety Pretraining and When Should We Introduce Safety Interventions During Pretraining?; the latter finds that the best timing depends on the setting. These are empirical results, not irreversible-safety guarantees. Distinguish Emergent Misalignment, whose original experiments used insecure-code training, from Subliminal Learning, where traits can transfer through apparently innocuous data.

ideas.original_title: November 4 follow-up: safety fine-tuning as a data-selection game.
ideas.original_text:
To sharpen the durable-safety question, I would fix the adversary’s data sampler and allowed fine-tuning procedure, then ask how many candidate examples it must inspect before finding data that make the model unsafe. The defender chooses safety data while preserving useful capabilities. I would distinguish selecting a dataset from a sampled pool, accepting or rejecting examples while training, and replaying examples already collected. Discarded examples count toward the sampling budget. This measures sampling difficulty; computational hardness would require a separate restriction on the search.

The accompanying notes solve initialization-only versions of these games in a quadratic model, assuming useful initial states that safety training can reach and imposing no post-attack utility constraint. The attacker chooses the largest examples for a single batch update, or accepts state-increasing examples in the sequential game; the smallest feasible initial state is an optimal defense. The limitation is informative: a state immune to every one-step attack can still fail after repeated training. With unrestricted replay and no training-step budget, one example beyond the unsafe threshold eventually suffices, and the optimal acquisition cost is independent of the initialization. The general safety-data design problem remains open. A next model should allow safety training to change the subsequent gradient dynamics more substantially, or explicitly bound the attacker’s training effort.

Start with (three pages); see (six pages) for precise statements and complete proofs. Both PDFs and their standalone LaTeX sources are in the project’s folder.

ideas.original_text: Are AI-powered cyberattacks more of the familiar competition between attackers and defenders? ideas.original_title: Robotics, planning, and the role of mathematics.
ideas.original_text:
I also asked Hamed about robotics. He said he has not been keeping up with the area, although he knows people working on it. His impression was that LeCun’s approach is somewhat outside the mainstream, while much of the current work uses vision–language models (VLMs) and vision–language–action models (VLAs). The rough picture we discussed was a relatively small language model, perhaps around 7B parameters, connected to a robot. This was an informal characterization, not a survey of the field.

I wondered whether these systems can do the real-time planning needed for safe household robotics, and whether model predictive control offers a useful connection. My concern about model size was tentative; we did not establish that size is the obstacle. Data is another problem, especially for generalizing outside the training distribution. There seem to be many questions here, but I do not yet know which call for foundational mathematics of the kind Rohan and I could contribute, and which mainly concern engineering, latency, architecture search, or data collection.

ideas.original_title: What mathematical language do we need?
ideas.original_text:
We questioned whether modern ML is best understood as a statistical discipline, leaning toward no while recognizing uses for statistical thinking, such as choosing data proportions. Perhaps AI calls for new primitives, as earlier problems motivated game theory, decision theory, and information theory. What would such a primitive let us understand that the existing language obscures?

The AIAS launch made me think about the role of mathematics in alignment. In my debrief, I contrasted the institute’s search for mathematical foundations with an earlier group discussion, where safety had been viewed primarily as an engineering challenge likely to advance through heuristics. We should examine both positions. A useful mathematical result need not replace an effective engineering practice: it might explain its limits, identify the assumptions responsible for its success, or reveal a failure that familiar evaluations miss. In his October 19 reply, Hamed encouraged me to discuss what I had learned and expressed interest in mathematically rigorous ideas.

My concern about deploying “pet tools” is really about how we choose problems. An elegant application of game theory, cryptography, control, or statistical calibration is valuable only insofar as it addresses a consequential feature of the setting. We should identify that feature before committing to a method. Of course, learning an unfamiliar tool can also reveal a question that was previously difficult to see. Avoiding tools altogether would miss the point.

The standard for progress should therefore include useful definitions and explanatory or impossibility results, as well as constructions. In my debrief, I explicitly defended research that clarifies a phenomenon without delivering a new method. A particularly valuable formulation would separate several failures that currently share the label “misalignment” and indicate which interventions could address each one.

Hamed’s reply, October 19, 2026; Sunay’s AIAS debrief, October 20, 2026. Related entries: B174, B205.

Related work. Skalse and colleagues ask when improving a proxy reward can make the underlying objective worse. Their characterization changes with the class of policies available to the agent [reference in Storage]. Before calling a proxy safe, I would want to say which changes in behavior the claim covers.

ideas.original_title: A personal laboratory with AI
ideas.original_text:
One of my childhood dreams was to have some type of secret laboratory where I would go and do secret experiments: a shed that, to the outside world, appeared to hold lawn-mowing supplies, but that turned into a frontier lab when I clicked a secret button. There is something special about directly communing with the universe through scientific inquiry. I wonder if that is possible now: go away to the woods, do math with an AI tool, do physics with an AGI tool, and discover things directly. But a big part of the childhood dream was also building something. Somehow that got lost after years of dry mathematical inquiry, which in its current form can feel divorced from technology.[1]

[1] November 8 audio messages, approximately 03:01–06:40 in the merged recording.

ideas.original_title: What would economics study after extensive automation?
ideas.original_text:
Suppose technology could meet much of what we now regard as our material needs. What would economics study in that world? Even then, one can ask how we are going to organize ourselves and how we will get along with one another. The same mathematics, modeling, and ideation that have been directed at economic activity might instead be directed at broader social behavior. Which questions would remain fundamental, and which depend on the particular technological constraints of the present?[1]

[1] November 8 audio messages, approximately 06:40–10:55, especially 09:59–10:55.

ideas.original_title: How does the startup ecosystem work?
ideas.original_text:
How is San Francisco structured so that someone can show up and, in a couple of months, be a founder? I can analyze, quantify, code, do statistics, and mathematically model things. How does someone with those skills find their people? What makes the ecosystem a dynamo of entrepreneurship? Am I accurate in thinking that an ambitious newcomer has a decent chance after a few tries, or is that a radical simplification that misses the connections and networks that determine who gets an opportunity? The question is especially about deep technology and transformative companies.[1]

[1] November 8 audio messages, approximately 16:09–20:08, especially 18:18–20:08.

ideas.original_title: Is theoretical statistics a finite subject?
ideas.original_text:
Looking through Savage’s collected writings, I wondered whether the theory of statistics is a finite subject. Could we eventually say that we have pushed the theory to its limit, and then spend our time applying it or move to adjacent areas of probability and analysis? There are clearly very hard problems in deep learning theory, but perhaps deep learning will itself help solve them. More generally, for a given subject, how would I know whether it is finite or infinite? What kinds of theoretical work would remain after AI can solve much of the existing agenda?[1]

[1] November 8 audio messages, approximately 24:53–28:24, especially 25:38–27:08; the final question also reflects my November 9 follow-up discussion.

ideas.original_title: Creativity, execution, and signal-to-noise ratio
ideas.original_text:
People represent the world differently and work in different ways. I do not think one can impose a uniform structure on everyone, especially in a creative endeavor. Research should leave room for new ideas, new ways of thinking, and questioning fossilized modes of work. At the same time, perhaps getting three things done a day, keeping the signal-to-noise ratio high, and repeating that process can eventually add up to a breakthrough. How should I balance open-ended thinking with disciplined execution? Is creativity something separate from that process, or does sustained execution help produce it? Does the same organization of time make sense for a CEO and for someone working on blue-skies research?[1]

[1] November 8 audio messages, approximately 28:24–35:10, especially 29:20–32:43 and 34:26–34:56.

ideas.title: Intentional and unintentional human mistakes
ideas.scope: Design a controlled task separating misunderstanding, limited attention, execution failure, and deliberate shortcuts through observable interventions.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Human recruitment and an identifiable design are not established; a cognitive-science contribution may fit other venues better.
ideas.impact_reason: Could improve causal interpretation of errors and motivate more informative comparisons with model behavior.
ideas.gate: Identify interventions that distinguish hypotheses without relying solely on people’s retrospective explanations.
ideas.rated_version: Design a controlled task separating misunderstanding, limited attention, execution failure, and deliberate shortcuts through observable interventions.
ideas.audit_reason: The human-error distinction is substantive; identifying causes requires interventions and participant access not established in the notes.
ideas.F_note: Recruitment and interventions separating knowledge, attention and deliberate shortcuts are not established; retrospective explanations would not identify the causes.
ideas.I_note: A causal separation of error mechanisms would inform behavioral measurement and human-model comparisons within a bounded task.
ideas.original_title: Intentional and unintentional mistakes
ideas.original_text:
Why do we humans make mistakes? I want to distinguish unintentional mistakes from deliberate shortcuts. We might misunderstand a task, hold a mistaken belief, forget a constraint, or fail to carry out a plan correctly. We might also understand what is required but decide that doing it carefully is not worth the effort. Even then, deliberately taking a shortcut is different from deliberately producing a bad result: we may expect the shortcut to work.

How much of human error comes from limited knowledge and attention, and how much comes from competing objectives? What evidence would let us distinguish these explanations?

ideas.title: Do language models take shortcuts?
ideas.scope: Use a fixed editing tool and checkable preservation constraints to distinguish tool limitations, observation failures, and checking choices under controlled incentives.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Controlled tool-use experiments are feasible, but identifying strategic checking beyond competence and observation failures remains the major uncertainty.
ideas.impact_reason: A convincing behavioral distinction would inform agent reliability; ordinary verification gains are already well studied.
ideas.gate: Demonstrate that the agent can recognize the defect when forced to inspect; manipulate incentives without changing task information or tool competence.
ideas.rated_version: Use a fixed editing tool and checkable preservation constraints to distinguish tool limitations, observation failures, and checking choices under controlled incentives.
ideas.audit_reason: Fixed-tool tests are practical, but verification interventions already have extensive empirical work. Distinguishing deliberate shortcuts from ability and observation failures is unresolved.

audit_evidence.establishes: 17 harness verification designs include visual tasks and measured accuracy-cost tradeoffs.
audit_evidence.does_not_establish: Whether agents strategically skip checking as detection risk changes.

audit_evidence.establishes: A position paper already frames under-verification in marginal cost and risk terms.
audit_evidence.does_not_establish: Empirical identification of stable agent preferences.

ideas.F_note: A fixed tool and checkable constraints make the experiment accessible; identifying checking choices separately from competence and observation is the hard part.
ideas.I_note: A convincing intervention-based distinction could improve agent reliability broadly, whereas ordinary gains from added verification are already well studied.
ideas.original_title: Do language models take shortcuts?
ideas.original_text:
Why do language models make mistakes when asked to complete a task? For example, suppose I ask an image editor to change one part of an image while preserving everything else. If it changes unrelated details, did it misunderstand the instruction, lack the ability to preserve those details, fail to inspect its output, or knowingly accept an inaccurate result?

Do models prefer to be “lazy” in any useful behavioral sense? Are they weighing the expected reward of taking a shortcut against the expected punishment from a user who notices inaccuracies? Or can training produce behavior that looks like this without any such calculation during the task? I would like to separate the behavior of the language model directing the edit from the limitations of the image-editing tool itself.

ideas.title: When is utility maximization a useful model?
ideas.scope: Fit a restricted checking-choice utility model in some conditions and test held-out cost/detection predictions against competence and instruction-following alternatives.
ideas.feasibility_reason: Controlled evaluations are affordable; separating utility, beliefs, competence, and instruction-following beyond existing coherence studies remains unresolved.
ideas.impact_reason: Could clarify when utility models predict verification choices; the initial result would support a bounded behavioral claim.
ideas.gate: Require out-of-sample predictions and compare utility against equally flexible nonutility models; announced detection probability is not observed subjective belief.
ideas.rated_version: Fit a restricted checking-choice utility model in some conditions and test held-out cost/detection predictions against competence and instruction-following alternatives.
ideas.audit_reason: The source proposes held-out cost/detection tests of stable utility. Existing preference-coherence work is a baseline, not a resolution of actual tool-checking choices.

audit_evidence.establishes: Preference utility fits are compared with free-form choices; the paper also studies instrumentality.
audit_evidence.does_not_establish: That held-out tool-checking choices obey stable utility under cost and detection interventions.

audit_evidence.establishes: Learned policies respond to designed correction incentives.
audit_evidence.does_not_establish: Equivalence between reward training and inference-time utility maximization.

ideas.F_note: The held-out checking-choice design is concrete and affordable; competence, beliefs and equally flexible alternative models remain difficult controls.
ideas.I_note: A stable out-of-sample utility model would sharpen agent-behavior evaluation without equating reward training with online optimization.
ideas.original_title: When is utility maximization a useful model?
ideas.original_text:
More broadly, do language models act as if they maximize utility? Being trained to obtain reward seems different from evaluating expected rewards while completing a particular task. When does the first produce the second?

Almost any behavior can be rationalized by choosing a suitable utility function after observing it. The more interesting question is whether a reasonably stable utility predicts a model’s choices across tasks, instructions, and opportunities for verification. Could we test this by varying the cost of checking an output and the probability that an error will be noticed, while holding the task and available tools fixed?

Question and follow-up discussion, November 10, 2026.
